terms: Genotype
Allele combination (e.g. Aa, AA)
Phenotype
Observable trait from genotype + environment
Homozygous
Two identical alleles (AA or aa)
Heterozygous
Two different alleles (Aa)
Codominance
Both alleles fully expressed (e.g. blood AB)
Sex linkage
Gene on X chromosome (e.g. haemophilia)
Point mutation
Single base substitution (missense, nonsense)
Frameshift
Insertion/deletion shifts reading frame
PCR
Polymerase chain reaction amplifies DNA
Gel electrophoresis
Separates DNA fragments by size
Restriction enzyme
Cuts DNA at specific sequence
Transgenic
Organism with foreign gene inserted
Chromosome
DNA + histone protein; carries genes
Homologous pair
Two chromosomes carrying same genes
Allele
Variant of a gene at a given locus
Meiosis
Reduction division: 2n → n
Crossing over
Exchange of segments in prophase I
Chiasma
Visible crossover point
ADH
Antidiuretic hormone from posterior pituitary; inserts aquaporins in collecting duct increasing water reabsorption.
Antibody
Y-shaped immunoglobulin produced by plasma cells; variable region binds specific antigen.
Clonal selection
B lymphocyte with matching receptor proliferates after antigen binding (Burnet 1957).
Kidney nephron
Functional unit: glomerulus, Bowman's capsule, proximal tubule, loop of Henle, distal tubule, collecting duct.
Spermatogenesis
Meiotic production of sperm in seminiferous tubules; takes ~74 days in humans; regulated by FSH and testosterone.
Ultrafiltration
High-pressure filtration at glomerulus; basement membrane retains proteins; filtrate enters Bowman's capsule.
Crossing over
Exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes at chiasmata in prophase I.
Homologous chromosomes
Chromosomes of same length, centromere position and gene loci; one maternal, one paternal.
Independent assortment
Random orientation of bivalents at metaphase I yields 2^n combinations (n=23 in humans).
Karyotype
Photographic display of all chromosomes arranged in homologous pairs by size and banding.
Meiosis
Two successive divisions producing four haploid gametes from one diploid cell; halves chromosome number.
Non-disjunction
Failure of homologues or chromatids to separate; causes aneuploidy (e.g., trisomy 21 in Down syndrome).
Calvin cycle
Stromal carbon fixation: RuBisCO joins CO2 to RuBP (Calvin & Benson 1948-50 using carbon-14).
Chemiosmosis
ATP synthesis driven by proton gradient across membrane (Mitchell 1961 chemiosmotic hypothesis).
Electron transport chain
Inner mitochondrial membrane; electrons pass through complexes I-IV pumping H+; O2 final acceptor.
Glycolysis
Cytoplasmic conversion of glucose to two pyruvate, net 2 ATP and 2 NADH.
Krebs cycle
Mitochondrial matrix oxidation of acetyl-CoA producing CO2, NADH, FADH2, ATP (Krebs 1937).
Light-dependent reactions
Thylakoid membrane; photosystems II and I split water, produce ATP via chemiosmosis and NADPH.
Genetic material

The molecule in which the heritable information of an organism is stored and from which it is copied and expressed. In all living organisms the genetic material is DNA; the base sequence of DNA carries the information.
Virus (in relation to genetic material)

A non-cellular infectious particle consisting of genetic material inside a protein coat. Some viruses have RNA rather than DNA as their genetic material, but viruses are not considered to be living, so they are not exceptions to the rule that DNA is the genetic material of all living organisms.
Nucleotide

The monomer of nucleic acids, made of three covalently bonded components: a pentose sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base. The pentose sugar is in the centre, with the phosphate group and the base each bonded to it. In diagrams, a circle represents the phosphate, a pentagon the pentose sugar and a rectangle the base.
Pentose sugar

A five-carbon sugar. In nucleotides the pentose is ribose (in RNA) or deoxyribose (in DNA); it is the central component of the nucleotide to which both the phosphate group and the nitrogenous base are bonded.
Phosphate group

The acidic, negatively charged component of a nucleotide, bonded to the pentose sugar. When nucleotides are linked, the phosphate of one nucleotide is bonded to the sugar of the next, forming the sugar–phosphate backbone.
Sugar–phosphate bond

The covalent bond formed by condensation between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the pentose sugar of the next nucleotide in the same strand (also called a phosphodiester bond). It links nucleotides into a polynucleotide.
Sugar–phosphate backbone

The continuous chain of alternating pentose sugars and phosphate groups, covalently bonded, that runs along each strand of DNA or RNA. Because every atom in the chain is covalently bonded, the backbone is strong; the bases project from it.
Nitrogenous bases

The nitrogen-containing components of nucleotides that carry the genetic code. DNA contains adenine (A), cytosine (C), guanine (G) and thymine (T); RNA contains adenine, cytosine, guanine and uracil (U) in place of thymine.
Base sequence

The order of nitrogenous bases along a nucleic acid strand. Because the sugar–phosphate backbone is the same along the whole strand, it is the sequence of bases alone that forms the basis of the genetic code.
Condensation reaction

A reaction in which two molecules are joined by a covalent bond with the release of a molecule of water. Nucleotides are joined into RNA (and DNA) by condensation between the phosphate group of one nucleotide and the pentose sugar of the next.
RNA polymer (polynucleotide)

A single strand of ribonucleotides linked by sugar–phosphate bonds formed by condensation. In a diagram the strand is drawn as an alternating sugar–phosphate chain with a base attached to each sugar; a molecule of n nucleotides is held together by n − 1 sugar–phosphate bonds.
Double helix

The structure of DNA: two polynucleotide strands wound around each other, with their sugar–phosphate backbones on the outside and the bases pointing inwards, where each base is hydrogen-bonded to its complementary base on the other strand.
Antiparallel

Describes the two strands of a DNA double helix, which run in opposite directions: one strand is oriented one way and the other strand the opposite way. In diagrams the strands are drawn antiparallel, with the sugars pointing in opposite directions.
Complementary base pairing

The specific pairing of bases between the two strands of DNA: adenine (A) always pairs with thymine (T), and guanine (G) always pairs with cytosine (C). The pairs are held together by hydrogen bonds, and the pairing is what makes the two strands complementary.
Hydrogen bond (between bases)

A weak, non-covalent attraction between a complementary pair of bases on opposite strands of DNA. Individually weak, hydrogen bonds are numerous along the molecule and together hold the two strands of the double helix together while allowing them to be separated when required.
Ribose and deoxyribose

The pentose sugars of RNA and DNA respectively. Deoxyribose has one fewer oxygen atom than ribose: in a sketch, the carbon at one position of the ring carries a hydrogen atom (–H) in deoxyribose where ribose carries a hydroxyl group (–OH).
Differences between DNA and RNA
DNA is usually double-stranded, contains deoxyribose and has the bases A, C, G and T. RNA is usually single-stranded, contains ribose and has the bases A, C, G and U (uracil in place of thymine).
Examples of nucleic acids

DNA, and the RNAs of a cell: messenger RNA (mRNA), which carries a copy of a gene's base sequence to a ribosome; transfer RNA (tRNA), which carries amino acids to the ribosome; and ribosomal RNA (rRNA), which forms part of the structure of ribosomes.
Template strand

A strand of DNA whose base sequence is used to direct the assembly of a new complementary strand of DNA (in replication) or of RNA (in transcription). The new strand is complementary to the template, not identical to it.
Complementarity in replication and expression

Because each base can hydrogen-bond stably only with its complementary base, a template strand determines the sequence of any strand built against it. In replication both strands act as templates, producing two identical DNA molecules; in transcription one strand acts as the template for a complementary mRNA, whose sequence is then translated.
Diversity of base sequences

Any of the four bases can occupy any position in a DNA strand, so a strand of n nucleotides has 4ⁿ possible sequences. Since a DNA molecule can be of any length, the number of possible sequences has no upper limit.
Information storage capacity of DNA

The ability of DNA to store an enormous amount of information with great economy: each nucleotide stores one of four possibilities in a space of less than a nanometre along the molecule, and a molecule can be of any length and any sequence.
Genetic code

The set of rules by which the base sequence of DNA (and of the mRNA transcribed from it) is translated into the amino acid sequence of a polypeptide: each group of three bases specifies one amino acid or a stop signal.
Universality of the genetic code

The same base triplets specify the same amino acids in essentially all living organisms, so a gene from one organism can be expressed correctly in another. This conservation of the code across all life forms is evidence of universal common ancestry.
Universal common ancestry

The conclusion that all living organisms are descended from a single ancestral population. The genetic code is shared across all life forms although there is no chemical necessity for any particular triplet to specify a particular amino acid, which is best explained by inheritance of the code from a common ancestor.
5' end and 3' end

The two ends of a nucleic acid strand, named after the carbon atoms of the pentose sugar: the 5' end has a phosphate group attached to the 5' carbon of its terminal sugar, and the 3' end has a free hydroxyl (–OH) group on the 3' carbon of its terminal sugar. In the backbone each phosphate links the 3' carbon of one sugar to the 5' carbon of the next.
Directionality of nucleic acid synthesis

Nucleotides can be added only to the free 3' hydroxyl group of a growing strand, so DNA and RNA are synthesized in the 5' to 3' direction. The template strand is therefore read in the 3' to 5' direction, and mRNA is translated by the ribosome in the 5' to 3' direction.
Purine
A nitrogenous base with a two-ring structure. Adenine and guanine are purines. In DNA a purine on one strand is always paired with a pyrimidine on the other.
Pyrimidine

A nitrogenous base with a single-ring structure. Cytosine, thymine and uracil are pyrimidines. Because every base pair in DNA is one purine bonded to one pyrimidine, A–T and C–G pairs have equal length, so the helix has the same three-dimensional structure regardless of the base sequence.
Nucleosome

The basic unit of DNA packaging in eukaryotes: a length of DNA wrapped around a core of eight histone proteins, held in place by an additional histone protein that is attached to the linker DNA where the DNA enters and leaves the core.
Histone

A protein around which DNA is wound in eukaryotic chromosomes. Eight histone proteins form the core of a nucleosome, with the DNA wrapped around the outside of the core; an additional histone attached to the linker DNA holds the DNA in place.
Linker DNA
The stretch of DNA between one nucleosome core and the next. An additional histone protein attached to the linker DNA holds the DNA on the core of the nucleosome.
Hershey–Chase experiment

An experiment (1952) using bacteriophages, which consist only of DNA and protein, to find which of the two enters a bacterium and directs the production of new viruses. Phage DNA was labelled with radioactive phosphorus (³²P) and phage protein with radioactive sulfur (³⁵S); after infection and separation, the ³²P was found inside the bacteria and the ³⁵S outside, supporting the conclusion that DNA is the genetic material.
Bacteriophage

A virus that infects bacteria. The phage used by Hershey and Chase is made only of DNA enclosed in a protein coat, so tracing where each component goes during infection shows which component carries the genetic information.
Radioisotope labelling

The use of a radioactive isotope to trace a molecule. Because DNA contains phosphorus but not sulfur, and protein contains sulfur (in some amino acids) but not phosphorus, ³²P labels only DNA and ³⁵S labels only protein. The availability of radioisotopes as research tools is what made the Hershey–Chase experiment possible.
Chargaff's data

Measurements of the relative amounts of the four bases in DNA from diverse organisms. They showed that in every organism the amount of adenine equals the amount of thymine and the amount of guanine equals the amount of cytosine (so purines equal pyrimidines), but that the proportions of A–T and G–C differ between organisms.
Tetranucleotide hypothesis

The earlier hypothesis that DNA was a simple repeating sequence of the four nucleotides, which would make all four bases equally abundant in every organism. Chargaff's data, showing unequal base composition that varies between species, falsified this hypothesis.
Problem of induction and certainty of falsification

No number of confirming observations can prove a general hypothesis true (the problem of induction), but a single reliable observation that contradicts the hypothesis can show it to be false (the certainty of falsification). Chargaff's data falsified the tetranucleotide hypothesis in this way.
Auxin
Plant hormone (IAA) promoting cell elongation and phototropism (Went 1926 oat coleoptile).
Phloem
Living sieve tubes with companion cells; translocate sucrose from source to sink (Munch 1930 pressure flow).
Phytochrome
Photoreceptor pigment switching between Pr (red-absorbing) and Pfr (far-red) forms; controls flowering.
Stomata
Pores in epidermis flanked by guard cells; open when guard cells turgid via K+ uptake.
Transpiration
Evaporative loss of water from leaves through stomata; creates tension drawing water column up.
Xylem
Dead lignified vessels transporting water and minerals from roots upward via transpiration pull.
Water as the medium for life

The first cells originated in water, and water remains the medium in which most of the processes of life take place: the cytoplasm of every cell is an aqueous solution in which metabolic reactions occur, and substances are transported dissolved in water. This is as true of organisms living on land or in the air as of aquatic organisms, because their cells carry water inside them.
Polar covalent bond

A covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is drawn unequally towards one of the two atoms. In water, the oxygen atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly than each hydrogen atom, so the oxygen carries a partial negative charge (δ−) and each hydrogen a partial positive charge (δ+). The water molecule as a whole is therefore polar.
Polarity notation (δ+ and δ−)

The notation used to show polarity when representing water molecules: δ− (delta minus) is written beside the oxygen atom and δ+ (delta plus) beside each hydrogen atom. A hydrogen bond between molecules is shown as a dashed line joining a δ+ hydrogen of one molecule to the δ− oxygen of a neighbouring molecule. The δ symbol indicates a partial charge, much smaller than the full charge of an ion.
Hydrogen bond

An attraction between molecules (an intermolecular force) in which a δ+ hydrogen atom that is covalently bonded to a strongly electronegative atom is attracted to a δ− atom of a neighbouring molecule. In water, hydrogen bonds form between the δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and the δ− oxygen of another; each water molecule can form up to four. An individual hydrogen bond is weak compared with a covalent bond and, in liquid water, hydrogen bonds continually break and re-form, but the very large number present gives water its cohesive, adhesive, solvent and thermal properties.
Cohesion

The attraction between molecules of the same substance. Water molecules cohere because of the hydrogen bonds between them. Cohesion allows water to be pulled up xylem vessels as a continuous column under tension and gives the surface of water a high surface tension.
Surface tension

The effect that makes the surface of a liquid behave like a stretched elastic film. Water molecules at the surface are pulled by hydrogen bonds to the molecules beside and beneath them, but not by the air above, so the surface resists being broken. Water's surface tension is high enough for small animals such as pond skaters to stand and move on the surface, so the water surface can be used as a habitat.
Transport of water under tension in xylem

Tension is a pulling force (a pressure below atmospheric). Evaporation of water from the cell walls of leaf cells during transpiration draws water out of the xylem, placing the column of water in each xylem vessel under tension. Because hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules together (cohesion), the tension is transmitted down the continuous column, so water is pulled up from the roots without the column breaking.
Adhesion

The attraction between water molecules and molecules of a different substance. Water adheres to surfaces that are polar or charged, because the δ+ and δ− parts of water molecules are attracted to charges or partial charges on the surface (for example, by hydrogen bonding to the hydroxyl groups of cellulose). Water does not adhere to non-polar surfaces such as the wax of a leaf cuticle.
Capillary action

The movement of water through narrow spaces, including against gravity, caused by adhesion of water to the polar or charged walls of the spaces together with cohesion between the water molecules. Capillary action moves water through the narrow spaces between soil particles, making it available to roots, and through the spaces between cellulose fibres in plant cell walls; in a leaf, water drawn into cell walls by capillary action replaces the water that evaporates from them.
Hydrophilic

Describes a substance that is attracted to water and dissolves in it (or, if solid, is wetted by it) because its molecules are polar or carry charges, so that water molecules form hydrogen bonds with them or are attracted to their charges. Glucose, amino acids, sodium chloride and most proteins are hydrophilic. Because a wide variety of hydrophilic substances dissolve in water, water is the medium for metabolism (most enzymes catalyse reactions in aqueous solution) and for transport in blood plasma, xylem sap and phloem sap.
Hydrophobic

Describes a substance that is not attracted to water and does not dissolve in it because its molecules are non-polar, with no charges or significant partial charges. Lipids and the hydrocarbon tails of phospholipids are hydrophobic. Water does not repel such molecules: they are excluded because water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other more strongly than they are attracted to a non-polar molecule. The functions of some molecules depend on their being hydrophobic and insoluble, for example the phospholipid tails that form the core of membranes.
Buoyancy

The upward force (upthrust) that a fluid exerts on a body immersed in it, equal to the weight of fluid displaced. Water is roughly 800 times denser than air, so it provides substantial support for the body of an aquatic animal such as a ringed seal, whereas air provides negligible support and an animal on land must bear its full weight through its skeleton and limbs.
Viscosity

The resistance of a fluid to flow, due to friction between its moving layers. Water is about 50 times more viscous than air, so an animal moving through water meets far more resistance than one moving through air; a streamlined shape, as in the ringed seal, reduces this resistance. Air's low viscosity offers little resistance to a bird in flight or to an animal walking on land.
Thermal conductivity

A measure of how rapidly heat is conducted through a substance. Water conducts heat about 25 times faster than air, so an animal loses heat to water much faster than to air at the same temperature. Aquatic mammals such as the ringed seal have a thick layer of blubber as insulation, and a diving bird such as the black-throated loon relies on air trapped in its feathers.
Specific heat capacity

The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (1 °C). Water's specific heat capacity, about 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, is roughly four times that of air per kilogram, and because water is also far denser, a body of water needs a very large energy input to change its temperature. Aquatic habitats therefore have stable temperatures that change slowly, whereas air temperature can change rapidly between day and night.
Black-throated loon (Gavia arctica) and ringed seal (Pusa hispida)

The guide's paired examples for contrasting water with air. The black-throated loon is a bird that flies through air, dives through water to catch fish, and comes ashore to nest; because air provides negligible upthrust, its wings must generate lift to support its full weight in flight and its skeleton and legs must bear it on land, while its wings meet little resistance in the low-viscosity air, and it loses heat much faster while diving than while flying. The ringed seal is an Arctic mammal that lives in water: upthrust supports most of its weight, its streamlined body reduces the resistance of viscous water, and a thick layer of blubber insulates it against rapid heat loss to the highly conductive water, whose temperature nonetheless stays stable because of water's high specific heat capacity. Either the common name or the scientific name may be used in an examination.
Asteroid hypothesis for the origin of Earth's water

The hypothesis that most of the water on Earth is of extraplanetary origin: it was delivered by asteroids containing water that collided with the early Earth. The abundance of water over the billions of years of Earth's history since then has allowed life to evolve.
Retention of water on Earth

Earth has kept its water for billions of years for two reasons: its gravity is strong enough to prevent water molecules in the atmosphere from escaping into space, and its surface temperatures are low enough for water vapour to condense, so most of the water is held as liquid in the oceans rather than as vapour that could be lost. A body with weak gravity, or one that is too hot for water to condense, cannot retain water.
Goldilocks zone

The range of distances from a star within which the surface temperature of an orbiting planet could allow water to exist as a liquid: neither so close to the star that water would boil away nor so far that it would be permanently frozen (also called the habitable zone). Because life as we know it requires liquid water as its medium, the search for extraterrestrial life concentrates on planets within this zone. The distance of the zone from a star depends on how much energy the star emits, so it is not the same for every star.
Pre-biotic Earth

The Earth before life existed, more than about 4 billion years ago. Its atmosphere contained no free oxygen and therefore no ozone, and had higher concentrations of carbon dioxide and methane than today. These greenhouse gases kept temperatures higher than at present, and without ozone, ultraviolet light penetrated to the surface. Under these conditions a variety of carbon compounds may have formed spontaneously by chemical processes that do not now occur.
Ozone and ultraviolet penetration

Ozone (O₃) is produced in the upper atmosphere from oxygen (O₂) by the action of ultraviolet light, and it absorbs much of the ultraviolet radiation arriving from the Sun. Because pre-biotic Earth had no free oxygen there was no ozone, so ultraviolet light penetrated to the surface of land and water. This radiation supplied energy for chemical reactions but also broke down complex molecules.
Pre-biotic formation of carbon compounds

The spontaneous formation of carbon compounds such as amino acids, sugars and nucleotide bases from simple inorganic molecules by chemical processes, without any living organism. On pre-biotic Earth, energy from ultraviolet light, lightning and volcanic heat acting on gases such as methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour could produce these compounds. Because the atmosphere now contains free oxygen, which oxidizes such compounds, and because these gases are far less abundant, the same processes do not now occur naturally.
Cell as the smallest unit of self-sustaining life

A cell is the smallest unit that can carry out all the functions of life – metabolism, growth, response to the environment, homeostasis and reproduction – using its own machinery, given a supply of nutrients and energy. A cell contains the enzymes, genetic material and membranes that sustain it; nothing smaller, such as an organelle, a virus or a molecule, can maintain itself independently.
Virus

A non-cellular infectious particle consisting of genetic material (DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat (capsid), in some cases with a lipid envelope taken from a host cell membrane. Viruses have no cytoplasm, ribosomes or metabolism of their own and can only replicate by using the machinery of a host cell. They are considered non-living for these reasons, even though they carry genes and evolve by natural selection.
Cells from pre-existing cells

The principle that a new cell is produced only by division of a pre-existing cell. No process is known today that produces a cell directly from non-living matter, and cells are highly complex, which is why explaining the spontaneous origin of the first cells is a challenge.
Requirements for the evolution of the first cells

Four processes that must have arisen for the first cells to evolve: catalysis (speeding up chemical reactions, before enzymes made by cells existed), self-replication of molecules (copying of information-carrying molecules such as RNA), self-assembly (spontaneous organization of molecules into structures such as bilayers) and the emergence of compartmentalization (enclosure of molecules by a membrane so that the chemistry inside could differ from that outside).
Protocell

A hypothesized self-organized, membrane-bound compartment containing self-replicating molecules, regarded as a precursor of the first true cells. Protocells had no hard parts and did not fossilize, so their existence is inferred from experiments and from the properties of living cells rather than observed directly.
Testability of scientific claims

The requirement that a scientific hypothesis or theory must make predictions that could in principle be shown to be wrong by observation or experiment. Hypotheses about the origin of cells are difficult to test because the exact conditions on pre-biotic Earth cannot be replicated and the first protocells did not fossilize, so scientists test them indirectly through laboratory simulations, model systems and evidence from the genomes of living organisms.
Miller–Urey experiment

An experiment carried out in 1953 in which Stanley Miller and Harold Urey circulated a mixture of methane, ammonia, hydrogen and water vapour, representing the early atmosphere, past electrical sparks that simulated lightning. Water was boiled to supply vapour and a condenser returned the products to a flask representing the ocean. After a week the water contained amino acids and other carbon compounds, showing that carbon compounds needed by life can form from inorganic molecules under conditions that may have existed on pre-biotic Earth.
Evaluation of the Miller–Urey experiment

Strengths: it was the first demonstration that carbon compounds used by living organisms, including several amino acids, form spontaneously from inorganic gases given an energy source, and reanalysis of Miller's stored samples with modern methods found more amino acids than were originally reported. Limitations: the early atmosphere is now thought to have contained more carbon dioxide and nitrogen and less methane and ammonia than the mixture used; the experiment produced only small molecules, not polymers, self-replicating molecules or cells; and the products were an undirected mixture that included many compounds, such as amino acids not used in proteins, that living organisms do not use to build their macromolecules. Later experiments using revised gas mixtures also produced amino acids, so the central conclusion stands.
Amphipathic fatty acid

A molecule with a hydrophilic (polar) part and a hydrophobic (non-polar) part is amphipathic. A fatty acid is amphipathic: its carboxyl group is hydrophilic and its hydrocarbon chain is hydrophobic. In water, amphipathic molecules arrange themselves so that the hydrophilic parts remain in contact with water and the hydrophobic parts are excluded from it.
Vesicle

A small spherical sac of fluid enclosed by a membrane. Fatty acids in water can coalesce spontaneously into a bilayer, with hydrophobic tails pointing inwards and hydrophilic heads facing the water on both surfaces, and the bilayer closes on itself to form a sphere. This self-assembly needs no enzymes and creates a membrane-bound compartment in which the internal chemistry can become different from that of the surrounding water.
RNA world hypothesis

The hypothesis that RNA was the first genetic material and that the earliest cells used RNA both to store hereditary information and to catalyse reactions, before DNA and protein enzymes evolved. It rests on two properties of RNA: it can be replicated by complementary base pairing, and some RNA molecules have catalytic activity.
Ribozyme

An RNA molecule that acts as a catalyst. In the ribosome, the formation of peptide bonds between amino acids during translation is catalysed by ribosomal RNA in the large subunit, not by protein. This surviving ribozyme is evidence that RNA could have acted as the enzymes of the earliest cells.
Last universal common ancestor (LUCA)

The most recent organism from which every organism alive today is descended. LUCA was not the first living cell: other forms of life are likely to have evolved before or alongside it, but they became extinct through competition from LUCA and its descendants, leaving LUCA's lineage as the only one with living descendants.
Universal genetic code

The correspondence between the 64 mRNA codons and the amino acids or stop signals they specify, which is the same in all organisms apart from a few minor variations. Because the assignment of codons to amino acids is largely arbitrary rather than chemically necessary, a shared code is best explained by inheritance from a common ancestor. The presence of shared genes across all organisms, such as those for ribosomal RNA, is a second line of evidence for LUCA.
Dating the first living cells

The oldest widely accepted evidence of cells is microfossils and stromatolites (layered structures built up by microbial communities) in rocks about 3.5 billion years old. These are dated by radiometric dating of the surrounding rock, using the known decay rate of long-lived isotopes such as uranium-238; radiocarbon dating cannot be used because carbon-14 decays away within about 50 000 years. Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, so cells existed within the first billion years and life has been evolving for most of Earth's history.
Molecular clock

A method of estimating the time since two lineages diverged from the number of differences between their DNA or protein sequences, assuming that mutations accumulate at a roughly constant rate that can be calibrated using fossils of known age. Applied to genes shared by all organisms, molecular clocks estimate that LUCA lived roughly 4 billion years ago, but such estimates carry wide uncertainty and cannot be checked against a fossil of LUCA itself.
Hydrothermal vent

A fissure in the seafloor from which water heated by magma below emerges, carrying dissolved minerals and reduced compounds such as hydrogen and hydrogen sulfide that precipitate to build chimney-like structures. Vents supply chemical energy, temperature and chemical gradients and mineral catalysts in the absence of sunlight, and are the environment in which LUCA is thought to have evolved.
Fossilized evidence from vent precipitates

Microscopic tubes and filaments of iron oxide found in rocks that formed from seafloor hydrothermal vent precipitates in the Nuvvuagittuq belt of Quebec, Canada, dated at least 3.77 billion years old, resemble the iron-oxidizing bacteria that live around vents today. They are interpreted as fossils of some of the earliest life, in the kind of environment in which LUCA is thought to have evolved.
Conserved sequence

A DNA or protein sequence that has stayed very similar across widely separated lineages because natural selection removes changes to it. Genes found in both bacteria and archaea are inferred to have been present in LUCA. Genomic analysis of such conserved genes indicates that LUCA lived without oxygen, at high temperatures, and used hydrogen and carbon dioxide as its sources of energy and carbon, all of which fit the conditions at hydrothermal vents.
Cell theory

The theory that cells are the basic structural unit of all living organisms: every living organism consists of one or more cells, and all cells arise from pre-existing cells. Because it is a general theory, it can be used to make predictions about organisms that have not yet been examined.
Deductive reasoning (NOS)

Reasoning from a general theory to a specific prediction that can then be tested by observation. From cell theory, a biologist can deduce that a newly discovered organism will consist of one or more cells before it has been examined under a microscope. Deduction runs from the general to the particular; induction runs the other way, from many particular observations to a general statement.
Magnification

How many times larger an image is than the object it shows: magnification = size of image ÷ actual size of object, with both sizes converted to the same units before dividing. Rearranged, actual size = size of image ÷ magnification. Magnification has no units and is written as, for example, ×400.
Eyepiece graticule and stage micrometer

An eyepiece graticule is a scale of equally spaced divisions fitted inside the eyepiece, so it appears superimposed on the specimen. It has no fixed value in micrometres: it must be calibrated for each objective lens by lining it up with a stage micrometer, a slide carrying a scale of known length (for example 100 µm divided into 100 divisions of 1 µm). Once the value of one graticule division is known for that objective, the actual size of a specimen is the number of divisions it spans multiplied by that value.
Scale bar

A line drawn on a micrograph or drawing that represents a stated actual length in the specimen, for example 10 µm. Its drawn length equals the actual length it represents multiplied by the magnification, so a 10 µm scale bar on a ×2000 image is 20 000 µm (20 mm) long. A scale bar allows actual sizes to be judged directly from the image without stating the magnification.
Temporary mount and staining

A temporary mount is a specimen placed in a drop of water or stain on a slide and covered with a coverslip for immediate viewing. Most cell structures are almost transparent, so stains such as iodine solution or methylene blue are used to increase contrast between structures; a stain does not increase magnification or resolution.
Coarse and fine adjustment

The two focusing controls of a light microscope. The coarse adjustment moves the stage or objective through large distances and is used only with the low-power objective to bring the specimen roughly into focus. The fine adjustment moves through very small distances and is used to sharpen the image, and is the only control used with high-power objectives, where the lens is close to the slide and coarse movement could break the slide or damage the lens.
Quantitative observation (NOS)

An observation that produces a numerical value, such as measuring the length of a cell in graticule divisions or in micrometres. Measurement using instruments such as a calibrated microscope is a form of quantitative observation, as opposed to a qualitative observation, which describes without measuring.
Resolution

The smallest distance between two points at which they can still be seen as separate. Resolution is limited by the wavelength of the radiation used: visible light gives a light microscope a resolution of about 200 nm, whereas an electron beam has a far shorter wavelength and gives an electron microscope a resolution below 1 nm. Higher magnification cannot reveal detail below the resolution limit; it only makes an unresolved image larger.
Electron microscopy

Microscopy using a beam of electrons instead of light. Its advantage is very much higher resolution and magnification, revealing ultrastructure such as ribosomes, membranes and the internal structure of organelles that a light microscope cannot resolve. Specimens must be dead, fixed, dehydrated and usually stained with heavy metals, and are viewed in a vacuum, so living cells cannot be observed and the images have no natural colour.
Freeze fracture

A technique in which a specimen is frozen very rapidly, then fractured with a blade. The fracture plane tends to run through the weak hydrophobic interior of membranes, between the two layers of the phospholipid bilayer. The exposed surfaces are coated with a thin layer of metal to make a replica, which is examined by electron microscopy. Freeze fracture revealed membrane proteins as particles embedded within the bilayer, which gave evidence for the fluid mosaic model.
Cryogenic electron microscopy

Electron microscopy of specimens that have been frozen so rapidly that water solidifies as a glass-like solid without forming ice crystals, and are kept at very low temperature while being imaged. No chemical fixation or staining is needed, so molecules are preserved close to their natural state. Images of many identical molecules are combined by computer to produce three-dimensional structures of proteins and other large molecules at near-atomic resolution.
Fluorescent stains

Dyes that absorb light of one wavelength and emit light of a longer wavelength. When a fluorescent stain that binds to a particular component, such as DNA, is used with a fluorescence light microscope, that component glows brightly against a dark background. Different fluorescent stains emitting different colours can be used together to show several components in the same cell.
Immunofluorescence

A light microscopy technique in which antibodies that bind specifically to one protein are linked to a fluorescent marker. When the antibodies are applied to cells, the marker glows only where that protein is located, so the distribution of a single protein inside cells or tissues can be seen with a fluorescence microscope.
Structures common to all cells

Typical cells of all living organisms have DNA as their genetic material, a cytoplasm composed mainly of water, and a plasma membrane composed of lipids. DNA stores the information for making the cell's proteins in a stable form that can be replicated and passed to daughter cells. Water is the solvent in which the reactions of metabolism take place and in which substances dissolve and move. Phospholipids have hydrophobic tails that form a bilayer barrier to water-soluble substances, so the membrane keeps the cell contents separate from the surroundings and controls what enters and leaves.
Prokaryotic cell

A cell with no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles. The structure required is that of Gram-positive eubacteria such as Bacillus and Staphylococcus: a cell wall outside the plasma membrane, cytoplasm, naked DNA in a single loop lying in the cytoplasm, and 70S ribosomes. Prokaryotic cells are typically about 1–10 µm in size and much smaller than most eukaryotic cells. Prokaryote cell structure varies between groups, but the details of the variations are not required.
Naked DNA

DNA that is not associated with histone proteins. The DNA of a prokaryote is a single naked loop (a circular molecule) lying in a region of the cytoplasm called the nucleoid; it is not enclosed by a membrane. 'Naked' refers to the absence of histones, not to the absence of a nuclear membrane.
70S ribosomes

The ribosomes of prokaryotic cells, which are smaller than the 80S ribosomes of the eukaryotic cytoplasm. The S value (Svedberg unit) describes the rate at which a particle sediments in a centrifuge and so reflects size. Prokaryotes carry out protein synthesis on 70S ribosomes; ribosomes are not membrane-bound, so their presence is consistent with the absence of membrane-bound organelles.
Gram-positive eubacteria

Bacteria such as Bacillus (rod-shaped) and Staphylococcus (spherical, in clusters) whose cell wall consists of a thick layer of peptidoglycan outside the plasma membrane. The cell wall of a prokaryote is not made of cellulose. These genera are the model for the prokaryotic cell structure required.
Nucleus

The organelle that contains the chromosomes of a eukaryotic cell. Each chromosome is a DNA molecule bound to histone proteins. The nucleus is enclosed by a double membrane (the nuclear envelope) that is perforated by nuclear pores, through which RNA and proteins pass between the nucleus and the cytoplasm.
80S ribosomes

The ribosomes in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells, larger than the 70S ribosomes of prokaryotes. Some lie free in the cytoplasm and make proteins used within the cytoplasm; others are attached to the endoplasmic reticulum, making it rough endoplasmic reticulum, and make proteins for secretion, for membranes or for lysosomes.
Cytoskeleton

A network of protein fibres in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells, consisting of microtubules (hollow tubes of the protein tubulin) and microfilaments (thin fibres of the protein actin). The fibres are dynamic: they assemble and disassemble as needed to change cell shape, move organelles and vesicles, separate chromosomes during division and move cilia and flagella.
Lysosome

A vesicle bounded by a single membrane that contains hydrolytic enzymes. Lysosomes are one of the variety of vesicles found in eukaryotic cells; they digest material taken into the cell and break down worn-out organelles, keeping the enzymes separated from the rest of the cytoplasm.
Endoplasmic reticulum

A network of membrane tubules and flattened sacs continuous with the outer membrane of the nucleus. Rough endoplasmic reticulum has 80S ribosomes attached to its outer surface and synthesizes proteins that are transported in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus; smooth endoplasmic reticulum lacks ribosomes and synthesizes lipids.
Golgi apparatus

A stack of flattened, curved membrane sacs (cisternae), not studded with ribosomes, with vesicles budding from its edges. It receives proteins in vesicles from the rough endoplasmic reticulum, modifies and sorts them, and packages them into vesicles, including secretory vesicles that carry proteins to the plasma membrane for release.
Mitochondrion

An organelle bounded by a double membrane, the inner membrane being folded into cristae that project into a fluid matrix. Mitochondria are the site of aerobic cell respiration, producing ATP for the cell.
Functions of life

The processes that all living organisms, including unicellular organisms, carry out: homeostasis (keeping internal conditions within limits), metabolism (the enzyme-catalysed reactions of the cell, both synthesis and breakdown), nutrition (obtaining food or making it), movement, excretion (removal of the waste products of metabolism), growth, response to stimuli and reproduction. In a unicellular organism all of these are carried out within one cell.
Homeostasis in a unicellular organism

Keeping the internal conditions of the cell within limits. In a freshwater unicellular organism such as Paramecium, water enters continuously by osmosis; a contractile vacuole collects this water and expels it from the cell, keeping the water content of the cytoplasm within limits. This is homeostasis, not excretion, because the water expelled is not a waste product of metabolism.
Cell wall composition

Plant cells have a cell wall made of cellulose; fungal cells have a cell wall made of chitin; animal cells have no cell wall. The cell wall lies outside the plasma membrane and gives the cell strength and a fixed shape.
Vacuoles in animal, fungal and plant cells

Plant cells typically have a single large permanent vacuole filled with cell sap, which stores substances and maintains the turgor pressure that supports the cell. Animal cells have small, temporary vacuoles, such as those formed when material is taken in by endocytosis. Fungal cells also have vacuoles.
Plastids

A group of organelles found in plant cells but not in animal or fungal cells. Chloroplasts, the site of photosynthesis, are the best-known plastids, but there are others, such as amyloplasts that store starch and chromoplasts that contain pigments. Chloroplasts are present only in plant cells that are exposed to light, such as leaf cells, not in every plant cell.
Centrioles, cilia and flagella

Structures built from microtubules. Centrioles occur in pairs in animal cells and are involved in organizing the spindle during cell division; plant cells lack centrioles and still form a spindle. Cilia and flagella are projections from the cell surface that move the cell or move fluid past it; they are found in many animal cells and in some unicellular eukaryotes, but not in the cells of plants or fungi, with rare exceptions such as the swimming sperm of mosses and ferns.
Aseptate fungal hyphae

Thread-like fungal filaments that are not divided by cross-walls (septa), so that many nuclei share one continuous cytoplasm. This arises because nuclei divide repeatedly without the cytoplasm being divided, giving one long multinucleate cell.
Skeletal muscle fibre

A very long muscle cell containing many nuclei. It forms during development by the fusion of many separate cells, so the nuclei of all of them lie within one plasma membrane, spread along the length of the fibre.
Red blood cell

A mature mammalian red blood cell has no nucleus: the nucleus is lost as the cell develops in the bone marrow, leaving more of the cell's volume for haemoglobin. Without a nucleus the cell cannot make new proteins or divide, and it has a limited lifespan.
Phloem sieve tube element

A living plant cell in phloem that has lost its nucleus and most other organelles as it matured, leaving a cell with cytoplasm and a plasma membrane but no nucleus, through which sap can flow. It is kept alive by an adjacent companion cell, which retains its nucleus.
Identifying cell types in micrographs

A prokaryotic cell is recognized by its small size, a cell wall, a nucleoid region of DNA not enclosed by a membrane, and the absence of a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles. A plant cell is recognized by a cell wall, a large sap vacuole and, in photosynthetic cells, chloroplasts. An animal cell has no cell wall and no chloroplasts, may show microvilli, and has a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles such as mitochondria.
Identifying organelles in electron micrographs

Nucleus: a large body bounded by a double membrane with pores, containing chromatin. Mitochondrion: a double membrane with the inner membrane folded into cristae. Chloroplast: a double membrane enclosing stacks of flattened thylakoids (grana). Rough endoplasmic reticulum: flattened sacs studded with ribosomes. Smooth endoplasmic reticulum: tubules without ribosomes. Golgi apparatus: a discrete stack of curved, flattened sacs with vesicles budding from the edges and no ribosomes. Ribosomes: small dense granules. Sap vacuole: a large membrane-bound space in a plant cell. Microvilli: finger-like projections of the plasma membrane.
Nucleoid region

The region of the cytoplasm of a prokaryotic cell in which the naked DNA loop lies. In electron micrographs it appears as a paler, fibrous area not enclosed by a membrane, which distinguishes a prokaryote from a eukaryote with a membrane-bound nucleus.
Annotation

A label on a drawing that gives information about the structure, in particular its function, rather than just its name. For example: rough endoplasmic reticulum — synthesizes proteins for secretion; Golgi apparatus — modifies proteins and packages them into vesicles; mitochondrion — site of aerobic cell respiration producing ATP; chloroplast — site of photosynthesis; sap vacuole — stores substances and maintains turgor; nucleus — contains the chromosomes and controls the cell's activities; plasma membrane — controls entry and exit of substances; cell wall — supports and protects the cell.
Secretory vesicle

A small membrane-bound sac that buds from the Golgi apparatus carrying proteins to the plasma membrane. When it fuses with the plasma membrane its contents are released from the cell by exocytosis. Secretory vesicles differ from lysosomes, which contain hydrolytic enzymes and remain inside the cell.
Microvilli

Finger-like projections of the plasma membrane of some animal cells, such as those lining the small intestine, that greatly increase the surface area for absorption. Unlike cilia, microvilli do not beat or move.
Endosymbiosis

The process by which mitochondria and, later in some lineages, chloroplasts originated: a prokaryotic cell was taken into a larger cell by endocytosis and, instead of being digested, survived and reproduced inside it, becoming an organelle. Evidence suggests all eukaryotes evolved from a common unicellular ancestor that already had a nucleus and reproduced sexually; mitochondria then evolved by endosymbiosis of an aerobic prokaryote, and in some eukaryotes chloroplasts subsequently arose by endosymbiosis of a photosynthetic prokaryote.
Evidence for endosymbiosis

Mitochondria and chloroplasts contain naked circular DNA, like the DNA of prokaryotes; they contain 70S ribosomes, like prokaryotes, rather than the 80S ribosomes of the surrounding cytoplasm; and they replicate by dividing in two, independently of the division of the cell. They are also bounded by a double membrane, the inner membrane being derived from the plasma membrane of the engulfed prokaryote and the outer from the vesicle membrane of the host cell, and they are similar in size to prokaryotic cells.
Strength of a theory (NOS)

The strength of a scientific theory comes from the range of observations it explains and the predictions it supports, not from direct observation of the events it proposes. The theory of endosymbiosis accounts for a wide range of observations about mitochondria and chloroplasts, and its predictions have been supported, which is why it is accepted even though the original endosymbiotic events happened over a billion years ago.
Cell differentiation

The process by which cells in a multicellular organism become specialized to form different tissues. Differentiated cells retain the whole genome; what differs between cell types is the pattern of gene expression, which determines which proteins are made and therefore the cell's structure and function.
Pattern of gene expression

The particular set of genes that is switched on in a cell. Different patterns of gene expression are the basis of differentiation, and they are often triggered by changes in the cell's environment, such as chemical signals from neighbouring cells or its position within the developing organism.
Multicellularity

The condition of an organism consisting of many cells. Multicellularity has evolved repeatedly and independently in different eukaryotic lineages: many fungi and eukaryotic algae are multicellular, and all plants and animals are multicellular, while many other eukaryotes remain unicellular.
Advantages of multicellularity

A multicellular organism can have a much larger body than a single cell, because each cell keeps a surface area to volume ratio adequate for exchange while the organism as a whole grows large. It also allows cell specialization: different cells differentiate to carry out different functions, which a single cell could not perform simultaneously and as efficiently.
Virus

A non-cellular infectious particle consisting of nucleic acid enclosed in a protein capsid, in some cases with an outer envelope. The few features shared by all viruses are a small, fixed size (most are tens to a few hundred nanometres across and do not grow); nucleic acid, either DNA or RNA, as genetic material; a capsid made of protein; no cytoplasm; and few or no enzymes. Because they have no metabolism of their own, viruses can only be replicated inside a living host cell.
Capsid

The protein coat of a virus, built from many copies of one or a few protein subunits, that encloses and protects the viral nucleic acid. Every virus has a capsid; it is protein, not a membrane. Capsid shape varies between viruses (for example helical or icosahedral), and in a bacteriophage the icosahedral head is joined to a protein tail.
Viral genetic material

The nucleic acid that carries a virus's genes. In any one virus it is either DNA or RNA, never both, and it may be single-stranded or double-stranded. It codes for the capsid proteins and for any enzymes the virus needs that the host cell cannot supply, but it does not code for the ribosomes or energy-transferring systems that the virus takes from the host.
Enveloped virus

A virus whose capsid is surrounded by a lipid bilayer envelope derived from a membrane of the host cell, acquired as the virus buds through that membrane on leaving the cell. Viral glycoproteins inserted in the envelope bind to receptors on the surface of a new host cell. Coronaviruses and HIV are enveloped; bacteriophage lambda is not enveloped, so its capsid is its outermost layer.
Bacteriophage lambda

A virus that infects the bacterium Escherichia coli. It has a linear double-stranded DNA genome of about 48 500 base pairs packed inside an icosahedral protein head, which is joined to a flexible protein tail through which the DNA is injected into the host. It is not enveloped. Lambda is a temperate phage: after infecting a cell it may follow either the lytic cycle or the lysogenic cycle.
Coronavirus

A group of enveloped viruses with a single-stranded RNA genome, among the largest of any RNA virus, enclosed in a helical nucleocapsid. Club-shaped spike glycoproteins projecting from the envelope give the crown-like appearance in electron micrographs and bind to receptors on host cells. The RNA is copied by an RNA-dependent RNA polymerase and is not converted into DNA. Coronaviruses cause respiratory diseases in humans, including COVID-19.
Human immunodeficiency virus (HIV)

An enveloped retrovirus with two copies of a single-stranded RNA genome inside a cone-shaped protein capsid, together with a few viral enzymes, including reverse transcriptase, integrase and protease. Glycoproteins in the envelope bind to receptors on helper T lymphocytes. After entry, reverse transcriptase copies the RNA into DNA, which is integrated into the host cell's DNA. HIV carries only these few enzymes and relies on the host cell for everything else, illustrating the general rule that viruses have few or no enzymes.
Obligate intracellular parasitism of viruses

The mode of existence in which a virus can only be replicated inside a living host cell. Viruses have no ribosomes, no source of ATP and few or no enzymes, so they rely on the host cell for energy supply (ATP from the host's cell respiration), nutrition (nucleotides and amino acids), protein synthesis (host ribosomes, transfer RNA and RNA polymerase) and other life functions. Outside a cell a virus is inert.
Lytic cycle (bacteriophage lambda)

The cycle in which a virus multiplies and destroys its host cell. In lambda the phases are: attachment, in which the tail binds to a specific receptor protein on the surface of an E. coli cell; DNA entry, in which the linear DNA is injected through the tail into the cytoplasm while the capsid stays outside, after which the DNA forms a circle; synthesis, in which host RNA polymerase transcribes the phage genes, host ribosomes translate them into phage proteins, and the phage DNA is replicated using host nucleotides and ATP; assembly, in which capsid proteins self-assemble around copies of the DNA to form new phages; and lysis, in which phage-encoded proteins break down the cell wall and membrane so the cell bursts, releasing on the order of a hundred new phages.
Lysogenic cycle (bacteriophage lambda)

The cycle in which the phage DNA, instead of directing the synthesis of new phages, is inserted into the host cell's chromosome by a phage-encoded integrase enzyme and remains there as a prophage. A phage repressor protein keeps the genes for the lytic cycle switched off, so the genes for phage structural proteins and lysis are not expressed and no phage particles are made and the host cell is not harmed. The prophage is replicated along with the host chromosome at every cell division and passed to both daughter cells, so a whole population of E. coli can come to carry the phage genome.
Prophage

The genome of a phage such as lambda when it is integrated into the chromosome of a bacterial host cell during the lysogenic cycle. It is part of the host's DNA, not a separate loop, and is copied by the host's DNA replication machinery whenever the chromosome is copied. A bacterium carrying a prophage is called a lysogen.
Induction

The switch of a prophage from the lysogenic cycle to the lytic cycle. In lambda it is triggered when the host's DNA is damaged, for example by ultraviolet light: the host's DNA-damage response leads to destruction of the phage repressor, the prophage DNA is excised from the chromosome, and the genes for the lytic cycle are expressed, so new phages are made and the cell lyses. Induction shows that lysogeny is a reversible state, not a separate kind of virus.
Convergent evolution of viral features

The independent evolution of similar features in unrelated lineages because they face the same selective pressures. All viruses share an extreme form of obligate parasitism, which favours a minimal particle: small, fixed size, a protective protein capsid and reliance on the host for metabolism. The features all viruses have in common could therefore have arisen separately in several lineages, so they cannot be taken as evidence that all viruses descend from one common ancestor.
Several origins of viruses

The hypothesis that viruses did not arise once but on several separate occasions from cellular organisms, for example from fragments of cellular genetic material that gained the ability to move between cells, or by loss of structures from parasitic cells. Two lines of evidence support an origin from cellular organisms and several origins rather than one: viruses use the same genetic code as living organisms, which indicates that they are derived from them; and viruses are extremely diverse, with genomes of single- or double-stranded RNA or DNA and very different structures, which is hard to reconcile with descent from a single ancestral virus.
Reasons for rapid evolution in viruses

Some viruses, especially RNA viruses such as influenza viruses and HIV, evolve far faster than cellular organisms because: the enzymes that copy their genomes (RNA-dependent RNA polymerase in influenza, reverse transcriptase in HIV) lack the proofreading of DNA polymerases, so the mutation rate per base per replication is very high; generation times are short, with each infected cell releasing large numbers of new virions; the resulting enormous populations contain many variants for natural selection to act on; and the host's immune responses and antiviral drugs exert strong selection. Influenza viruses can also exchange genome segments between strains.
Antigenic drift (influenza)

The gradual change in the surface antigens of influenza viruses, haemagglutinin and neuraminidase, caused by the accumulation of point mutations in the genes coding for them during error-prone replication. Variants whose antigens are no longer recognised by antibodies in the population are favoured by natural selection. Drift is why the strains circulating change from one season to the next and why the influenza vaccine is reformulated every year.
Antigenic shift (influenza)

A sudden, major change in the surface antigens of influenza A viruses produced by reassortment: the genome consists of eight separate RNA segments, and when two different strains (for example a human strain and a strain from birds or pigs) infect the same cell, new virions can be assembled containing a mixture of segments from both. The new subtype has antigens to which few people have immunity, so shift is associated with pandemics, such as the 2009 H1N1 pandemic strain, which combined segments derived from swine, avian and human influenza viruses.
Consequences of rapid viral evolution for treatment

Because rapidly evolving viruses generate resistant or antigenically altered variants quickly, treatment must be designed around this. HIV is treated with a combination of several antiretroviral drugs acting on different targets (for example reverse transcriptase, protease and integrase), because resistance to any single drug arises readily by mutation but a single virion is very unlikely to carry mutations conferring resistance to all of them at once. Influenza vaccines are reformulated each year to match the antigens of the strains predicted to circulate. The antigenic diversity of HIV, which differs even between variants within one patient, is one of the reasons no effective HIV vaccine has yet been produced.
Variation

Differences in traits between individual organisms. Variation is a defining feature of life: no two individuals, not even identical twins or members of a clone, are identical in all their traits, because genetic differences (mutation, recombination) and environmental influences both act on every organism. The patterns of variation are complex, with many traits varying independently, and these patterns are the basis on which organisms are named and classified.
Morphological species concept

The original concept of a species, as used by Linnaeus: a species is a group of organisms that share a set of traits (morphology, meaning form and structure) that distinguish them from other groups. It is still the practical basis for identifying most organisms, but it gives no rule for how much difference counts as a separate species, and it can be misled by variation within a species (for example between males and females) or by close resemblance between different species.
Binomial system

The two-part system of naming species introduced by Linnaeus. The first part of the name is the genus and the second part distinguishes the species within that genus, so Panthera leo (lion) and Panthera tigris (tiger) are two species in the same genus. The genus name is given an initial capital letter, the species name is lowercase, and the whole name is written in italics (or underlined when handwritten). Because the second part is only meaningful together with the genus, the same species word can be used in different genera.
Genus

A group of closely related species that share similar traits, named by the first part of the binomial. Species in the same genus, such as Panthera leo and Panthera tigris, resemble one another more closely than species in different genera, but they remain separate species.
Biological species concept

The definition of a species as a group of organisms that can breed with one another and produce fertile offspring. Two populations belong to different species if they cannot interbreed, or if they interbreed but produce only infertile offspring. It is one of several competing species concepts and has known challenges: it cannot be applied to fossils, to organisms that reproduce only asexually, or to populations that are separated geographically and so never have the chance to interbreed, and hybridization between recognized species sometimes produces fertile offspring.
Interspecific hybrid

An offspring produced when members of two different species breed. Under the biological species concept the test is whether the hybrid is fertile: a mule, produced by a horse and a donkey, is infertile, so horse and donkey remain separate species even though they can breed together.
Speciation

The splitting of one species into two or more species. It usually happens gradually rather than by a single act: populations that stop interbreeding accumulate differences in their traits over many generations, and at some point they are regarded as different species. Because the divergence is continuous, there is no precise moment at which speciation is complete.
Population

A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time, and so able to interbreed. A species may consist of many populations; when populations stop interbreeding and diverge, it can become an arbitrary decision whether they are still populations of one species or have become separate species.
Diploid chromosome number

The number of chromosomes in a body cell of a species, in which chromosomes are present in homologous pairs (one of each pair from each parent). It is an even number in a diploid cell because the chromosomes come in pairs. Chromosome numbers vary widely between plant and animal species and are not a measure of complexity: humans have 46 chromosomes and chimpanzees have 48.
Karyotype

The number and appearance of the chromosomes in the cells of an organism, described by chromosome number, and by the length, centromere position and banding pattern of each chromosome. Karyotyping is the process of finding an organism's karyotype, usually from cells arrested in metaphase of mitosis when the chromosomes are condensed and visible.
Karyogram

An image in which the chromosomes from one cell, photographed at metaphase, have been cut out and arranged in homologous pairs in a standard order, usually by decreasing length, with the sex chromosomes last. Homologous chromosomes are matched by their length, the position of the centromere and the pattern of bands produced by staining, so that a pair cannot be matched on length alone.
Chromosome 2 fusion hypothesis

The hypothesis that human chromosome 2 arose by end-to-end fusion of two chromosomes that were separate in the shared ancestor of humans and chimpanzees (the two chromosomes that were numbered 12 and 13 in the chimpanzee, now called 2A and 2B), which explains why humans have 46 chromosomes while chimpanzees have 48. Its predictions can be tested: human chromosome 2 should carry telomere-like sequences near its middle, a second (inactive) centromere region, and banding patterns that match the two chimpanzee chromosomes laid end to end. It is therefore a testable hypothesis.
Testable hypothesis

A proposed explanation from which predictions can be derived and checked against observations or experiments, so that the hypothesis could in principle be shown to be false. The origin of chromosome 2 by fusion is testable because it predicts specific, observable sequence and banding features. A statement that makes no checkable prediction, or that concerns values or preferences rather than the natural world, is non-testable and lies outside what science can decide.
Genome

All the genetic information of an organism: the complete base sequence of its DNA, including genes and non-coding regions, in the nucleus and in mitochondria and chloroplasts. Organisms of the same species share most of their genome, but no two individuals (other than clones) have identical genomes.
Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)

A position in the genome at which a single base differs between individuals of the same species. SNPs are the commonest source of genome diversity within a species; most fall in non-coding DNA or do not change the amino acid coded for, so they need not affect the phenotype, although some do.
Genome size

The total amount of DNA in one copy of an organism's genome, measured in base pairs (or picograms of DNA). Eukaryote genomes vary enormously in size, and this variation is not a simple reflection of the number of genes or of the organism's complexity, because much of the DNA in a large genome is non-coding or repetitive. Genomes also vary in base sequence, and the differences between species are much larger than the differences between individuals within a species.
Genome size database

An online database, such as the Animal Genome Size Database or the NCBI Genome resource, from which the genome size of species in different taxonomic groups can be extracted for comparison. Comparing the values shows that genome size does not increase in step with organism complexity: some amphibians and flowering plants have genomes tens of times larger than the human genome.
Whole genome sequencing

Determining the complete base sequence of an organism's DNA. Its speed has increased and its cost has fallen dramatically: the first human genome took over a decade and a project budget of around three billion dollars, whereas a human genome can now be sequenced in about a day for a few hundred dollars. Current uses include research into evolutionary relationships by comparing the genomes of different species; a potential future use is personalized medicine.
Personalized medicine

A potential future use of whole genome sequencing in which a person's own genome sequence is used to guide their medical care, for example predicting their risk of particular diseases, choosing the drug and dose most likely to work for them, or matching a cancer treatment to the mutations in their tumour. It is a probabilistic tool, because for most diseases the genome affects risk rather than determining the outcome.
Horizontal gene transfer

The movement of genetic material between organisms other than from parent to offspring, for example the transfer of plasmid DNA between bacteria, including between bacteria of different species. Because genes can pass between species, bacterial species do not have the sealed gene pools that the biological species concept assumes.
Asexual reproduction and the species concept

Organisms that reproduce only asexually (for example many bacteria, and some plants, fungi and animals such as bdelloid rotifers) produce offspring genetically identical to the parent without breeding, so the test of whether they can breed and produce fertile offspring cannot be applied. Their species are defined instead on morphological, ecological or genetic (DNA sequence) similarity.
Chromosome number as a shared trait

All members of a species normally have the same number of chromosomes, so chromosome number is a trait shared within a species. Closely related species can have different numbers, and cross-breeding between them is unlikely to produce fertile offspring, because the hybrid inherits an unequal set of chromosomes from its two parents and these cannot form homologous pairs in meiosis, so viable gametes are not made. A horse (64 chromosomes) and a donkey (62) produce a mule with 63 chromosomes, which is almost always sterile.
Dichotomous key

An identification tool consisting of a series of numbered steps, each offering exactly two contrasting choices based on a trait that is fixed and easily observed, with each choice leading either to the name of an organism or to another step. A good key uses traits that do not vary with age, season or the individual (such as leaf arrangement or the number of legs) rather than variable traits such as size or colour, and is built by engaging with the local plant or animal species it is meant to identify.
DNA barcode

A short, standardized section of DNA, sequenced from a sample, whose base sequence identifies the species it came from by comparison with a reference database. Different regions are used for different groups, for example part of the mitochondrial COI gene for animals and chloroplast genes such as rbcL and matK for plants. A barcode is not the whole genome: it is a region that varies enough between species, but little enough within a species, to serve as a label.
Environmental DNA (eDNA)

DNA collected from an environmental sample such as water, soil or air, rather than from an organism itself, shed in skin cells, mucus, faeces, pollen or other material. Barcoding eDNA reveals which species have left DNA in a habitat, allowing its biodiversity to be surveyed rapidly and without capturing or seeing the organisms, although a detection shows only that DNA of the species was present in the sample, not where or when the organism itself was.
Taxon

Any named group of organisms in a classification, at any level; the plural is taxa. In the traditional hierarchy every organism belongs to one taxon at each rank, from kingdom down to species, and each taxon at one rank is contained within a single taxon of the rank above.
Traditional hierarchy of taxa

The ranked series kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus and species, in which each rank is nested within the one above. The hierarchy was constructed largely from morphology before evolutionary relationships were known, so it does not always correspond to patterns of divergence generated by evolution. A fixed ranking is also arbitrary, because there is no natural criterion that makes a family in one group equivalent to a family in another: the ranks are imposed on a gradation of variation.
Cladistics

An approach to classification in which organisms are grouped into clades on the basis of shared common ancestry, deduced most objectively from base sequences of genes or amino acid sequences of proteins. Clades are unranked: they nest inside one another to any depth and are not assigned to kingdom, phylum, class or any other fixed rank. Cladistics offers an alternative to the traditional ranked hierarchy rather than a redrawing of it.
Paradigm shift

A change in the fundamental framework of assumptions and methods within which a science is practised, rather than a refinement of details inside the existing framework. The replacement of classification by fixed ranks with classification by unranked clades, defined by common ancestry, is an example of the paradigm shift that sometimes occurs in scientific theories.
Classification corresponding to evolutionary relationships

The ideal classification, in which every taxonomic group consists of organisms that have all evolved from a common ancestor, so that the groups mirror the branching pattern of evolution. Its advantage is predictive: because characteristics are shared within a clade, the characteristics of an organism can be predicted from the group it belongs to, including characteristics that have not yet been studied in that species.
Common ancestor

A species from which two or more later species have descended. All the members of a group in an evolutionary classification share a common ancestor that is not shared with organisms outside the group, and the characteristics inherited from that ancestor are what the members have in common.
Molecular clock

The method of estimating when two clades diverged from a common ancestor from the number of differences between their base sequences or amino acid sequences, on the basis that sequence differences accumulate gradually over time in each lineage. Both lineages accumulate changes after they separate, so the differences between two living species are shared between the two lineages. The clock can only give estimates, because mutation rates are affected by the length of the generation time, the size of a population, the intensity of selective pressure and other factors.
Cladogram

A branching tree diagram that shows the most probable pattern of divergence of a set of organisms into clades, constructed from base sequences of genes or amino acid sequences of proteins (or, less objectively, from morphological traits). A cladogram is a hypothesis about evolutionary relationships: different genes or different criteria for judgement can lead to different cladograms for the same organisms.
Parsimony analysis

The criterion used to select the most probable cladogram from the alternatives: the cladogram in which the observed sequence variation between clades is accounted for with the smallest number of sequence changes is chosen. The number of changes is totalled over all positions in the sequences, so a tree favoured by one position may be rejected because it needs more changes at others.
Root

The base of a cladogram, representing the common ancestor of all the organisms shown. Every lineage on the cladogram descends from the root, so all the living organisms at the tips have been evolving for the same length of time since it.
Node

A branching point on a cladogram, representing a hypothetical common ancestor of the lineages that arise from it. The node is inferred from the data, not an identified fossil or a living species. All the organisms on the branches beyond a node form a clade, and the more recent the node at which two organisms' lineages join, the more closely related they are. Branches can be rotated about a node without changing the relationships shown.
Terminal branch

A branch of a cladogram that ends at one of the organisms or groups being compared, rather than at a further node. The left-to-right order of terminal branches carries no information about relatedness, and a terminal branch far from the root does not represent a more advanced organism.
Convergent evolution

The independent evolution of similar characteristics in lineages that do not share a recent common ancestor, usually because they are subject to similar selective pressures. Similarities due to convergent evolution can suggest a classification that groups unrelated organisms together; cladistic analysis of base sequences can show such a classification to be false, as happened with the figwort family (Scrophulariaceae), which was defined by floral morphology and from which several genera were transferred to other families.
Falsification

The rejection of a theory or other scientific knowledge claim when it is contradicted by evidence. A classification is a knowledge claim about evolutionary relationships and may eventually be falsified: cladistics tests whether the members of a named group form a clade, and where they do not, as in the traditional figwort family, the classification is revised.
Domain

The highest taxonomic level, introduced above the kingdoms in the reclassification proposed in 1977. Each domain contains one or more kingdoms, so the domains added an extra level to the hierarchy rather than replacing the kingdoms.
Three domains: Bacteria, Archaea and Eukarya

The three groups into which all organisms are classified. Bacteria and Archaea are both prokaryotic, but their rRNA base sequences are as different from each other as either is from Eukarya, so they are separate domains. Eukarya contains all eukaryotes, including the plant, animal and fungal kingdoms. The three-way division was proposed in 1977 by Carl Woese and colleagues from rRNA sequence comparisons; the term domain and the current names were adopted later.
Ribosomal RNA (rRNA) as classification evidence

RNA that forms part of the structure of ribosomes in every organism. Because all organisms have ribosomes, and because rRNA genes change only slowly, their base sequences can be compared across the whole of life. Comparison of rRNA base sequences was the evidence used to propose the three domains: it revealed that prokaryotes fall into two groups, Bacteria and Archaea, that are not distinguishable by cell structure but are deeply separated in sequence.
Evolution
