Change in the heritable characteristics of a population over generations. The unit that evolves is the population, not the individual: the frequencies of alleles, and therefore of the heritable characteristics they determine, change from one generation to the next. Characteristics acquired during an organism's lifetime and not genetic in origin are not passed on, so changes in them are not regarded as evolution.
Acquired characteristic

A feature that develops in an individual during its lifetime as a result of its activities or environment, such as enlarged muscles from training, a suntan or a learned skill. Acquired characteristics are not genetic in origin and are not inherited, so a change in them, however widespread in a population, is not evolution.
Lamarckism

The pre-Darwinian idea that characteristics acquired by an organism during its life through use or disuse of its organs are passed on to its offspring, so that a species changes by inheriting acquired characteristics. Defining evolution as change in heritable characteristics distinguishes Darwinian evolution from Lamarckism, because acquired changes that are not genetic in origin cannot be inherited.
Theory (nature of science)

In science, a well-supported explanation that predicts and explains a broad range of observations. The theory of evolution by natural selection is unlikely ever to be falsified, but the nature of science makes it impossible to prove formally that it is true by correspondence with every fact. It is therefore accepted as a pragmatic truth and still called a theory, despite all the supporting evidence; the word does not mean a guess or an untested idea.
Sequence evidence for common ancestry

Evidence for evolution obtained by comparing the base sequences of DNA or RNA, or the amino acid sequences of proteins, in different species. Differences in a sequence accumulate over time after two lineages split from a common ancestor, so species with fewer sequence differences share a more recent common ancestor than species with more differences. The pattern of similarity across many species matches a branching tree of descent, which gives powerful evidence of common ancestry.
Common ancestor

A species from which two or more later species are descended. Living species are not the ancestors of other living species: two present-day species that share many features or sequences do so because both inherited them from the same ancestral population that lived in the past.
Selective breeding

The deliberate choice by humans of which individuals of a domesticated animal or crop plant are allowed to breed, based on the heritable characteristics wanted. Repeated over generations it changes the heritable characteristics of the population, so it is evolution driven by artificial rather than natural selection. The breeder does not create the variation but selects among the heritable variation already present, including new mutations.
Breed or variety

A population of a domesticated animal species (a breed) or crop plant species (a variety) that differs in heritable characteristics from other populations of the same species because of selective breeding. The differences between breeds and varieties, and between them and the original wild species (such as the differences between dog breeds and the grey wolf, or between cabbage, kale, broccoli, cauliflower, kohlrabi and Brussels sprouts and wild cabbage, Brassica oleracea), show how rapidly evolutionary change can occur; the breeds and varieties remain members of one species.
Homologous structures

Structures in different species that are similar because they were inherited from a common ancestor, even if they now perform different functions. Their shared underlying pattern is not explained by function, since each could have been built differently, but is explained by descent with modification from the same ancestral structure, so homologous structures are evidence for evolution.
Pentadactyl limb

The limb pattern shared by amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals: a single bone in the upper limb, two bones in the lower limb, a group of wrist or ankle bones, and five digits each made of a series of small bones. The human arm, the wing of a bat, the flipper of a whale and the leg of a horse are all pentadactyl limbs adapted to different functions, so they are homologous structures inherited from a common ancestor.
Analogous structures

Structures in different species that have the same function but different evolutionary origins. They resemble each other because similar selection pressures favoured similar solutions, not because they were inherited from a common ancestor. Examples include the wings of insects and of birds, and the streamlined bodies and fins of sharks and dolphins.
Convergent evolution

The independent evolution of similar features in species that are not closely related, because they live in similar environments or have similar ways of life and experience similar selection pressures. Convergent evolution is the origin of analogous structures; the species remain separate and do not become more closely related to each other.
Speciation

The splitting of a pre-existing species into two or more species that can no longer interbreed. This is the only way in which new species have appeared, so each speciation event increases the total number of species on Earth. Gradual evolutionary change within a single species, without splitting, is not speciation.
Extinction

The disappearance of a species when its last member dies. Extinction decreases the total number of species on Earth, while speciation increases it, so the number of species alive at any time is the outcome of these two processes.
Reproductive isolation

The absence of interbreeding between two populations, so that alleles cannot pass between their gene pools. It is the starting condition for speciation: while gene flow continues, differences that arise in one population spread to the other, but once populations are reproductively isolated they can diverge until they are separate species.
Differential selection

Different selection pressures acting on two reproductively isolated populations, for example because their environments, food sources or competitors differ, so that different heritable characteristics are favoured in each. Over generations the populations diverge, and if divergence continues they become unable to interbreed. Bonobos, living south of the Congo River, and common chimpanzees, living north of it, diverged from one ancestral population in this way after the river separated them: neither species swims, and conditions on the two sides differ, for example bonobos have no gorillas competing for food in their range.
Geographical isolation

Separation of populations by a physical barrier such as a river, a mountain range or a stretch of sea that members of the species cannot cross. It is one means of achieving reproductive isolation: the Congo River separates bonobos from common chimpanzees because neither species swims.
Allopatric speciation

Speciation in which the populations that diverge are in different places, having been reproductively isolated by a geographical barrier. Once gene flow has stopped, differential selection in the two areas causes the gene pools to diverge until the populations can no longer interbreed.
Sympatric speciation

Speciation in which the diverging populations live in the same area. Reproductive isolation is achieved without a geographical barrier, for example by behavioural isolation, by temporal isolation, or in plants by polyploidy. As in allopatric speciation, reproductive isolation prevents gene flow and the gene pools then diverge.
Behavioural isolation

Reproductive isolation caused by differences in behaviour, particularly courtship: individuals only mate with partners whose courtship signals, such as song, display or scent, are those of their own group, so populations sharing an area do not interbreed.
Temporal isolation

Reproductive isolation caused by differences in the timing of reproduction, such as flowering, mating or spawning at different times of the day or year, so that populations sharing the same area cannot interbreed. It refers to timing within the lives of present-day organisms, not to living in different periods of Earth's history.
Adaptive radiation

The rapid diversification of a single ancestral species into many species, each adapted to a different niche, typically where vacant niches are available, for example after colonization of an island group or after an extinction event. Because each species specializes on a different resource or habitat, closely related species can coexist without competing, so adaptive radiation increases biodiversity in the ecosystem.
Vacant niche

A role in an ecosystem, defined by the resources, habitat and way of life it involves, that no species currently occupies. Vacant niches remove competition from occupying them, which allows descendants of a colonizing species to specialize in different ways and is the condition under which adaptive radiation occurs.
Interspecific hybrid

An offspring produced by mating between members of two different species, such as a mule, which is the offspring of a horse and a donkey. Hybrids are usually rare because barriers such as differences in courtship behaviour prevent mating, and when they are produced they are usually sterile, so alleles do not mix between the gene pools of the two species.
Hybrid sterility

The inability of an interspecific hybrid to produce viable gametes. A horse has 64 chromosomes and a donkey 62, so a mule has 63; the chromosomes inherited from the two parent species are not homologous pairs and cannot all pair up during meiosis, so functional gametes are not formed. The mule is healthy and vigorous but cannot breed, so its horse and donkey alleles reach no further generation.
Courtship behaviour as a barrier

Species-specific signals such as songs, displays, colours or scents that precede mating and are recognized only by members of the same species. Because individuals do not respond to the courtship of another species, courtship behaviour often prevents hybridization in animals, so it acts as a barrier that keeps the alleles of different species from mixing.
Polyploidy

Possession of more than two complete sets of chromosomes in each cell. In plants, a sterile hybrid between two species can become fertile if its chromosome number doubles, because every chromosome then has a homologous partner to pair with in meiosis. The polyploid cannot produce fertile offspring with either parent species, so it is reproductively isolated from both and is a new species.
Abrupt speciation

The formation of a new species in a single generation rather than by gradual divergence over many generations. In plants it occurs by hybridization between two species followed by polyploidy: the fertile polyploid hybrid is immediately isolated from both parent species. The knotweeds or smartweeds, genus Persicaria, contain many species that have been formed by these processes.
Biodiversity

The variety of life in all its forms, levels and combinations. It includes ecosystem diversity (the range of ecosystems in a region or on Earth), species diversity (the number of species and their relative abundance) and genetic diversity (the variety of alleles within a species).
Ecosystem diversity

The variety of ecosystems in an area, each with its own community of species and abiotic environment. A coastline with coral reef, mangrove, seagrass meadow and lowland rainforest has higher ecosystem diversity than one with rainforest alone, and losing any one of these ecosystems reduces biodiversity even if no species is lost.
Species diversity

The number of species in a community (species richness) together with the relative abundance of each species (species evenness). A community dominated by one species has lower species diversity than a community in which the same species are present in similar numbers.
Genetic diversity

The variety of alleles within a species or population. High genetic diversity gives a population more scope to adapt to changing conditions and resist disease. A species can persist while losing genetic diversity: the cheetah survives as a species, but its individuals are so genetically alike that skin grafts between unrelated animals are not rejected.
Described species

A species that has been discovered, given a binomial name and formally described in a publication. Around two million species have been described, but estimates of the total number of species on Earth are several times higher, so many more species remain to be discovered, especially among insects, fungi and microorganisms. Fossil evidence suggests that more species are alive today than at any time in the past.
Splitters and lumpers

Terms for taxonomists who classify the same observations in different ways. A splitter treats small but consistent differences as grounds for recognizing separate species and so recognizes more species in a group; a lumper treats the same differences as variation within a species and so recognizes fewer. Neither is simply wrong: classification is pattern recognition, and the same observations can be classified in different ways (NOS).
Sixth mass extinction

The current episode of species extinction, in which the rate of extinction is far above the background rate estimated from the fossil record. Unlike the five earlier mass extinctions, whose causes were non-anthropogenic, its causes are human activities: hunting and other over-exploitation, destruction of habitat, pollution and the spread of pests, diseases and invasive alien species.
North Island giant moa (Dinornis novaezealandiae)

A flightless bird of New Zealand, the females standing up to about 2 m tall, which had evolved with no mammalian predators, matured slowly and laid few eggs. Polynesian settlers arrived around 1300 CE, hunted moa for meat, took their eggs and burned areas of forest; the species was extinct within about two centuries. It is the guide's example of the anthropogenic loss of terrestrial megafauna.
Caribbean monk seal (Neomonachus tropicalis)

A seal of the Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico, killed by Europeans from the 1490s for the oil in its blubber and for its meat and skin; later, its remaining colonies were disturbed by coastal settlement and its fish prey depleted by fishing. The last confirmed sighting was in 1952 and it was declared extinct in 2008. It is the guide's example of the anthropogenic extinction of a marine species.
Passenger pigeon (Ectopistes migratorius)

A North American bird whose flocks numbered in the billions in the early 1800s. Commercial hunting for meat, made possible by the railway and the telegraph, together with the clearance of the eastern forests in which it nested, drove it to extinction; the last individual died in Cincinnati Zoo in 1914. It shows that even an extremely abundant species can be driven to extinction by anthropogenic causes. (A third case study from an area familiar to students is required; this is a widely taught example, and a local one may be substituted.)
Ecosystem loss

The destruction or degradation of an ecosystem so that its characteristic community and processes disappear, even if some organisms or tree cover remain. Causes may be directly anthropogenic, such as clearance for agriculture or urbanization, or indirectly anthropogenic, such as fires that spread through land that logging and drainage have made flammable.
Mixed dipterocarp forest

The lowland rainforest of Borneo, Sumatra and the Malay Peninsula, dominated by tall trees of the family Dipterocarpaceae. It has been lost through logging for hardwood timber, followed by clearance and burning to create oil palm and pulpwood plantations, with fires during droughts spreading through logged and drained land. It is the guide's compulsory case study of ecosystem loss in Southeast Asia.
Aral Sea (lost ecosystem case study)

An inland sea in Central Asia whose ecosystem was lost when, from the 1960s, the rivers feeding it were diverted to irrigate cotton and other crops. The sea shrank to a fraction of its former area and split into separate basins, its salinity rose several-fold, its fishery collapsed as the native fish species disappeared from the sea, and the exposed seabed became a salt desert from which dust and salt storms spread. It is a directly anthropogenic ecosystem loss. (A second case study from an area familiar to students is required by the guide if possible; this is a widely taught example, and a local one may be substituted.)
IPBES

The Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform on Biodiversity and Ecosystem Services, an intergovernmental body that assesses published evidence on the state of biodiversity. Its 2019 Global Assessment concluded that around one million species are threatened with extinction and that nature is declining at rates unprecedented in human history.
Species richness

The number of different species present in a community or area. It records nothing about how abundant each species is, so two surveys can record the same richness while the community has changed greatly.
Species evenness

How evenly the individuals in a community are distributed among the species present. A community in which most individuals belong to one species has low evenness, even when its species richness is high. Evidence of change in richness or evenness requires surveys repeated over time using the same method.
Citizen science

The collection of scientific data by members of the public rather than professional scientists, for example in national garden-bird or butterfly counts. It allows surveys over far larger areas and longer periods than scientists alone could cover, but brings methodological concerns: variable identification skill, uneven sampling effort and non-random choice of sites, which must be accounted for before the data are used as evidence (NOS).
Verifiable evidence

Evidence that others can check. To be verifiable, evidence usually has to come from a published source that has been peer-reviewed (examined by independent experts before publication) and that describes its methodology in enough detail for the work to be checked or repeated (NOS).
Over-exploitation

Harvesting a species faster than its population can replace itself, by hunting, fishing or collecting. Hunting and other forms of over-exploitation are among the specific causes of the current biodiversity crisis.
Invasive alien species

A species carried by human activity to a region outside its natural range, where it establishes, spreads and harms native species by predation, competition or disease. Global transport, for example in ships' ballast water or with traded goods, spreads invasive alien species and also pests and diseases; this spread is one of the specific causes of the biodiversity crisis.
In situ conservation

Conservation of species in their natural habitats, for example through the management of nature reserves. It keeps species within the ecological interactions and selection pressures of their own environment and conserves the habitat along with the species. Management is active: controlling invasive species, regulating grazing or fire, and maintaining corridors between reserves.
Ex situ conservation

Conservation of species away from their natural habitat, in zoos, botanic gardens and seed or tissue banks. It protects individuals and germ plasm from threats in the wild and allows captive breeding for reintroduction, but it does not conserve the habitat, holds limited genetic diversity and cannot by itself secure a species' future.
Rewilding

Restoring natural processes to an area so that the ecosystem becomes self-sustaining with less need for continuing management, often by reintroducing species that had been lost, such as large herbivores or predators, and by removing barriers to their movement.
Reclamation of degraded ecosystems

Restoring an ecosystem that has been damaged or destroyed, for example by replanting cleared forest, re-flooding drained wetland or removing pollutants from a river, so that native communities can re-establish.
Germ plasm

Living genetic material, such as seeds, pollen, spores, cultured tissue, sperm, eggs or embryos, stored so that a species' genes are preserved. Seed banks store dried seeds at low temperature; tissue banks store cultured tissue or frozen cells, and are needed for species whose seeds cannot survive drying and freezing. Different species therefore require different measures.
EDGE of Existence programme

A conservation programme, run by the Zoological Society of London, that prioritizes species which are both Evolutionarily Distinct and Globally Endangered. The rationale is that losing a species with few close living relatives removes a disproportionate amount of unique evolutionary history from the tree of life, and that such species are often overlooked by conservation focused on well-known animals.
Evolutionary distinctiveness

A measure of how much unique evolutionary history a species represents, based on the length of the branches of the phylogenetic tree that it shares with few or no other living species. A species with no close living relatives, such as the aye-aye, has high evolutionary distinctiveness; a species in a large group of close relatives has low. It is not a measure of how old or how 'primitive' a species is.
Global endangerment

A species' risk of extinction, taken in the EDGE programme from its IUCN Red List category, from Least Concern through Near Threatened, Vulnerable and Endangered to Critically Endangered. Combining it with evolutionary distinctiveness gives the EDGE priority; deciding which species to prioritize also has ethical, political, social, cultural and economic implications that need to be debated (NOS).
Covalent bond

A chemical bond in which two atoms share a pair of electrons, each atom contributing one electron to the shared pair. Covalent bonds are strong, so the carbon skeletons of biological molecules are stable; they hold the atoms of a single molecule together, in contrast to the weaker intermolecular attractions such as hydrogen bonds.
Bonding of carbon

A carbon atom has four electrons in its outer shell and forms up to four covalent bonds, either as four single bonds or as a combination of single and double bonds, with other carbon atoms or with atoms of other non-metallic elements such as hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus. Because carbon–carbon bonds can be repeated indefinitely, carbon compounds can be unbranched chains (fatty acids), branched chains (amylopectin, glycogen), single rings (glucose, ribose) or multiple rings (steroids, the purine bases adenine and guanine), which is the basis of the diversity of the compounds on which life depends.
SI prefixes as international conventions

Prefixes attached to SI units to show a multiple or fraction of the unit: kilo (10³), centi (10⁻²), milli (10⁻³), micro (10⁻⁶) and nano (10⁻⁹). Their meanings are not facts discovered about nature but conventions fixed by international agreement, so that a measurement such as 7 µm has the same meaning to every scientist regardless of language or country (a nature-of-science point).
Monomer, polymer and macromolecule

A monomer is a small molecule that can be linked to others of the same kind; a polymer is a large molecule made of many monomers joined by covalent bonds; a macromolecule is any very large molecule. Polysaccharides, polypeptides and nucleic acids are polymers, and therefore macromolecules. Lipids such as triglycerides are large but are not polymers, because they are built from a fixed small number of different components rather than from a repeating monomer.
Condensation reaction

A reaction in which two molecules are joined by a covalent bond with the release of a water molecule, formed from an -OH group of one molecule and an -H from the other. Monomers are linked into polymers by repeated condensation reactions, each forming one bond and releasing one water molecule, so joining n monomers into a chain releases n − 1 water molecules. Condensation reactions in cells are catalysed by enzymes.
Polysaccharide, polypeptide and nucleic acid

The three classes of biological polymer produced by condensation. Polysaccharides (starch, glycogen, cellulose) are polymers of monosaccharides linked by glycosidic bonds; polypeptides are polymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds; nucleic acids (DNA and RNA) are polymers of nucleotides linked by covalent bonds between the phosphate of one nucleotide and the sugar of the next.
Hydrolysis reaction

A reaction in which a covalent bond between two parts of a molecule is broken by the addition of water: the water molecule is split, and the -H is added to one product and the -OH to the other, which is why the reaction is named hydrolysis ("splitting with water"). Digestion breaks polymers into monomers by enzyme-catalysed hydrolysis, so hydrolysing a chain of n monomers uses n − 1 water molecules. Hydrolysis is the reverse of condensation.
Monosaccharide (pentose and hexose)

A single sugar unit, the monomer of polysaccharides. Monosaccharides are classified by the number of carbon atoms they contain: a pentose has five (ribose and deoxyribose) and a hexose has six (glucose, fructose and galactose). In molecular diagrams they are usually drawn in ring form, in which one oxygen atom forms part of the ring and one or more carbon atoms lie outside it, so the class is found by counting all the carbon atoms, in and outside the ring, not by counting the atoms that make up the ring.
Properties of glucose in relation to its use

Glucose (a hexose) is the main respiratory substrate and transport sugar in many organisms because of four properties: it is soluble in water, since its polar hydroxyl (-OH) groups form hydrogen bonds with water; it is therefore transportable, dissolved in blood plasma or other fluids; it is chemically stable, so it does not break down during transport or storage unless enzymes act on it; and its oxidation in cell respiration to carbon dioxide and water yields a large amount of energy.
Starch

The energy storage polysaccharide of plants, a polymer of alpha-glucose made of amylose (unbranched chains that coil into a helix) and amylopectin (chains with occasional branches). Coiling and branching make starch compact, so much glucose is stored in a small volume; its large molecular size makes it relatively insoluble, so it has no osmotic effect on the cell; and alpha-glucose monomers can be added by condensation or removed by hydrolysis at chain ends with relative ease, so the store can be built up or mobilized as needed.
Glycogen

The energy storage polysaccharide of animals (and fungi), a polymer of alpha-glucose similar to amylopectin but more frequently branched. Its branching makes it compact and provides many chain ends at which glucose can be added by condensation or removed by hydrolysis at the same time, allowing rapid mobilization; its large size makes it relatively insoluble, so glycogen granules in liver and muscle cells do not disturb the cell's osmotic balance.
Alpha-glucose and beta-glucose

Two forms (isomers) of glucose with the same molecular formula, C₆H₁₂O₆, that differ only in the orientation of the hydroxyl group on carbon atom 1 in the ring form: below the plane of the ring in alpha-glucose and above it in beta-glucose. Starch and glycogen are polymers of alpha-glucose; cellulose is a polymer of beta-glucose, and this small difference determines whether the polymer coils and branches or forms straight chains.
Cellulose

The structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls, an unbranched polymer of beta-glucose. Because of the orientation of the hydroxyl group on carbon 1 of beta-glucose, each successive monomer is rotated 180° relative to its neighbours, so the chain is straight rather than coiled. Straight chains lie side by side and are grouped into bundles (microfibrils) cross-linked by many hydrogen bonds between chains, giving cellulose the high tensile strength that lets the cell wall resist the pressure of the cell contents.
Glycoprotein

A protein with one or more carbohydrate chains covalently attached. Glycoproteins in the plasma membrane have their carbohydrate part projecting outwards from the cell surface, where the particular sequence of sugars acts as a marker that other cells and the immune system can recognize, so glycoproteins are the basis of cell–cell recognition, including the recognition of cells as belonging to the organism itself.
ABO antigens

Glycoproteins (and glycolipids) on the surface of red blood cells whose carbohydrate chains determine a person's ABO blood group. The A antigen and the B antigen share the same base chain and differ only in the monosaccharide added at its end, by an enzyme encoded by the person's ABO alleles. Group A cells carry the A antigen, group B cells the B antigen, group AB cells both; group O cells carry the unmodified base chain and neither the A nor the B antigen, so there is no separate "O antigen". Recognition of these antigens by antibodies is why transfused blood must be matched.
Lipid

A substance in living organisms that dissolves in non-polar solvents but is only sparingly soluble in aqueous (water-based) solvents. Lipids are defined by this solubility rather than by a single structure, and include fats (triglycerides that are solid at about 20°C), oils (triglycerides that are liquid at that temperature), waxes and steroids.
Hydrophobic

Describes a molecule or region of a molecule that does not dissolve in or associate with water. Lipids are hydrophobic because they consist mostly of carbon and hydrogen atoms joined by non-polar covalent bonds, with few or no polar groups able to form hydrogen bonds with water; water molecules hydrogen-bond to one another and the non-polar molecules are excluded, so they cluster together. Lipids are not insoluble because they are large: a triglyceride is far smaller than a soluble protein.
Triglyceride

A lipid formed when one glycerol molecule is linked by condensation reactions to three fatty acid molecules. Each of the three hydroxyl groups of glycerol reacts with the carboxyl group of a fatty acid to form an ester bond and release a water molecule, so three water molecules are released in total. Fats and oils are triglycerides. A triglyceride is not a polymer, because it is made from a fixed number of components rather than a chain of repeating monomers.
Phospholipid

A lipid formed by condensation reactions in which one glycerol molecule is linked to two fatty acid molecules and one phosphate group. The two fatty acid tails are hydrophobic and the phosphate head is hydrophilic, so the molecule is amphipathic and forms the bilayers of cell membranes.
Saturated, monounsaturated and polyunsaturated fatty acids

Fatty acids are classified by the number of carbon–carbon double bonds (C=C) in their hydrocarbon chain: a saturated fatty acid has none (every carbon carries as many hydrogen atoms as it can), a monounsaturated fatty acid has one and a polyunsaturated fatty acid has two or more. The C=O double bond of the carboxyl group is present in every fatty acid and does not count towards unsaturation.
Effect of C=C double bonds on melting point

Each C=C double bond puts a kink in the hydrocarbon chain of a fatty acid, so molecules of unsaturated fatty acids and the triglycerides made from them cannot pack closely together; the intermolecular attractions between them are weaker and the melting point is lower. Saturated chains are straight, pack closely and melt at higher temperatures. Plants, which are at environmental temperature, store energy as oils rich in unsaturated fatty acids that remain liquid when it is cool; endotherms, which maintain a high, constant body temperature, store fats with a higher proportion of saturated fatty acids, which are solid at room temperature but sufficiently fluid at body temperature.
Triglycerides as long-term energy stores

Triglycerides stored in adipose tissue suit long-term energy storage because they release about twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates when oxidized, they are insoluble so they can be stored in large amounts without osmotic effects and without the water that accompanies glycogen, and they are chemically stable. Glycogen is used for shorter-term storage from which glucose can be mobilized quickly.
Triglycerides as thermal insulators

Adipose tissue beneath the skin is a poor conductor of heat, so it slows the loss of heat from the body to the surroundings. It is valuable to endotherms, which maintain a body temperature above that of their habitat: the colder the habitat relative to body temperature, the thicker the layer that is useful, as in the blubber of seals and whales in polar seas. The insulating layer is not the source of the heat it retains, which comes from the animal's metabolism, and it is of little use for retaining heat in ectotherms, whose body temperature is close to that of their surroundings.
Amphipathic

Describes a molecule that has both a hydrophilic (water-attracting) region and a hydrophobic (water-excluded) region. A phospholipid is amphipathic: its phosphate head is hydrophilic and its two fatty acid tails are hydrophobic. The term does not mean that the molecule is both an acid and a base.
Phospholipid bilayer

The double layer of phospholipids that forms the basis of all cell membranes. In water, amphipathic phospholipids spontaneously arrange themselves so that the hydrophilic heads face the water on both surfaces and the hydrophobic tails face inwards, away from water, forming the interior of the bilayer. The arrangement forms and is maintained because the tails are excluded from water, not because phospholipids are covalently bonded to one another, so the bilayer is stable yet fluid.
Steroid

A lipid whose molecules are built on four fused rings of carbon atoms, three six-membered and one five-membered, which is how a steroid is recognized in a molecular diagram. Steroids are non-polar (hydrophobic), so they can pass through the hydrophobic interior of a phospholipid bilayer by simple diffusion and reach receptors inside cells.
Oestradiol and testosterone

Steroid hormones, both built on the four fused carbon rings that characterize steroids: oestradiol is the main oestrogen and testosterone the main androgen. Being non-polar steroids, they diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer of their target cells and bind to receptors inside the cell, unlike protein hormones, which cannot cross the bilayer.
Amino acid (generalized structure)

The monomer from which polypeptides are built. Every amino acid has a central alpha carbon atom to which four things are bonded: an amine group (–NH₂), a carboxyl group (–COOH), a hydrogen atom and an R-group. The amine group, carboxyl group and hydrogen are the same in every amino acid; only the R-group differs.
Alpha carbon

The central carbon atom of an amino acid, which carries the amine group, the carboxyl group, a hydrogen atom and the R-group. Because the amine and carboxyl groups are on the same carbon, the alpha carbon becomes part of the repeating backbone of a polypeptide when amino acids are linked.
R-group

The variable side group attached to the alpha carbon of an amino acid. Each of the 20 amino acids coded for in the genetic code has a different R-group, and it is the R-group alone that distinguishes one amino acid from another.
Amine group and carboxyl group

The two functional groups present in every amino acid. The amine group (–NH₂) is a nitrogen atom bonded to the alpha carbon and to two hydrogen atoms; the carboxyl group (–COOH) is a carbon atom bonded to the alpha carbon, double-bonded to one oxygen and bonded to a hydroxyl group. The amine group can bind a hydrogen ion to become –NH₃⁺ and the carboxyl group can dissociate to –COO⁻.
Condensation reaction (amino acids)

The reaction that links two amino acids: the carboxyl group of one reacts with the amine group of the other, forming a peptide bond and releasing one molecule of water. Word equation: amino acid + amino acid → dipeptide + water. Repeating the reaction adds further amino acids one at a time, so a chain of n amino acids is formed with the release of n − 1 water molecules.
Peptide bond

The covalent bond formed by a condensation reaction between the carbon of the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the nitrogen of the amine group of the next. In a polypeptide the peptide bonds join the alpha carbons into a continuous backbone; the R-groups project from the backbone and are not part of the bond.
Dipeptide

Two amino acids linked by a single peptide bond. A generalized dipeptide has a free amine group at one end, a free carboxyl group at the other end, two alpha carbons each carrying a hydrogen and an R-group, and the peptide bond (–CO–NH–) between them.
Essential amino acid

An amino acid that cannot be synthesized in the body and must therefore be obtained from protein in food. A diet that lacks any essential amino acid limits the synthesis of proteins that contain it, however much other protein is eaten.
The 20 coded amino acids

The 20 different amino acids that are coded for in the genetic code and assembled into polypeptides by ribosomes. Because a peptide chain can contain any number of amino acids, from a few to thousands, and the amino acids can be in any order, the number of possible different polypeptides is effectively infinite: for a chain of n amino acids there are 20ⁿ possible sequences.
Polypeptide

A chain of many amino acids linked by peptide bonds. Examples span a wide range of lengths: the two chains of insulin have 21 and 30 amino acids (51 in total); lysozyme, an enzyme in tears and egg white, has 129; the alpha and beta chains of haemoglobin have 141 and 146; each polypeptide of collagen has around 1000; and titin, a muscle protein, has more than 30 000. A protein consists of one or more polypeptides.
Denaturation

A change in the three-dimensional shape (conformation) of a protein caused by high temperature or by a pH away from the range the protein is adapted to, so that the protein can no longer carry out its function. Heat makes the molecule vibrate more strongly, breaking the weak bonds that hold the folded shape; a change in pH alters the charges on the protein and so disrupts the bonds that depend on them. Peptide bonds are not broken, so the amino acid sequence is unchanged, but the change of shape is in most cases permanent.
Hydrophobic R-group

A non-polar R-group that does not form hydrogen bonds with water and is therefore not attracted to it. In an aqueous environment, amino acids with hydrophobic R-groups tend to be positioned away from water. Because R-groups determine the properties of assembled polypeptides, the pattern of hydrophobic and hydrophilic R-groups along a chain largely decides how it folds.
Hydrophilic R-group (polar or charged; acidic or basic)

An R-group that is attracted to water. Hydrophilic R-groups are either polar but uncharged, forming hydrogen bonds with water, or charged. Charged R-groups are acidic, if they contain a carboxyl group that can dissociate to release a hydrogen ion and become negatively charged, or basic, if they contain an amine group that can bind a hydrogen ion and become positively charged.
Primary structure

The sequence of amino acids in a polypeptide, from the amine end to the carboxyl end, held together by peptide bonds. The primary structure determines every higher level of structure: the identity and precise position of each amino acid decides where the chain can coil, pleat and fold, and which R-groups end up close enough to bond.
Conformation

The three-dimensional shape adopted by a protein. Because it is determined by the amino acid sequence, the conformation of a given protein is precise, predictable and repeatable: every molecule of a protein with the same primary structure folds into the same shape, despite the complexity of that shape.
Secondary structure

Regular coiling or pleating of parts of a polypeptide chain, stabilized by hydrogen bonds at regular positions between the C=O group of one peptide bond and the N–H group of another in the backbone. The R-groups are not involved. The two main forms are the alpha helix and the beta-pleated sheet, and a single polypeptide may contain both, joined by less regular regions.
Alpha helix

A secondary structure in which the polypeptide backbone is coiled into a right-handed spiral, held by hydrogen bonds between the C=O group of each peptide bond and the N–H group of the peptide bond four amino acids further along the chain. The R-groups project outwards from the helix.
Beta-pleated sheet

A secondary structure in which two or more lengths of polypeptide (strands) lie side by side and are held together by hydrogen bonds between the C=O and N–H groups of the backbones of neighbouring strands, giving a pleated sheet with the R-groups projecting above and below it.
Tertiary structure

The overall three-dimensional folding of a whole polypeptide, including its regions of secondary structure, into its functional conformation. It is held by interactions between R-groups that the folding brings close together: hydrogen bonds between polar R-groups, ionic bonds between oppositely charged R-groups, disulfide covalent bonds between pairs of cysteines, and hydrophobic interactions between non-polar R-groups.
Disulfide bond

A covalent bond formed between the sulfur atoms of the R-groups of two cysteines that lie close together in the folded polypeptide (or in two different polypeptides). It is much stronger than the other interactions that hold tertiary structure and is not broken by moderate heating or by changes in pH, but it can be broken by reducing agents.
Ionic bond (in protein structure)

An attraction between a positively charged and a negatively charged R-group. Amine groups in R-groups become positively charged by binding hydrogen ions and carboxyl groups in R-groups become negatively charged by dissociation of hydrogen ions; the charged groups can then form ionic bonds. Because the charges depend on the binding and release of hydrogen ions, a change in pH can remove them and break the ionic bonds.
Hydrophobic interaction

The association of non-polar R-groups with one another away from water. Water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other rather than to non-polar groups, so non-polar R-groups are excluded from the water and end up packed together; this helps hold the tertiary structure of a protein in an aqueous environment.
Hydrophobic core of a globular protein

In a protein that is soluble in water, the amino acids with hydrophobic R-groups are clustered in the centre of the folded molecule, away from the surrounding water, while amino acids with hydrophilic R-groups are mainly on the surface, where they interact with water and keep the protein in solution.
Integral protein

A protein embedded in a membrane. It has one or more regions in which the amino acids have hydrophobic R-groups; these regions sit within the hydrophobic centre of the phospholipid bilayer and anchor the protein in the membrane, while regions with hydrophilic R-groups project into the aqueous solution on either side.
Quaternary structure

The association of two or more polypeptides, each with its own tertiary structure, into a single functional protein. The polypeptides are held together by the same kinds of interaction as tertiary structure. Insulin (two polypeptides linked by disulfide bonds) and collagen (three polypeptides wound around each other) have quaternary structure; a protein made of a single polypeptide does not.
Conjugated and non-conjugated proteins

A conjugated protein contains one or more non-polypeptide components (prosthetic groups) in addition to its polypeptides: haemoglobin is conjugated because each of its four polypeptides carries a haem group, which is not made of amino acids and contains an iron ion. A non-conjugated protein consists of polypeptides only: insulin and collagen are non-conjugated proteins.
Cryogenic electron microscopy (NOS)

A technique in which a sample is frozen very rapidly and imaged with an electron microscope, allowing the structure of single protein molecules, and of proteins interacting with other molecules, to be worked out. It illustrates that technology allows the imaging of structures that would be impossible to observe with the unaided senses, and so extends what can be known.
Globular protein

A protein whose polypeptide(s) fold into a compact, rounded shape. Globular proteins are generally soluble in water, with hydrophilic R-groups on the surface, and their precise three-dimensional shape lets them bind specifically to other molecules: insulin is a globular protein whose shape allows it to bind to insulin receptors on target cells, so that it can act as a hormone carried in the blood.
Fibrous protein

A protein with a long, narrow, elongated shape. Fibrous proteins are generally insoluble in water and have structural roles: collagen consists of three polypeptides wound together into a rope-like triple helix, and many collagen molecules are linked into fibres that give tendons, ligaments, skin and bone high tensile strength.
Phospholipid

A lipid made of a glycerol molecule linked to two fatty acid chains and a phosphate group. The phosphate head is hydrophilic and the two hydrocarbon tails are hydrophobic, so the molecule is amphipathic. Phospholipids are the main lipid of cell membranes.
Amphipathic

Describes a molecule that has both a hydrophilic (water-attracting) region and a hydrophobic (water-repelling) region. Phospholipids and other amphipathic lipids naturally arrange themselves in water so that their hydrophilic parts face the water and their hydrophobic parts are kept away from it.
Lipid bilayer

A continuous sheet two molecules thick that phospholipids and other amphipathic lipids form spontaneously in water. The hydrophilic heads of both layers face the aqueous solutions on either side and the hydrophobic tails point inwards, forming a hydrophobic core. The bilayer is held together by hydrophobic interactions and other weak forces, not by covalent bonds between the lipids, and is the basis of all cell membranes.
Hydrophobic core

The central region of a membrane, formed by the hydrocarbon chains of the fatty acids of the two layers of phospholipids. Because it contains no water and no charges, it has low permeability to large molecules and to hydrophilic particles such as ions and polar molecules.
Membrane permeability

The ease with which a particular substance can cross a membrane. A pure lipid bilayer is readily permeable to small non-polar molecules, only slightly permeable to small polar molecules such as water, and almost impermeable to ions and large polar molecules, so it functions as an effective barrier between the aqueous solutions on its two sides.
Simple diffusion

The net movement of particles from a region of higher concentration to a region of lower concentration as a result of their random movement, without any transport protein and without energy from ATP. Oxygen and carbon dioxide are small non-polar molecules that cross membranes by simple diffusion, passing between the phospholipids of the bilayer.
Integral protein

A membrane protein that is embedded in the lipid bilayer, in one of the two lipid layers or spanning both. The part of the protein within the bilayer has hydrophobic amino acid R-groups on its surface, which interact with the hydrocarbon tails. Integral proteins include channels, pumps, receptors and enzymes.
Peripheral protein

A membrane protein that is not embedded in the hydrophobic core but is attached to one or other surface of the bilayer, either to the hydrophilic heads of phospholipids or to the exposed part of an integral protein. Peripheral proteins are found on both the cytoplasmic and the extracellular faces of membranes.
Osmosis

The net movement of water molecules across a membrane that is permeable to water but not to the solute, from a solution with a lower solute concentration to a solution with a higher solute concentration. Water molecules move randomly in both directions; the net movement arises because the side with the lower solute concentration has a higher proportion of free water molecules, so more water molecules cross from that side than return.
Aquaporin

An integral membrane channel protein with a narrow pore that allows water molecules, but not ions or other solutes, to pass through. Aquaporins greatly increase the permeability of a membrane to water, so cells that must move water rapidly by osmosis, such as some kidney tubule cells, have many aquaporins in their membranes.
Facilitated diffusion

The passive movement of particles across a membrane, down their concentration gradient, through a channel protein or carrier protein. It requires no energy from ATP, but because each protein allows only a specific particle through, it makes the membrane selectively permeable to that particle.
Channel protein

An integral protein with a central pore through which specific ions or other hydrophilic particles diffuse across the membrane. The diameter of the pore and the charges on the amino acids lining it determine which particle can pass. Many channels are gated: they can be open or closed, and ions diffuse through only when the channel is open.
Active transport

The movement of specific particles across a membrane against their concentration gradient, using energy released by the hydrolysis of ATP. It is carried out by pump proteins and stops if the cell can no longer supply ATP.
Pump protein

An integral membrane protein that uses energy from ATP to change its shape and so transfer a specific particle from one side of the membrane to the other. Because energy is supplied, a pump can move its particle from a lower to a higher concentration, which no form of diffusion can do.
Selective permeability

The property of a membrane that allows some substances to cross while others cannot. Selectivity comes from the transport proteins: each channel, carrier or pump handles specific particles, so facilitated diffusion and active transport are selective. Permeability by simple diffusion is not selective; it depends only on the size of a particle and on whether it is hydrophobic or hydrophilic.
Glycoprotein

A membrane protein with a carbohydrate chain covalently attached. The carbohydrate part is always on the extracellular side of the plasma membrane, where it takes part in cell recognition and cell adhesion.
Glycolipid

A membrane lipid with a carbohydrate chain covalently attached to its hydrophilic head. Like the carbohydrate of glycoproteins, the carbohydrate of a glycolipid projects from the extracellular surface of the plasma membrane and contributes to cell recognition and cell adhesion.
Cell recognition and cell adhesion (roles of membrane carbohydrates)

The two roles of the carbohydrate chains of glycoproteins and glycolipids. In cell recognition, the pattern of carbohydrates on a cell surface identifies the cell, for example as belonging to the organism's own body. In cell adhesion, carbohydrates and proteins on adjacent cells bind to each other, helping to hold cells together.
Fluid mosaic model

The accepted model of membrane structure: a phospholipid bilayer in which phospholipids and proteins can move laterally (fluid), with integral and peripheral proteins scattered irregularly through and on the bilayer (mosaic). A two-dimensional drawing shows the bilayer with hydrophilic heads outwards and hydrophobic tails inwards, integral proteins embedded in it, peripheral proteins on its surfaces, glycoproteins with carbohydrate on the extracellular side and cholesterol between the phospholipids.
Hydrophilic and hydrophobic regions of a membrane

The hydrophilic regions are the two surfaces of the membrane, formed by the phosphate heads of the phospholipids, which face the aqueous cytoplasm on one side and the aqueous extracellular fluid on the other. The hydrophobic region is the core, formed by the hydrocarbon tails of both layers. Membrane proteins likewise have hydrophobic regions where they contact the core and hydrophilic regions where they contact water.
Membrane fluidity

The freedom with which the phospholipids and proteins of a membrane move within the plane of the bilayer. Fluidity depends on temperature and on the composition of the membrane, and must be maintained for membranes to be flexible, to allow vesicles to form and fuse, and for membrane proteins to function.
Unsaturated fatty acid (in membranes)

A fatty acid with one or more double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain, which put a kink in the chain so that neighbouring phospholipids cannot pack closely. Lipids rich in unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points, so a bilayer containing them stays fluid and therefore flexible at the temperatures a cell experiences, including low temperatures.
Saturated fatty acid (in membranes)

A fatty acid with no double bonds in its hydrocarbon chain, so the chain is straight and neighbouring phospholipids pack closely together. Lipids rich in saturated fatty acids have higher melting points, so they make a membrane stronger and less fluid, which is an advantage at higher temperatures. Organisms adjust the ratio of saturated to unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes to suit the temperature of their habitat: for example, fish living in cold water have a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids in their membranes than related fish in warm water.
Cholesterol (in membranes)

A steroid lipid found in animal cell membranes, positioned between the phospholipids with its small hydrophilic hydroxyl group next to the phosphate heads and its rigid hydrophobic ring structure and hydrocarbon tail among the fatty acid tails. Cholesterol acts as a modulator (adjustor) of membrane fluidity: at higher temperatures it restricts the movement of phospholipids and so stabilizes the membrane, and at lower temperatures it prevents the fatty acid tails from packing closely and so prevents the membrane from stiffening.
Endocytosis

The process in which a region of the plasma membrane surrounds material outside the cell and pinches off to form a vesicle inside the cell. It requires ATP and depends on the fluidity of the membrane. Examples are the engulfing of a bacterium by a phagocytic white blood cell and the uptake of droplets of extracellular fluid.
Exocytosis

The process in which a vesicle inside the cell moves to the plasma membrane and fuses with it, releasing the contents of the vesicle outside the cell. It requires ATP and depends on the fluidity of the membrane, which allows the vesicle membrane to merge with the plasma membrane. Examples are the secretion of digestive enzymes by pancreatic cells and the release of neurotransmitter from a neuron at a synapse.
Vesicle

A small sac of fluid enclosed by a single membrane, formed by a region of membrane budding off from a larger membrane. Vesicles can form from and fuse with membranes only because the phospholipid bilayer is fluid and can be reshaped, rejoining as a continuous sheet after pinching off or merging.
Neurotransmitter-gated ion channel (nicotinic acetylcholine receptor)

A channel protein that opens when a specific neurotransmitter binds to it. The nicotinic acetylcholine receptor, in the membrane of a postsynaptic neuron or muscle fibre, opens its pore when two molecules of acetylcholine bind to it, allowing sodium ions to diffuse into the cell down their concentration gradient. The acetylcholine itself does not pass through the channel.
Voltage-gated ion channel

A channel protein that opens or closes in response to a change in the membrane potential rather than to the binding of a chemical. Voltage-gated sodium channels and voltage-gated potassium channels in the membrane of a neuron open when the membrane depolarizes, allowing the ions to diffuse down their concentration gradients; no ATP is used by the channels themselves.
Sodium–potassium pump

An integral protein that, for each molecule of ATP hydrolysed, moves three sodium ions out of the cell and two potassium ions into the cell, both against their concentration gradients. Binding of sodium ions inside the cell and phosphorylation by ATP change the pump's shape so that the sodium ions are released outside; binding of potassium ions outside and loss of the phosphate return it to its original shape, releasing the potassium ions inside.
Exchange transporter

A transport protein that moves one type of particle across a membrane in one direction while moving a different type in the opposite direction. The sodium–potassium pump is an exchange transporter that uses ATP to swap sodium ions for potassium ions.
Membrane potential

A difference in electrical charge between the two sides of a membrane. In a resting neuron the inside of the membrane is negative relative to the outside. Sodium–potassium pumps are important in generating this potential: they move three positive sodium ions out for every two positive potassium ions in, and they maintain the concentration gradients of the two ions on which the potential depends.
Sodium-dependent glucose cotransporter

A membrane protein that binds a sodium ion and a glucose molecule on the outside of the cell and transfers both to the inside. The sodium ion moves down its concentration gradient and the energy this releases carries glucose against its concentration gradient. These cotransporters absorb glucose from the lumen of the small intestine into the epithelial cells and reabsorb glucose from the filtrate into the cells lining the nephron.
Indirect active transport

Movement of a particle against its concentration gradient that is driven not by ATP directly but by the movement of a second particle down a gradient that was itself established by an ATP-using pump. In sodium-dependent glucose cotransport, the sodium gradient is maintained by sodium–potassium pumps, so ATP is used, but only indirectly.
Cell-adhesion molecule (CAM)

A membrane protein that binds to a cell-adhesion molecule on the surface of an adjacent cell, holding the two cells together so that they can form a tissue. Different forms of CAM are used to build the different types of cell–cell junction.
Organelle

A discrete subunit of a cell that is adapted to perform a specific function. Organelles include the nucleus, mitochondria, chloroplasts, vesicles, ribosomes and the plasma membrane; an organelle may or may not be bounded by a membrane. The cell wall, the cytoskeleton and the cytoplasm are not considered organelles.
Cytoskeleton

The network of protein filaments and microtubules that runs through the cytoplasm, giving the cell its shape and moving organelles and chromosomes. Although it has clear functions, it is a continuous framework rather than a discrete subunit, so, like the cytoplasm and the cell wall, it is not considered an organelle.
Cell fractionation

The separation of the components of cells so that the function of each type of organelle can be studied on its own. Cells are broken open in a cold, isotonic, buffered solution and the homogenate is spun in an ultracentrifuge at a series of increasing speeds: larger, denser organelles such as nuclei form a pellet at lower speeds, and smaller ones such as ribosomes only at very high speeds. Study of the function of individual organelles became possible once ultracentrifuges had been invented and these methods developed, an example of progress in science following the development of a new technique.
Nucleus as a separate compartment

The nucleus holds the DNA of a eukaryotic cell inside a double membrane, and functional ribosomes are found only in the cytoplasm (ribosomal subunits are assembled in the nucleolus but join into working ribosomes only after leaving the nucleus). Transcription therefore takes place in the nucleus and translation in the cytoplasm, so newly transcribed mRNA does not meet ribosomes until it has left the nucleus, and it can be modified before that happens.
Post-transcriptional modification

Changes made to mRNA in the nucleus after transcription and before translation, for example the removal of some sections of the RNA and the addition of protective groups at its ends. It is possible in eukaryotes because the nuclear membrane keeps new mRNA away from ribosomes. In prokaryotes, which have no nucleus, this is not possible: mRNA may meet ribosomes immediately and be translated while it is still being transcribed.
Compartmentalization

The division of the cytoplasm of a eukaryotic cell into membrane-bound compartments such as organelles and vesicles. Its advantages include concentrating the enzymes and metabolites of a process together in a small volume, so that reactions proceed rapidly, and separating biochemical processes that are incompatible with each other, for example keeping hydrolytic enzymes inside lysosomes apart from the rest of the cytoplasm.
Lysosome

A small membrane-bound vesicle containing hydrolytic enzymes at a concentration far higher than could safely exist in the cytoplasm, together with the conditions those enzymes need. Lysosomes fuse with phagocytic vacuoles to digest their contents and also break down damaged organelles; the lysosome membrane keeps the enzymes from hydrolysing the cell's own structures.
Phagocytic vacuole

A vacuole formed when a cell engulfs material such as a bacterium or a food particle by endocytosis. Lysosomes fuse with the phagocytic vacuole, delivering hydrolytic enzymes at high concentration into a compartment where they digest the contents without acting on the rest of the cell; the products of digestion are then absorbed into the cytoplasm.
Cristae

The folds of the inner mitochondrial membrane, which greatly increase its surface area. The inner membrane holds the electron transport chain and ATP synthase, so the large area of the cristae allows a mitochondrion to carry out oxidative phosphorylation at a high rate.
Intermembrane space

The narrow compartment between the outer and inner membranes of a mitochondrion. The electron transport chain pumps protons into it from the matrix; because its volume is small, a relatively small number of protons produces a steep concentration gradient across the inner membrane, which drives ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis.
Mitochondrial matrix

The fluid enclosed by the inner mitochondrial membrane. The enzymes and substrates of the link reaction and the Krebs cycle are compartmentalized in the matrix at high concentration, so these reactions proceed rapidly, and the reduced NAD they produce is generated close to the electron transport chain in the inner membrane.
Thylakoid

A flattened, membrane-bound sac inside a chloroplast, arranged in stacks called grana. The thylakoid membranes have a large total surface area and hold the photosystems and electron carriers of the light-dependent reactions; the small volume of fluid inside each thylakoid allows a proton gradient to build up quickly for ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis.
Stroma

The fluid surrounding the thylakoids inside a chloroplast. The enzymes and substrates of the Calvin cycle are compartmentalized in the stroma, where the ATP and reduced NADP produced by the thylakoid membranes are used to fix carbon dioxide and produce carbohydrate.
Nuclear envelope

The double membrane that bounds the nucleus, consisting of two phospholipid bilayers. It separates transcription from translation, is perforated by nuclear pores that allow selected materials to pass between nucleus and cytoplasm, and breaks into vesicles during mitosis and meiosis so that spindle microtubules can attach to and move the chromosomes, re-forming around each set of chromosomes afterwards.
Nuclear pore

A channel that passes through both membranes of the nuclear envelope. Large molecules cannot cross the phospholipid bilayers themselves, so pores are needed to allow mRNA and ribosomal subunits to leave the nucleus and to allow proteins such as polymerases and histones, and the nucleotides needed for replication and transcription, to enter it.
Free ribosome

A ribosome in the cytoplasm that is not attached to a membrane. Free ribosomes synthesise proteins that are retained in the cell, such as the enzymes of glycolysis and other proteins that function in the cytoplasm or the nucleus.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum

A network of flattened membrane sacs, continuous with the outer membrane of the nuclear envelope, with ribosomes bound to its cytoplasmic surface. Polypeptides made by these membrane-bound ribosomes pass into the lumen of the rough ER, from which they are carried in vesicles to the Golgi apparatus. These are proteins for transport within the cell, for insertion into membranes, or for secretion from the cell.
Golgi apparatus

A stack of flattened membrane sacs (cisternae) that receives protein from the rough endoplasmic reticulum in vesicles, processes it, for example by modifying the carbohydrate groups attached to it, and packages it into vesicles that bud off from the opposite face of the stack. Vesicles from the Golgi apparatus carry the protein to the plasma membrane, where it is secreted by exocytosis.
Vesicle

A small, spherical, membrane-bound sac that buds off from a membrane such as the plasma membrane, the endoplasmic reticulum or the Golgi apparatus, carries material within the cell and delivers it by fusing with another membrane. Vesicles are formed in endocytosis, transport protein from the rough ER to the Golgi apparatus and from the Golgi apparatus to the plasma membrane, and release their contents from the cell in exocytosis, when the vesicle membrane becomes part of the plasma membrane.
Clathrin

A protein that assembles into a lattice on the cytoplasmic side of a membrane, causing the membrane to bend into a coated pit that pinches off as a vesicle. The clathrin coat is shed once the vesicle has formed, so that the vesicle can fuse with its target membrane.
Differentiation

The development of an unspecialized cell into a specialized cell with a particular structure and function. The cells produced by the early divisions of the zygote are unspecialized; differentiation happens when a cell expresses some of its genes and not others, so that it makes the proteins characteristic of one cell type. The genome is not changed: every differentiated cell keeps the full set of genes but uses only part of it.
Gradient in an early-stage embryo

A concentration gradient of a signalling chemical (a morphogen) across the early embryo, produced because the chemical is made or deposited in one region and spreads out from it. A cell's position in the gradient determines the concentration it experiences, and different concentrations switch on different genes, so cells in different positions express different genes and differentiate into different cell types.
Stem cell

An undifferentiated cell that has two defining properties: it can divide endlessly, producing more cells by mitosis without exhausting its capacity to divide, and it can differentiate along different pathways to produce specialized cell types.
Stem cell niche

A specific location in a tissue of an adult where stem cells are kept, and where signals from the surrounding cells and extracellular environment control what the stem cells do. The niche can maintain the stem cells in an undifferentiated, non-dividing state, or it can promote their proliferation and their differentiation into the cell types the tissue needs.
Bone marrow stem cell niche

A niche in the red bone marrow inside bones where haematopoietic stem cells are maintained and, when signalled to, proliferate and differentiate to replace the blood cells (erythrocytes, white blood cells and platelet-producing cells) that are continually lost. It is one of the two example locations of adult stem cell niches used in this topic.
Hair follicle stem cell niche

A niche in the bulge region of a hair follicle, below the skin surface, where stem cells are kept in a maintained state between hair growth cycles. When a new hair begins to grow, or the follicle is damaged, niche signals promote proliferation of the stem cells and their differentiation into the cells that build the new hair and its sheath.
Totipotent stem cell

A stem cell that can differentiate into any cell type of the organism, including the extra-embryonic cells that form the placenta and membranes around the embryo. The zygote and the cells of the very early embryo, up to the first few divisions, are totipotent.
Pluripotent stem cell

A stem cell that can differentiate into any of the cell types of the body of the organism but not into the extra-embryonic tissues such as the placenta. Cells of an early-stage animal embryo soon lose totipotency and become pluripotent; the cells of the inner cell mass of the blastocyst are pluripotent embryonic stem cells.
Multipotent stem cell

A stem cell that can differentiate into only a limited range of cell types, typically the cell types of one tissue. Stem cells in adult tissues such as bone marrow are multipotent: bone marrow stem cells produce the different types of blood cell but not, for example, neurons or muscle.
Range of cell size in humans

Human cells vary in size by several orders of magnitude, and size is one aspect of a cell's specialization. A sperm cell has a head about 5 µm long and 3 µm wide, with a tail bringing its total length to about 50 µm; the egg cell is about 100 µm in diameter, the largest human cell by volume, because it stores cytoplasm and nutrients for the early embryo. Red blood cells are about 7–8 µm across; white blood cells are mostly larger, about 10–20 µm, although small lymphocytes are close to the size of a red blood cell. A neuron has a cell body of ordinary size but an axon that can be over a metre long, and a striated muscle fibre can be several centimetres long and 10–100 µm wide.
Surface area-to-volume ratio

The surface area of a cell divided by its volume. As the linear size of a cell increases, its surface area increases with the square of the length but its volume increases with the cube, so the ratio falls. For a cube of side L the surface area is 6L², the volume is L³ and the ratio is 6/L.
Constraint on cell size

The limit that surface area-to-volume ratio places on how large a cell can be. Exchange of materials (nutrients, oxygen, wastes, heat) across the cell surface depends on the area of that surface, whereas the need for exchange depends on the volume of cytoplasm carrying out metabolism. As a cell grows, its volume and its needs increase faster than its surface area, so beyond a certain size the surface can no longer supply the volume and the cell must stop growing, divide, or change shape.
Cube model of surface area-to-volume ratio

Cubes of different side lengths used as a simplified model of cells of different sizes. Doubling the side length multiplies the surface area by four and the volume by eight, so the ratio halves. The model is deliberately simpler than a real cell (NOS: models are simplified versions of complex systems), but the scale factors operate in the same way for any shape, so the conclusion that larger objects have smaller surface area-to-volume ratios applies to real cells.
Flattening of cells

An adaptation in which a cell is flattened so that no part of its cytoplasm is far from the surface, increasing the surface area-to-volume ratio and shortening diffusion distances. The erythrocyte is the example: it is a biconcave disc about 7–8 µm wide but only about 2 µm thick, so it has a much larger surface area than a sphere of the same volume, which speeds the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
Microvilli

Finger-like projections of the plasma membrane, each supported by cytoskeleton, that greatly increase the surface area of one face of a cell without adding much volume. Cells of the proximal convoluted tubule of the nephron have dense microvilli (a brush border) on the surface facing the tubule lumen, increasing the area of membrane available for reabsorbing glucose, ions, water and other useful substances from the filtrate.
Invagination

Infolding of the plasma membrane into the cell, which increases the surface area without increasing the volume. Cells of the proximal convoluted tubule have deep invaginations of the membrane on their basal side, with mitochondria packed between the folds, increasing the area of membrane through which reabsorbed substances are transported out of the cell towards the blood.
Type I pneumocyte

The extremely thin, flattened cell that forms most of the surface of the alveolar epithelium. Its thinness, with the cytoplasm stretched into a very thin layer, minimizes the distance that oxygen and carbon dioxide must diffuse between the air in the alveolus and the blood in the capillaries.
Type II pneumocyte

A thicker, roughly cuboidal cell of the alveolar epithelium whose cytoplasm contains many secretory vesicles called lamellar bodies. The lamellar bodies discharge surfactant into the alveolar lumen, so that the alveolar surface is coated with surfactant.
Tissue with more than one cell type

A tissue in which two or more differently adapted cell types are present because no single cell type could carry out the overall function of the tissue. The alveolar epithelium is the example: gas exchange needs the extreme thinness of type I pneumocytes, while surfactant secretion needs the many lamellar bodies of type II pneumocytes, and one cell could not be both extremely thin and packed with secretory vesicles.
Myofibril

A contractile structure running the length of the cytoplasm of a muscle cell or fibre, made of repeating units of overlapping protein filaments whose sliding produces contraction. Myofibrils are present in both cardiac muscle cells and striated (skeletal) muscle fibres, and give both a striated appearance.
Cardiac muscle cell

A relatively short, branched muscle cell of the heart wall containing myofibrils, usually with one nucleus (occasionally two). Cells are joined end to end where their branches meet, so that a network is formed. The hypothesis for the branching is that it lets contraction and the electrical signal that triggers it spread through the heart wall in all directions, so that the wall contracts as a coordinated unit.
Striated muscle fibre

A very long, unbranched, cylindrical unit of skeletal muscle containing many parallel myofibrils and many nuclei spread along its length. It is formed during development by the fusion of many separate cells (myoblasts). The hypothesis for its length is that a fibre spanning the length of a muscle can contract as one unit, and for its many nuclei that a single nucleus could not supply enough mRNA and protein for such a large volume of cytoplasm. Because it has one continuous plasma membrane and cytoplasm but arose from many cells, whether a striated muscle fibre is a cell or a multinucleate structure (syncytium) is a matter of debate.
Adaptations of the human sperm cell

A small, streamlined cell adapted to reach and enter the egg. It has a haploid nucleus in the head, an acrosome at the tip of the head containing enzymes that digest a path through the layers around the egg, a midpiece packed with mitochondria that supply ATP, and a long flagellum (tail) whose beating propels the cell. It has very little cytoplasm, so it is light and carries little to slow it down.
Adaptations of the human egg cell

A large, non-motile cell about 100 µm in diameter with a haploid nucleus and a large volume of cytoplasm containing stored nutrients (yolk droplets) that supply the embryo during its first divisions before it can obtain nutrients from the mother. It is surrounded by the zona pellucida, a layer of glycoproteins outside the plasma membrane that a sperm must penetrate, and it contains cortical granules beneath the membrane whose contents are released at fertilization to change the zona pellucida so that no further sperm can enter.
Gas exchange

The diffusion of gases across a surface between an organism and its environment: oxygen is taken up and carbon dioxide released by aerobic organisms, and the reverse by photosynthesizing tissue in the light. It is a vital function in all organisms, from unicellular organisms exchanging gases across the plasma membrane to large animals and plants with specialized exchange surfaces.
Surface area-to-volume ratio

The surface area of an organism or cell divided by its volume. As size increases, volume grows faster than surface area, so the ratio decreases: a cube of side 1 mm has a ratio of 6 mm⁻¹, a cube of side 2 mm a ratio of 3 mm⁻¹. A smaller ratio means less exchange surface is available to supply each unit of respiring volume, which is why larger organisms need specialized gas-exchange systems.
Diffusion distance

The distance a gas must diffuse between the exterior of an organism and the cells that use or produce it. Because the time taken for diffusion rises steeply with distance, gas exchange by diffusion alone is only adequate for small organisms; in a large organism the distance from the centre to the exterior is too great, so gases must be carried by a transport system to and from a specialized exchange surface.
Gas-exchange surface

A surface across which gases diffuse between an organism and its environment, such as the alveolar surface of a lung or the mesophyll cell surfaces bordering the air spaces of a leaf. Effective exchange surfaces are permeable to the gases, consist of a thin tissue layer so that the diffusion distance is short, are moist so that gases dissolve before crossing membranes, and have a large surface area so that much gas can cross at once.
Permeability

The property of a membrane or tissue layer that allows a substance to pass through it. A gas-exchange surface must be permeable to oxygen and carbon dioxide; both are small, non-polar molecules that pass freely through the phospholipid bilayer of the cells forming the surface, whereas a layer such as the waxy cuticle of a leaf is almost impermeable to them.
Concentration gradient

A difference in concentration of a substance between two regions. Net diffusion of oxygen across an exchange surface continues only while its concentration is higher on the outside than in the blood; if exchange were allowed to reach equilibrium, net diffusion would stop. Animals maintain the gradient by supplying fresh air or water to the outer side (ventilation) and by carrying blood continuously past the inner side through dense networks of blood vessels, so that oxygenated blood is replaced by deoxygenated blood.
Ventilation

The movement of the external medium across a gas-exchange surface so that the gas concentrations next to the surface stay close to those of the environment. Lungs are ventilated with air, which is drawn in and expelled; gills are ventilated with water, which is passed over the gill surfaces. Ventilation is distinct from gas exchange itself, which is the diffusion of gases across the surface.
Alveolus

One of the millions of tiny air sacs at the ends of the bronchioles in a mammalian lung, where gas exchange takes place. Each alveolus has a wall one cell thick, lined with a film of moisture and surrounded by an extensive capillary bed, so the diffusion distance between air and blood is very short. Together the alveoli provide a very large surface area for gas exchange.
Surfactant

A phospholipid-rich secretion from cells of the alveolar wall that forms a layer on the moist inner surface of the alveoli.
