It reduces the surface tension of the water film, which would otherwise tend to pull the walls of each small alveolus inward; this prevents the alveoli collapsing and allows them to expand easily during inspiration.
Bronchiole

One of the narrow airways formed by repeated branching of the bronchi within a mammalian lung. The branched network of bronchioles carries air to and from the alveoli at its ends; the branching allows a very large number of alveoli, and therefore a very large exchange surface, to be packed into the volume of the thorax. Gas exchange takes place across the alveolar walls, not the walls of the bronchioles.
Diaphragm

A sheet of muscle separating the thorax from the abdomen. When it contracts it flattens, increasing the volume of the thorax; when it relaxes it returns to a dome shape, decreasing the volume. In inspiration its contraction lowers the pressure in the lungs below atmospheric pressure so air flows in.
Intercostal muscles

Two layers of muscle between the ribs that act antagonistically. Contraction of the external intercostal muscles moves the ribs upward and outward, increasing the volume of the thorax during inspiration; contraction of the internal intercostal muscles moves the ribs downward and inward, decreasing the volume during forced expiration.
Abdominal muscles

The muscles of the abdominal wall, which contract during forced expiration. Their contraction raises the pressure in the abdomen and pushes the abdominal organs up against the relaxed diaphragm, so the diaphragm domes further into the thorax and the volume of the thorax decreases. They are relaxed during inspiration, when the contracting diaphragm pushes the abdominal organs downward.
Ventilation of the lungs

The cycle of inspiration and expiration that moves air into and out of the alveoli. Inspiration is active: the diaphragm and external intercostal muscles contract, the ribs rise, the thorax volume increases, pressure in the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure and air flows in. Quiet expiration is largely passive, driven by relaxation of these muscles and elastic recoil of the lungs; forced expiration uses contraction of the internal intercostal and abdominal muscles to reduce the thorax volume further. The lungs contain no skeletal muscle and cannot move air themselves.
Tidal volume
The volume of air moved into or out of the lungs in one breath during normal, relaxed breathing; typically about 0.5 dm³ in an adult at rest. It increases during exercise as breaths become deeper.
Vital capacity

The maximum volume of air that can be exhaled after the deepest possible inhalation. It is the sum of the tidal volume, the inspiratory reserve volume and the expiratory reserve volume, and is typically 3 to 5 dm³ in an adult. It is not the total volume of the lungs, because some air always remains in the lungs after a maximal exhalation.
Inspiratory reserve volume

The additional volume of air that can be inhaled after a normal tidal inhalation, measured from the top of a resting breath to the peak of the deepest possible inhalation. It does not include the tidal volume.
Expiratory reserve volume

The additional volume of air that can be exhaled after a normal tidal exhalation, measured from the bottom of a resting breath to the end of the deepest possible exhalation. It does not include the tidal volume.
Spirometer

An instrument that records the volume of air breathed in and out through a mouthpiece, producing a trace of lung volume against time. Tidal volume is read from the height of a resting breath, the reserve volumes from the extra movements above and below it when the subject inhales and exhales maximally, and vital capacity from the full excursion from deepest inhalation to deepest exhalation. Simpler measurements can be made by exhaling into a bag or through a tube into an inverted, water-filled container.
Waxy cuticle

A layer of wax secreted by the epidermal cells onto the outer surface of a leaf. It is impermeable to water and almost impermeable to gases, so it reduces water loss from the leaf surface; gases enter and leave the leaf through the stomata rather than across the cuticle.
Epidermis

The single layer of closely packed cells covering the upper and lower surfaces of a leaf. It protects the tissues inside, secretes the waxy cuticle and, in most dicotyledonous leaves, contains most of the stomata on its lower surface. Its cells are usually transparent and lack chloroplasts, apart from the guard cells.
Spongy mesophyll

The layer of loosely packed, irregularly shaped photosynthetic cells in the lower part of a leaf, separated by interconnected air spaces that open to the stomata. The moist surfaces of the mesophyll cells bordering the air spaces form the gas-exchange surface of the leaf: carbon dioxide dissolves and diffuses into the cells and oxygen diffuses out. The air spaces give the leaf a very large internal surface area and let gases reach the palisade cells above.
Stoma and guard cells

A stoma is a pore in the epidermis, bordered by a pair of guard cells, through which gases diffuse between the air spaces of the leaf and the atmosphere. The guard cells regulate the aperture: when they take up water and become turgid, their unevenly thickened walls make them curve apart and the pore opens; when they lose water and become flaccid, the pore closes. This allows the leaf to balance carbon dioxide uptake against water loss.
Leaf vein

A vascular bundle running through the mesophyll of a leaf, containing xylem and phloem. Xylem delivers water to the leaf, replacing the water lost by transpiration and keeping the mesophyll cell surfaces moist so that gases can dissolve; phloem carries away the sugars made in photosynthesis. Veins do not carry gases: oxygen and carbon dioxide move through the leaf by diffusion.
Plan diagram

A drawing that shows the outline and relative position of each tissue in a section, without drawing individual cells. A plan diagram of a transverse section of a dicotyledonous leaf shows, from the upper surface downward, the upper epidermis, the palisade mesophyll, the spongy mesophyll and the lower epidermis, with veins (vascular bundles) within the mesophyll; in a vein the xylem lies toward the upper surface and the phloem toward the lower surface.
Palisade mesophyll

The layer of closely packed, elongated cells, rich in chloroplasts, lying directly beneath the upper epidermis of a dicotyledonous leaf. It is the main photosynthetic tissue; its cells are positioned to absorb light entering through the transparent upper epidermis and obtain carbon dioxide from the air spaces of the spongy mesophyll below.
Transpiration

The loss of water vapour from the leaves and other aerial parts of a plant, mainly through the stomata. It is a consequence of gas exchange: stomata must be open for carbon dioxide to diffuse in for photosynthesis, and while they are open water vapour, evaporated from the moist surfaces of the mesophyll cells into the air spaces, diffuses out down its concentration gradient to the drier atmosphere.
Factors affecting the rate of transpiration

Temperature, humidity, wind and light intensity. Higher temperature increases the rate by increasing evaporation and the water-vapour concentration inside the leaf; higher humidity decreases the rate by reducing the concentration gradient between the air spaces and the atmosphere; wind increases the rate by removing the layer of humid air at the leaf surface; higher light intensity increases the rate because it causes the stomata to open.
Stomatal density

The number of stomata per unit area of leaf surface, usually expressed per mm². It is determined by counting the stomata visible in a field of view of known area, under a microscope at high power, and dividing the count by that area; counts from several fields of view are averaged before dividing.
Leaf cast

An impression of a leaf surface made by painting the surface with clear nail varnish or similar material, allowing it to dry, and peeling it off with adhesive tape. Mounted on a slide, the cast shows the outlines of the epidermal cells and stomata and can be used, like a micrograph of the epidermis, to count stomata and determine stomatal density.
Replicate measurements

Repeated measurements of the same quantity, such as counts of stomata in several different fields of view on the same leaf. Biological material is variable, so single counts differ from place to place; taking replicates reveals this variability and allows a mean to be calculated, which increases the reliability of the quantitative data.
Haemoglobin

The oxygen-transporting protein of red blood cells, consisting of four polypeptide subunits each carrying a haem group with an iron ion that can bind one oxygen molecule. One haemoglobin molecule can therefore carry up to four oxygen molecules; it loads oxygen where the oxygen concentration is high, in the lungs, and unloads it where the concentration is low, in respiring tissues.
Cooperative binding

The property of haemoglobin by which binding of an oxygen molecule to one haem group changes the conformation of the whole protein, increasing the affinity of the remaining haem groups for oxygen. Binding of the first oxygen is therefore the hardest and each subsequent oxygen binds more readily; the reverse occurs during unloading. Cooperative binding explains the S-shaped oxygen dissociation curve.
Allosteric binding of carbon dioxide

Binding of carbon dioxide to haemoglobin at sites other than the oxygen-binding haem groups, on the polypeptide chains. This binding changes the conformation of the protein and lowers its affinity for oxygen, promoting the release of oxygen in tissues where carbon dioxide concentration is high; carbon dioxide does not compete with oxygen for the haem groups.
Foetal haemoglobin

The form of haemoglobin in the red blood cells of a foetus, which has different polypeptide subunits from adult haemoglobin and a higher affinity for oxygen. At the oxygen concentration in the placenta, where maternal haemoglobin is releasing oxygen, foetal haemoglobin loads oxygen to a higher saturation, so oxygen passes from maternal blood to foetal blood; its dissociation curve lies to the left of the adult curve.
Bohr shift

The decrease in the affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen caused by an increase in carbon dioxide concentration, seen as a shift of the oxygen dissociation curve to the right. Carbon dioxide binds allosterically to haemoglobin and, by forming carbonic acid, lowers the pH of the blood; both effects change the protein's conformation so that more oxygen dissociates at any given oxygen concentration. Actively respiring tissues produce more carbon dioxide and therefore receive more oxygen from the blood that passes through them.
Oxygen dissociation curve

A graph of the percentage saturation of haemoglobin with oxygen against the oxygen concentration (partial pressure of oxygen) of the surroundings. The curve is S-shaped because of cooperative binding: at low oxygen concentration saturation rises slowly, then steeply once the first oxygen molecules bound have raised the affinity of the remaining haem groups, and finally it levels off as the haem groups approach full occupancy. The steep region corresponds to the oxygen concentrations found in respiring tissues, so a small fall in concentration there causes a large release of oxygen.
Affinity of haemoglobin for oxygen

The readiness with which haemoglobin binds and retains oxygen, shown by the position of its dissociation curve. A curve further to the left indicates higher affinity, because haemoglobin reaches a given saturation at a lower oxygen concentration; a curve further to the right indicates lower affinity, so more oxygen is released at a given oxygen concentration.
Capillary

The narrowest blood vessel, with a wall only one endothelial cell thick and a lumen so narrow that red blood cells pass through in single file. Capillaries branch repeatedly to form networks that penetrate every tissue, giving a very large total surface area for exchange of materials between the blood and the internal or external environment.
Fenestration

A pore through the endothelial cell of a capillary wall, found in capillaries where exchange needs to be particularly rapid, such as those of the kidney glomerulus and the villi of the small intestine. Fenestrations allow water and small solutes to pass out of the plasma quickly but are far too small for blood cells to leave the vessel.
Lumen

The central space of a blood vessel through which the blood flows. In a micrograph the thickness of the vessel wall compared with the diameter of the lumen distinguishes an artery (thick wall, narrow round lumen) from a vein (thin wall, wide and often irregular lumen).
Artery

A vessel that carries blood away from the heart. Its wall is thick relative to the lumen and contains layers of smooth muscle and elastic tissue, surrounded by an outer layer of collagen, so it can withstand and maintain the high, pulsing pressure of blood leaving the heart.
Vein

A vessel that carries blood back towards the heart at low pressure. Its wall is thin relative to its wide lumen, with only a little muscle and elastic tissue, and it contains valves that prevent backflow of blood.
Elastic tissue of the artery wall

Tissue containing elastic fibres in the wall of an artery. It stretches when the ventricle contracts and blood is forced in at high pressure, then recoils as the ventricle relaxes, so pressure is maintained and blood keeps flowing between heartbeats rather than falling to zero.
Smooth muscle of the artery wall

The layer of muscle in the artery wall that, together with the elastic tissue, helps the artery withstand high pressure. Contraction of the muscle narrows the lumen (vasoconstriction) and relaxation widens it (vasodilation), which helps to maintain and regulate blood pressure and to control how much blood flows to a tissue. The muscle does not pump the blood along; the heart does that.
Pulse

The wave of pressure that passes along the wall of an artery each time the left ventricle contracts and forces blood into the aorta. It can be felt with the fingertips where an artery lies close to the skin, such as the radial artery in the wrist or the carotid artery in the neck, so counting the pulse for a known time gives the heart rate in beats per minute.
Valve in a vein

A pocket-shaped flap of tissue in the wall of a vein that opens when blood moves towards the heart and closes when blood starts to move backwards, so blood can flow in one direction only. Valves are needed because blood pressure in veins is too low to prevent backflow on its own.
Coronary artery

One of the arteries that branch from the aorta just above the aortic valve and run over the surface of the heart, supplying the cardiac muscle itself with oxygenated blood. Blood in the chambers of the heart does not supply the heart wall; the coronary vessels do.
Occlusion of a coronary artery

Blockage of a coronary artery, usually when fatty deposits (atheroma) build up in the artery wall and narrow the lumen, and a blood clot then forms at the damaged site and blocks it completely. The cardiac muscle beyond the blockage is deprived of oxygen and dies, which is a myocardial infarction (heart attack).
Correlation coefficient

A number between -1 and +1 that quantifies how strongly two variables are related. The sign shows the direction of the relationship (positive when both rise together, negative when one rises as the other falls) and the size shows its strength, with values near zero showing little or no correlation. Even a strong correlation, such as that between saturated fat intake and coronary heart disease, does not prove that one variable causes the other.
Transpiration

The loss of water vapour from a plant, mainly through the stomata of the leaves. Water evaporates from the wet cellulose cell walls of mesophyll cells into the air spaces of the leaf and the vapour then diffuses out through open stomata.
Transpiration pull (tension)

The negative pressure potential generated in the xylem when water evaporates from leaf cell walls. Water is drawn out of the xylem vessels and through the cell walls by capillary action to replace what is lost, putting the whole column of water in the xylem under tension, and it is this tension that draws water up from the roots to the leaves.
Cohesion

The attraction between water molecules due to hydrogen bonding. Because water molecules hold on to one another, the column of water in a xylem vessel stays continuous when it is pulled upwards under tension instead of breaking apart.
Capillary action

The movement of water through narrow spaces, such as the gaps between cellulose fibres in a cell wall, driven by adhesion of water to the surfaces and cohesion between water molecules. In the leaf it draws water out of the xylem and through the cell walls towards the sites of evaporation.
Xylem vessel

A continuous tube for transport of water formed from a column of cells that have died and lost their cell contents. The end walls between the cells are incomplete or absent, so water flows through unimpeded, and the side walls are thickened with lignin.
Lignin

A hard, waterproof polymer deposited in the walls of xylem vessels. Lignified walls are strong enough to withstand the tension in the water column without the vessel collapsing inwards, and they also help support the plant.
Pit

A gap in the lignified wall of a xylem vessel where only the thin primary cell wall remains. Pits allow water to enter the vessel from the root cortex and to leave it into surrounding cells and neighbouring vessels in the stem and leaf.
Vascular bundle

A strand of vascular tissue containing xylem and phloem. In a transverse section of a dicotyledonous stem the vascular bundles are arranged in a ring near the outside, with the xylem on the inner side of each bundle and the phloem on the outer side.
Cortex

The region of unspecialized parenchyma cells that lies between the epidermis and the vascular tissue in both stems and roots. It is a storage and packing tissue, not a transport tissue; in a stem the outer cortex cells may also contain chloroplasts and photosynthesize.
Epidermis

The single outer layer of cells covering a stem or root. In a stem it is covered by a waxy cuticle that reduces water loss and protects against pathogens; in a root it lacks a cuticle and bears root hairs that absorb water and mineral ions.
Vascular cylinder of a root

The central core of vascular tissue in a transverse section of a dicotyledonous root. The xylem forms a star or cross shape at the centre and the phloem lies in separate groups between the arms of the xylem, all surrounded by the cortex and the epidermis. This differs from the ring of separate vascular bundles seen in a stem.
Tissue fluid

The fluid that bathes the cells of a tissue. It is formed by pressure filtration of plasma through the capillary wall and has the same composition as plasma except that it contains almost no plasma proteins and no blood cells. Cells exchange substances with tissue fluid, not directly with the blood.
Pressure filtration

The formation of tissue fluid when the hydrostatic pressure of blood at the arteriole end of a capillary forces water and small solutes out through gaps and fenestrations in the capillary wall, leaving plasma proteins and cells behind. At the venule end the blood pressure is lower, so tissue fluid drains back into the capillary.
Plasma

The liquid part of blood, in which the cells are suspended. It is mostly water with dissolved glucose, amino acids, mineral ions, dissolved gases, urea, hormones and plasma proteins such as albumin. Tissue fluid is plasma minus most of the plasma proteins.
Lymph

Excess tissue fluid that has drained into lymph ducts rather than back into the capillaries. Lymph ducts have thin walls with gaps through which tissue fluid enters and valves that prevent backflow, and the lymph is returned to the blood circulation through ducts that empty into veins near the heart.
Single circulation

The circulation of a bony fish, in which blood passes through the heart once in each complete circuit: heart to gills, where it is oxygenated, then directly on to the rest of the body and back to the heart. Pressure lost in the gill capillaries is not restored, so blood reaches the body tissues at low pressure.
Double circulation

The circulation of a mammal, in which blood passes through the heart twice in each complete circuit. The right side of the heart pumps deoxygenated blood to the lungs (pulmonary circulation) and the blood returns to the left side, which pumps it at high pressure to the rest of the body (systemic circulation).
Cardiac muscle

The specialized muscle of the heart wall. Its cells are branched and joined so that the electrical signal for contraction spreads rapidly from cell to cell, and it contracts rhythmically without fatigue for a lifetime. The thickness of cardiac muscle in each chamber matches the pressure that chamber must generate.
Pacemaker (sinoatrial node)

A group of specialized cardiac muscle cells in the wall of the right atrium that initiates each heartbeat by generating an electrical impulse without any signal from the nervous system. The impulse spreads across the atria, then to the ventricles, so contraction is coordinated.
Atrioventricular valves

The valves between each atrium and its ventricle. They are pushed open when atrial pressure exceeds ventricular pressure, so blood flows into the ventricles, and are forced shut when the ventricles contract and their pressure rises above that of the atria, preventing backflow into the atria.
Semilunar valves

The valves at the exit of each ventricle, at the base of the aorta and of the pulmonary artery. They open when ventricular pressure exceeds arterial pressure during ventricular contraction and close when the ventricles relax, preventing blood in the arteries from flowing back into the heart.
Septum

The wall of cardiac muscle that separates the right and left sides of the heart, so that deoxygenated blood on the right side cannot mix with oxygenated blood on the left side and the two circulations are kept at different pressures.
Systole and diastole

Systole is the phase of the cardiac cycle in which a chamber of the heart contracts; diastole is the phase in which it relaxes and fills. Atrial systole is followed by ventricular systole, and then all chambers are in diastole together while blood flows in from the veins.
Systolic and diastolic blood pressure

The two values in a blood pressure reading such as 120/80 mm Hg, both measured in an artery. Systolic pressure is the peak arterial pressure reached during ventricular systole; diastolic pressure is the minimum arterial pressure during ventricular diastole, which remains well above zero because of elastic recoil of the artery walls.
Root pressure

A positive pressure potential generated in the xylem of the root. Cells around the xylem actively transport mineral ions into the xylem, lowering its water potential so that water follows by osmosis, and the accumulating water pushes upwards. It moves water when transpiration is insufficient, for example in high humidity or in spring before the leaves of deciduous plants have opened.
Sieve tube element

A living phloem cell that forms part of a sieve tube. It has no nucleus and only a thin layer of cytoplasm with few organelles, so the sap can flow through it with little resistance, and its end walls are perforated sieve plates through which sap passes to the next element.
Companion cell

A phloem cell next to each sieve tube element, with a nucleus, dense cytoplasm and many mitochondria. It carries out the metabolic functions the sieve tube element cannot, and uses ATP from its mitochondria to load carbon compounds such as sucrose into the sieve tube at sources and to unload them at sinks.
Plasmodesmata
Channels of cytoplasm passing through the cell walls between a companion cell and its sieve tube element, through which sugars and other substances move from one cell to the other.
Source and sink

A source is a part of the plant that loads carbon compounds into the phloem, such as a photosynthesizing leaf or a storage organ releasing its reserves; a sink is a part that unloads and uses or stores them, such as a growing root, a fruit or a developing bud. Phloem sap flows from source to sink, in whichever direction that lies.
Atria

The two thin-walled upper chambers of the heart that collect blood returning in veins: the right atrium from the venae cavae and the left atrium from the pulmonary veins. Because the atria only have to push blood a short distance through the open atrioventricular valves into the ventricles directly below, their walls contain little cardiac muscle; atrial contraction completes the filling of the ventricles before ventricular systole begins.
Movement

A change in the position of an organism, or of part of its body, brought about by the organism itself. Adaptations for movement are a universal feature of living organisms: motile organisms move the whole body from place to place (locomotion), while sessile organisms and plants move parts of the body, using mechanisms such as muscle contraction, the beating of cilia or flagella, differential growth or reversible changes in cell turgor.
Motile species

A species whose individuals can move the whole body from place to place. Paramecium, a unicellular ciliate, swims by the coordinated beating of thousands of cilia; a fish or a cheetah moves by the contraction of skeletal muscle acting on a skeleton. Motility allows an organism to seek food, mates and favourable conditions and to escape from danger, and it is one of the two contrasting cases (motile and sessile) the guide asks students to explore.
Sessile species

A species whose adult individuals remain fixed in one place and do not move from place to place. The acorn barnacle, a crustacean, swims as a larva but cements itself to a rock as an adult; it still has adaptations for movement, using muscles to extend and beat its feathery cirri (modified legs) to sweep food from the water and to withdraw them and close its shell plates when disturbed. A sessile species shows that movement of body parts does not require locomotion.
Sarcomere

The repeating contractile unit of a myofibril in striated muscle, extending from one Z line (Z disc) to the next. Thin actin filaments are anchored to the Z lines and thick myosin filaments occupy the centre, giving a dark A band (the full length of the myosin filaments), a light I band (actin only, on either side of a Z line) and a paler H zone in the middle of the A band (myosin only). During contraction the sarcomere shortens because the filaments slide over one another: the A band keeps its width while the I band and H zone narrow.
Actin (thin filament)

The protein that forms the thin filaments of the sarcomere. Two chains of actin subunits twist around one another, and each subunit carries a site to which a myosin head can bind. In the relaxed sarcomere these sites are blocked by the regulatory protein tropomyosin, held in place by troponin; calcium ions binding to troponin move tropomyosin aside and expose the sites.
Myosin (thick filament)

The motor protein that forms the thick filaments of the sarcomere. Each myosin molecule has a long tail, which bundles with other tails to form the filament, and a globular head that projects outwards. The head binds and hydrolyses ATP, attaches to actin to form a cross-bridge and pivots in the power stroke that pulls the actin filament towards the centre of the sarcomere.
Sliding filament model

The explanation of muscle contraction in which the actin and myosin filaments do not shorten but slide past one another, pulling the Z lines closer together and shortening the sarcomere. Sliding is driven by repeated cross-bridge cycles: a myosin head binds to actin, pivots in the power stroke (pulling actin towards the centre of the sarcomere and releasing ADP and phosphate), binds a new ATP (which detaches the head from actin), hydrolyses the ATP (which re-cocks the head) and attaches again further along the actin filament. Many heads cycling out of step generate a smooth pull.
Role of calcium ions in contraction

An action potential spreading over the membrane of a muscle fibre causes calcium ions to be released from the sarcoplasmic reticulum into the cytoplasm around the myofibrils. Calcium ions bind to troponin, which shifts tropomyosin away from the myosin-binding sites on actin so that cross-bridges can form. When stimulation stops, calcium ions are pumped back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum by active transport, tropomyosin covers the binding sites again and the fibre relaxes.
Titin

An immense elastic protein, the largest known in humans, that runs from the Z line to the centre of the sarcomere (the M line) alongside the thick filaments and holds them in position. Titin acts as a molecular spring: when a sarcomere is stretched, titin is extended and stores potential energy, then recoils to return the sarcomere to its resting length when the stretching force is removed. Its resistance rises steeply as it is extended, so it also prevents the sarcomere from being overstretched to the point where the actin and myosin filaments no longer overlap.
Antagonistic muscles

A pair of muscles, or muscle groups, that produce opposite movements at a joint or in a body structure, such as the biceps and triceps at the elbow or the external and internal intercostal muscles of the ribcage. Muscle tissue can only exert force when it contracts, so a muscle cannot lengthen itself: it is stretched back to its resting length by contraction of its antagonist. When one member of the pair contracts, the other relaxes and is extended.
Motor unit

A single motor neuron together with all the skeletal muscle fibres it stimulates. The axon of the motor neuron branches, forming a neuromuscular junction with each fibre, so when the neuron fires every fibre in the unit contracts together. A muscle contains many motor units; units in muscles used for fine movements, such as those moving the eye, contain few fibres, while units in large limb muscles may contain more than a thousand. The force of a contraction is graded by the number of motor units recruited and by the frequency of impulses.
Neuromuscular junction

The chemical synapse between the terminal of a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre. An action potential arriving at the terminal causes release of the neurotransmitter acetylcholine into the synaptic cleft; acetylcholine binds to receptors on the membrane of the muscle fibre (the sarcolemma), depolarizing it and triggering an action potential that spreads over and into the fibre, causing release of calcium ions from the sarcoplasmic reticulum and hence contraction.
Muscle fibre

A single elongated, multinucleate cell of skeletal muscle, formed during development by the fusion of many cells. It is packed with parallel myofibrils, each made of sarcomeres in series, and is surrounded by a membrane (the sarcolemma) and a network of sarcoplasmic reticulum that stores calcium ions. Each fibre is stimulated by one motor neuron at one neuromuscular junction, and belongs to one motor unit.
Exoskeleton

A hard external skeleton, found in arthropods such as insects and crustaceans, made of plates of chitin-containing cuticle joined by flexible regions at the joints. Muscles attach to the inner surface of the exoskeleton on either side of a joint, so contraction moves one section of the skeleton relative to another. The exoskeleton provides anchorage for muscles, acts as a system of levers and also protects and supports the body.
Endoskeleton

An internal skeleton of bone or cartilage, found in vertebrates. Muscles attach to the outer surface of bones by tendons, usually spanning a joint, so that when the muscle contracts one bone moves relative to another. The endoskeleton provides anchorage for muscles, acts as a system of levers, supports the body and grows with the animal.
Skeleton as a lever

A bone or exoskeletal plate acts as a rigid bar that pivots at a joint. In the lever the joint is the fulcrum, the force exerted by the contracting muscle where its tendon attaches is the effort, and the weight of the body part or object moved is the load. Because a muscle exerts force only by contracting and pulling, the lever converts a short, strong pull near the joint into a larger, faster movement at the far end of the bone, as when the biceps flexes the elbow.
Synovial joint

A freely movable joint in which the ends of the bones are covered with smooth cartilage and enclosed in a capsule lined with a membrane that secretes synovial fluid. The human hip is a ball-and-socket synovial joint: the rounded head of the femur fits into a cup-shaped socket in the pelvis. Bones provide the rigid levers, cartilage reduces friction and absorbs shock, synovial fluid lubricates the joint, ligaments hold the bones together, and muscles attached by tendons across the joint provide the force for movement.
Ligament

A tough band of fibrous connective tissue that connects bone to bone across a joint. Ligaments hold the head of the femur in the socket of the pelvis, stabilize the hip joint and limit the range and direction of movement, helping to prevent dislocation. They are slightly elastic but do not contract.
Tendon

A cord of tough, inelastic connective tissue that attaches a muscle to a bone. The tendon transmits the force of muscle contraction to the bone, so that muscles anchored on the pelvis and femur can move the hip joint. Tendons do not contract.
Cartilage

Smooth, slightly compressible connective tissue covering the articulating surfaces of the femur and pelvis at the hip joint. It reduces friction between the moving bones and absorbs shock during walking and running. It has no blood supply of its own and is nourished by the synovial fluid.
Synovial fluid

A viscous fluid secreted by the synovial membrane that lines the capsule of a synovial joint. It lubricates the joint, reducing friction and wear on the cartilage, and supplies nutrients to the cartilage.
Range of motion

The extent of movement possible at a joint in a particular dimension, measured as the angle through which one bone can move relative to another from one extreme of the movement to the other. A joint's range of motion should be compared in several dimensions, for example flexion–extension, abduction–adduction and rotation at the hip: a ball-and-socket joint such as the hip moves through useful ranges in all three, while a hinge joint such as the knee moves mainly in one.
Goniometer

A protractor-like instrument with two arms and a pivot used to measure joint angles. The pivot is placed over the joint and the arms are aligned with the bones on either side; the angle is read at each extreme of the movement and the difference between the readings gives the range of motion. Joint angles can also be measured by computer analysis of photographs or video frames on which lines are drawn along the bones.
Intercostal muscles

Two layers of muscle between adjacent ribs whose fibres run in opposite diagonal directions. Contraction of the external intercostal muscles pulls the ribcage up and outwards, increasing the volume of the thorax for inhalation; contraction of the internal intercostal muscles pulls the ribcage down and inwards for forced exhalation. The two layers are antagonistic: when one contracts it stretches the other, storing potential energy in the titin of the stretched sarcomeres. They are an example of antagonistic muscle action producing an internal body movement rather than locomotion.
Locomotion

Movement of a whole organism from one place to another. Locomotion is energetically costly, and animals locomote for reasons that increase survival or reproduction: foraging for food (a hummingbird flying between flowers for nectar), escaping from danger (a gazelle sprinting from a cheetah), searching for a mate (a male emperor moth flying upwind towards pheromone released by a female) and migration (the Arctic tern flying between Arctic breeding grounds and Antarctic waters each year).
Migration

Regular, usually seasonal, movement of animals between two regions, typically between breeding grounds and feeding or overwintering areas, followed by a return journey. Examples include the Arctic tern, which flies between the Arctic and the Antarctic each year; wildebeest, which move across the Serengeti following seasonal rains and fresh grazing; and humpback whales, which travel between polar feeding grounds and tropical breeding waters. Migration is distinct from the one-way dispersal of young animals away from where they were born.
Foraging

Locomotion in search of food. Examples include a hummingbird flying between flowers to drink nectar, a wolf pack travelling long distances to track prey and a honey bee flying between the hive and patches of flowers.
Streamlining

A smooth, tapered (fusiform) body shape that reduces drag as an animal moves through water. Marine mammals such as dolphins and whales are streamlined: the body is spindle-shaped, the hind limbs have been lost, external ears and genitals are absent or withdrawn into the body, hair is almost absent and a layer of blubber smooths the outline of the body.
Flipper

A forelimb of a marine mammal modified for swimming. The flipper of a whale or dolphin contains the same bones as the forelimb of other mammals (humerus, radius, ulna and digits), but the bones are shortened and flattened and the whole limb is enclosed in a single paddle-shaped surface with no separate digits visible. In whales and dolphins the flippers are used for steering, braking and stability rather than for the main thrust.
Fluke

The horizontal, boneless tail fin of a whale or dolphin, formed from tough connective tissue. The fluke is moved up and down by powerful muscles along the back and belly that flex the spine vertically, in contrast to the side-to-side beat of the vertical tail fin of a fish. The up-and-down stroke provides the thrust for swimming.
Blowhole and periodic breathing

Marine mammals breathe air but spend most of their time submerged, so they breathe periodically: a series of rapid breaths at the surface, each exchanging a large proportion of the air in the lungs, separated by long dives during which they do not breathe. In whales and dolphins the nostrils have moved to the top of the head to form a blowhole, which is opened briefly at the surface and sealed shut by muscle while submerged, and the airway from the blowhole to the lungs is separated from the mouth and oesophagus, so that air is taken in only through the blowhole and food cannot enter the lungs.
Habitat

The place in which a community, species, population or organism lives. A description of a habitat can include its geographical location (for example the Atlantic coasts of western Europe), its physical location (for example the seaward slopes of foredunes) and the type of ecosystem (for example a coastal sand dune system).
Population
A group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time. A population lives in a habitat; it is not itself the habitat.
Community

All the populations of different species living and interacting in the same area. A community lives in a habitat; the habitat is the place, and the community is the living part of the ecosystem that occupies it.
Abiotic environment

The non-living physical and chemical conditions of a habitat, such as temperature, water availability, light intensity, salinity, soil or water pH, oxygen availability and wind. Organisms have adaptations, evolved by natural selection, that allow them to survive and reproduce within the abiotic conditions of their habitat.
Marram grass (Ammophila arenaria)

A grass species adapted to the abiotic environment of coastal sand dunes, where sand drains freely, wind and salt spray are strong, nutrients are scarce and sand is repeatedly deposited over the plant. Its leaves roll inwards in dry conditions, with the stomata in grooves on the inner surface and hairs that trap humid air, reducing transpiration; the outer surface has a thick waxy cuticle; extensive rhizomes and deep roots anchor the plant and stabilize the sand; and vertical growth is stimulated by burial, so the plant grows up through newly deposited sand.
Mangrove trees (Avicennia marina and Rhizophora)

Tree species adapted to mangrove swamps: tidal, saline, waterlogged mud that is low in oxygen. The grey mangrove (Avicennia marina) has pneumatophores for gas exchange and salt glands on its leaves that secrete excess salt; the red mangrove (Rhizophora) has stilt (prop) roots for support in soft mud and excludes most salt at its roots by ultrafiltration. Both maintain a low water potential in their cells so that water can be absorbed from seawater, and both produce propagules that germinate while still attached to the parent tree.
Pneumatophore

A vertical root that grows upward from the horizontal roots of a mangrove such as Avicennia marina and projects above the mud into the air. Pneumatophores carry pores (lenticels) through which oxygen diffuses into the root system, allowing aerobic respiration in roots buried in waterlogged, anaerobic mud.
Abiotic variable

A non-living factor of the environment that can vary from place to place or over time and affect where a species can live. Examples for plants include temperature, water availability, light intensity, soil pH, salinity and the availability of mineral nutrients; examples for animals include temperature, water availability, salinity, pH and, in aquatic habitats, the concentration of dissolved oxygen.
Range of tolerance

The range of values of an abiotic variable within which a species can survive, given by its adaptations. Within the range there is an optimum zone in which individuals grow and reproduce best, flanked by zones of stress in which they survive but with reduced growth or reproduction; beyond the limits of tolerance the species cannot survive, so it is absent from places where the variable lies outside its range.
Species distribution

The pattern of where a species is found. Distribution is affected by abiotic variables because each species has a range of tolerance for each variable: a species is restricted to places where every abiotic variable lies within its range of tolerance.
Limiting factor

An abiotic variable that restricts the distribution, growth or abundance of a species because its value lies at or beyond the edge of the species' range of tolerance. Along a gradient of an abiotic variable, the point at which a species disappears indicates a limit of its tolerance for that factor.
Transect

A line laid across a habitat along which the distribution of species is recorded, usually by placing quadrats at regular intervals and recording the abundance (for example percentage cover or counts) of each species in each quadrat. Abiotic variables such as temperature, light intensity and soil pH are measured at the same points, often with sensors, so that changes in the distribution of a species can be correlated with changes in an abiotic variable.
Semi-natural habitat

A habitat that has been influenced by humans but is dominated by wild rather than cultivated species, such as a hay meadow, a grazed heath or a coppiced woodland. Transect data for correlating species distribution with an abiotic variable should be collected from a natural or semi-natural habitat.
Correlation between distribution and an abiotic variable

A relationship in which the abundance of a species changes as an abiotic variable changes along a transect. A correlation is consistent with the variable limiting the species but does not prove that it does so: other variables that change along the same transect, or biotic factors, could be responsible, so an experiment is needed to establish cause.
Coral reef

A marine ecosystem built up from the calcium carbonate skeletons deposited by reef-building corals. Corals are colonial animals (cnidarians) whose polyps secrete calcium carbonate and contain zooxanthellae, so reef formation requires the physical conditions in which both the polyps and the zooxanthellae can function.
Zooxanthellae

Photosynthetic unicellular algae (dinoflagellates) that live inside the tissues of reef-building coral polyps in a mutualistic relationship. They supply the coral with carbon compounds from photosynthesis, which is why reef-building corals require shallow, clear water that light can penetrate.
Conditions for coral reef formation

Reef-building corals require: shallow water, generally less than about 50 m deep, so that light reaches the zooxanthellae; clear water, because suspended sediment reduces light and smothers polyps; warm water, typically between about 23 °C and 29 °C; salinity close to that of the open ocean, roughly 32 to 42 parts per thousand, so reefs do not form where rivers dilute seawater; and a pH of about 8.0 to 8.4, since a fall in pH lowers the carbonate ion concentration needed for calcification.
Biome distribution graph

A graph with mean annual temperature on one axis and mean annual precipitation on the other, on which the distribution of terrestrial biomes is plotted as regions. For any given combination of temperature and rainfall pattern, one natural ecosystem type is likely to develop; the graph therefore shows that these two abiotic factors are the main determinants of terrestrial biome distribution.
Biome

A group of ecosystems, which may be on different continents, that have similar communities because they experience similar abiotic conditions and because convergent evolution has produced organisms with similar adaptations. The species are not the same in each ecosystem of a biome; it is the community structure and the types of adaptation that are similar.
Convergent evolution

The independent evolution of similar features in lineages that are not closely related, because natural selection in similar environments favours similar adaptations. The water-storing stems and spines of cacti in the Americas and of euphorbias in Africa are an example: they arose separately in different plant families in response to similar hot desert conditions.
Climate conditions of the major biomes

Tropical forest: hot all year (mean annual temperature typically 20 to 30 °C) with very high rainfall, generally above 2000 mm a year, and little seasonal variation. Temperate forest: moderate temperatures with warm summers and cool winters, and rainfall of roughly 750 to 1500 mm a year spread through the year. Taiga (boreal forest): long, cold winters and short, mild summers, with low to moderate precipitation, much of it as snow. Grassland: rainfall too low or too seasonal to support forest, roughly 250 to 750 mm a year in temperate grassland, with a wide range of temperatures. Tundra: very cold, with mean annual temperatures below freezing, a growing season of only a few weeks, precipitation generally below about 250 mm a year and permanently frozen subsoil (permafrost). Hot desert: precipitation below about 250 mm a year, very high daytime temperatures and a large difference between day and night temperatures.
Hot desert adaptations: saguaro cactus (Carnegiea gigantea)

A plant of the Sonoran Desert adapted to extreme heat and scarce, unpredictable rainfall. Spines replace leaves, reducing the surface area for transpiration and deterring herbivores; the green stem photosynthesizes and is covered by a thick waxy cuticle; the stem is pleated, so it can swell to store water after rain; stomata open at night rather than during the hot day; and the roots are shallow but spread widely, absorbing rain from a large area before it drains away or evaporates.
Hot desert adaptations: fennec fox (Vulpes zerda)

A small mammal of the Sahara. Its very large ears, with many blood vessels close to the surface, radiate heat and cool the fox without loss of water, and also give acute hearing for locating prey; it is nocturnal, sheltering in a burrow during the heat of the day; its pale coat reflects sunlight; thick fur on the soles of the feet protects them from hot sand; and its kidneys produce concentrated urine, so it can obtain most of its water from food and rarely needs to drink.
Tropical rainforest adaptations: kapok tree (Ceiba pentandra)

An emergent tree that grows to over 60 m in tropical rainforest, where rainfall exceeds 2000 mm a year and most nutrients are held in living biomass rather than in the shallow, leached soil. Its buttress roots spread out above the ground and support the very tall trunk in shallow soil, while a wide, shallow network of roots absorbs nutrients from the thin layer of decomposing litter. It grows rapidly to reach full sunlight above the canopy and its smooth bark discourages climbing plants.
Tropical rainforest adaptations: black-handed spider monkey (Ateles geoffroyi)

A mammal of the canopy of Central American rainforest that feeds mainly on ripe fruit. Its prehensile tail, with a hairless friction pad near the tip, acts as a fifth limb and can support the whole body, freeing the hands to reach fruit at the ends of branches; its long limbs and hook-like hands with reduced thumbs allow it to swing beneath branches (brachiation) as it moves through the canopy; and it is active by day, when it can see ripe fruit.
Ecological niche

The role of a species in an ecosystem: the full set of biotic and abiotic interactions that influence its growth, survival and reproduction, including how it obtains food, what feeds on it, the other species it competes or cooperates with, and the range of abiotic conditions it tolerates. A niche is a role, not a place.
Biotic interaction

An interaction between a species and other living organisms that influences its growth, survival or reproduction, for example feeding on prey, being eaten by predators, competing for resources, being infected by pathogens, or pollination. Biotic interactions are part of a species' niche.
Abiotic interaction

An interaction between a species and the non-living components of its environment, such as temperature, light intensity, water availability, oxygen concentration, pH and salinity. The range of each abiotic factor a species can tolerate is part of its niche.
Obligate anaerobe
An organism that can grow only where oxygen gas is absent from its environment; oxygen is toxic to it, so it cannot tolerate aerobic conditions.
Facultative anaerobe

An organism that tolerates both the presence and the absence of oxygen gas: it uses oxygen for aerobic cell respiration when oxygen is available, and survives by anaerobic cell respiration when it is not.
Obligate aerobe
An organism that requires oxygen gas in its environment and can grow only in aerobic conditions, because it depends on aerobic cell respiration.
Autotroph

An organism that synthesizes its own carbon compounds from simple inorganic substances such as carbon dioxide and water, using an external energy source. Plants, algae and photosynthetic prokaryotes are autotrophs that use light energy.
Photosynthesis as a mode of nutrition

The autotrophic mode of nutrition in which light energy is used to synthesize carbon compounds from carbon dioxide and water. It is the mode of nutrition of plants, of algae and of several groups of photosynthetic prokaryotes; the prokaryotes do this without chloroplasts.
Heterotroph

An organism that obtains carbon compounds from other organisms, living or dead, rather than synthesizing them from inorganic substances. All animals are heterotrophic, as are fungi and many prokaryotes and protists.
Holozoic nutrition

The heterotrophic mode of nutrition used by animals, in which food is ingested (taken into the body), digested internally into small molecules, absorbed across the gut wall into the body and then assimilated into the organism's own tissues.
Assimilation

The final stage of holozoic nutrition, in which absorbed products of digestion, such as amino acids and monosaccharides, are taken up by cells and used to build the organism's own molecules and tissues. Assimilation is distinct from absorption, which is the passage of the products across the gut wall.
Mixotroph

An organism that uses both autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition, for example a protist that photosynthesizes and also ingests or absorbs carbon compounds from other organisms. Euglena is a well-known freshwater example, and many mixotrophic species are part of oceanic plankton.
Obligate and facultative mixotrophs

An obligate mixotroph must use both autotrophic and heterotrophic nutrition, because neither mode alone can sustain it. A facultative mixotroph can survive using one mode alone but uses the other when it is advantageous, for example photosynthesizing in the light and feeding heterotrophically in the dark.
Saprotroph

An organism that obtains carbon compounds from dead organic matter by secreting digestive enzymes onto it and absorbing the products of this external digestion. Saprotrophic nutrition is found in some fungi and bacteria.
Decomposer

A term that can be applied to fungi and bacteria with saprotrophic nutrition, because their external digestion of dead organic matter breaks it down and releases elements for recycling in the ecosystem.
Archaea
One of the three domains of life, alongside Bacteria and Eukaryota. Archaea are prokaryotes but are a separate domain from bacteria, and as a group they are metabolically very diverse.
Energy sources in archaea

Different archaea obtain the energy needed for ATP production in one of three ways: from light, from the oxidation of inorganic chemicals, or from the oxidation of carbon compounds obtained from other organisms.
Dentition

The number, type, size and arrangement of an animal's teeth. In hominids, large flat molars with thick enamel and a massive jaw with large chewing-muscle attachments indicate a herbivorous diet of tough plant material, whereas relatively small, unspecialised teeth with reduced canines indicate an omnivorous diet.
Deduction from theory (NOS)

Using an established theory to reach a conclusion about a case that cannot be observed directly. Observation of living mammals produced theories relating dentition to herbivorous or carnivorous diets; applying these theories to fossil skulls allows the diets of extinct hominids to be deduced.
Piercing and chewing mouthparts

Adaptations of leaf-eating insects for feeding on plants. Chewing mouthparts, as in caterpillars and grasshoppers, are mandibles that bite off and grind pieces of leaf. Piercing mouthparts, as in aphids, are needle-like stylets that penetrate the leaf to reach the sap.
Secondary compounds

Toxic substances produced by plants in seeds and leaves that are not part of the plant's basic metabolism but deter, poison or harm herbivores that eat them. Together with physical structures such as thorns, they are plant adaptations for resisting herbivory.
Detoxification adaptation

A metabolic adaptation of some herbivores that allows them to eat plants containing toxic secondary compounds: enzymes, in the liver for example, chemically break the toxins down into harmless products that can be excreted.
Predator adaptations

Chemical, physical and behavioural features that help a predator to find, catch and kill prey, for example venom (chemical), sharp teeth, claws, acute senses or speed (physical), and hunting in groups, ambushing or stalking (behavioural).
Prey adaptations

Chemical, physical and behavioural features that help a prey animal to resist predation, for example distasteful or poisonous secretions (chemical), camouflage, shells, spines or speed (physical), and living in groups, being active at night or freezing when threatened (behavioural).
Liana

A woody climbing plant rooted in the forest soil that uses the trunks and branches of trees for support, so that it reaches the light of the canopy without producing a thick self-supporting trunk of its own.
Epiphyte

A plant that grows on the branches of a tree, high in the forest where light is available, without roots in the soil. An epiphyte uses the tree only for support and obtains water and minerals from rain and debris; it does not take carbon compounds from the tree.
Strangler epiphyte

A plant, such as a strangler fig, that germinates from a seed deposited on a branch high in a tree and grows roots down the trunk to the soil. As the roots thicken and fuse around the trunk and its own leaves shade the host, the host tree may die, leaving the strangler standing in its place.
Shade tolerance

The ability of shrubs and herbs on the forest floor to photosynthesize and grow at the low light intensities that reach beneath the canopy, so that they can complete their life cycle without reaching the canopy themselves.
Fundamental niche
The potential niche of a species: the full range of conditions and resources it could use, based on its adaptations and tolerance limits, in the absence of competition from other species.
Realized niche

The actual extent of a species' niche when it is in competition with other species. The realized niche is the part of the fundamental niche that the species actually occupies; it can be no larger than the fundamental niche.
Competitive exclusion

The principle that two species cannot indefinitely occupy the same niche in the same place: if their niches overlap completely, one species uses the shared resources more effectively and the other is eliminated from that area.
Outcomes of competition between species

When the fundamental niches of two species overlap, competition has two possible outcomes: one species is eliminated from the area, or both species are restricted to a part of their fundamental niche, so that each occupies a realized niche that is unique to it.
Enzyme

A globular protein that acts as a biological catalyst, increasing the rate of one specific chemical reaction by lowering its activation energy. The enzyme is chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction, so a single enzyme molecule can catalyse the same reaction many times over.
Catalyst

A substance that increases the rate of a chemical reaction without being used up or permanently altered. The reaction could occur without the catalyst, but at the temperatures found in cells most metabolic reactions would be far too slow to sustain life, so cells depend on enzymes to bring rates up to a useful level.
Metabolism

The complex network of interdependent and interacting chemical reactions occurring in a living organism. Almost every reaction is catalysed by its own specific enzyme, so an organism needs many different enzymes, and it can exert control over metabolism by controlling the amount and activity of those enzymes.
Metabolic pathway

A sequence of enzyme-catalysed reactions in which the product of one reaction is the substrate of the next, arranged either as a linear chain or as a cycle. Pathways link with one another to form the network of metabolism.
Control of metabolism through enzymes

Regulation of the rate of a metabolic pathway by regulating its enzymes: how much of each enzyme is synthesized and whether each enzyme molecule is active. This is possible only because each reaction depends on a specific enzyme, so inhibiting or activating one enzyme adjusts one pathway without affecting the rest of metabolism.
Anabolism

The metabolic reactions that build larger molecules from smaller ones, including the formation of macromolecules from monomers by condensation reactions. Protein synthesis, glycogen formation and photosynthesis are anabolic. Anabolic reactions require an input of energy, usually from ATP.
Catabolism

The metabolic reactions that break larger molecules into smaller ones, including the hydrolysis of macromolecules into monomers during digestion and the oxidation of substrates such as glucose in cell respiration. Catabolic reactions release energy.
Condensation reaction

A reaction in which two molecules are joined by a covalent bond and a water molecule is released. Monomers are linked into macromolecules by condensation: amino acids into polypeptides by peptide bonds, and glucose into glycogen by glycosidic bonds.
Hydrolysis

A reaction in which a covalent bond within a molecule is broken by the addition of a water molecule. Macromolecules are digested into monomers by hydrolysis, for example starch into maltose and then glucose, and polypeptides into amino acids.
Globular protein

A protein folded into a compact, roughly spherical three-dimensional shape that is held by interactions between amino acids, including hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulfide bonds and hydrophobic interactions. Enzymes are globular proteins, and it is this folding that creates the active site.
Active site

The region of an enzyme to which the substrate binds and where catalysis occurs. It is composed of only a few amino acids, but interactions between amino acids throughout the folded three-dimensional structure of the enzyme hold those few amino acids in the positions that give the active site the shape and chemical properties needed for catalysis.
Induced fit

The model of enzyme-substrate binding in which the active site is not a rigid shape that exactly matches the substrate. As the substrate binds, interactions between it and the active site cause both the enzyme and the substrate to change shape, giving a closer fit and weakening bonds within the substrate so that the reaction is catalysed.
Enzyme-substrate complex

The temporary structure formed while a substrate is bound to the active site of an enzyme. Within the complex the substrate is converted to product, which is then released, leaving the active site free to bind another substrate molecule.
Substrate-active site collision

The random encounter of a substrate molecule with the active site of an enzyme, which must happen before binding can occur. Both substrate and enzyme move by random molecular motion in the fluid around them, and the rate of reaction depends on how often collisions occur with the substrate in an orientation that allows binding.
Immobilized enzyme

An enzyme held in a fixed position, for example by being embedded in a membrane. Catalysis still occurs because substrate molecules move randomly and collide with the active site. Conversely, some very large substrate molecules are effectively immobile, and it is the enzyme that moves to them.
Enzyme-substrate specificity

The property that each enzyme catalyses only one reaction or one type of reaction. It arises because the shape and the chemical properties (charge and polarity) of the active site are complementary to one substrate, so other molecules do not bind in a way that allows catalysis.
Denaturation

A change in the three-dimensional structure of a protein caused, for example, by high temperature or extreme pH, which breaks the hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds and other interactions that hold the folded shape; the peptide bonds remain intact. In an enzyme the active site loses its complementary shape, so the substrate can no longer bind and activity is lost, usually permanently.
Collision theory applied to enzymes

Reaction occurs when a substrate and an active site collide with sufficient energy and in the correct orientation. Factors that increase the frequency or energy of collisions, such as higher temperature or higher substrate concentration, increase the rate until some other factor, such as denaturation or saturation of active sites, limits it.
Optimum temperature

The temperature at which an enzyme's rate of activity is highest. Below it, rate rises with temperature because molecules move faster and so collide more often and with more energy. Above it, rate falls steeply because the enzyme is denatured.
Optimum pH

The pH at which an enzyme's rate of activity is highest; it differs between enzymes (about 2 for pepsin in the stomach, about 8 for trypsin in the small intestine). Away from the optimum, changes in hydrogen ion concentration alter the charges on amino acids, disrupting ionic and hydrogen bonds and changing the shape of the active site; at extreme pH the enzyme is denatured.
Saturation of active sites

The state reached at high substrate concentration when every active site is occupied almost all of the time. Rate rises with substrate concentration because collisions with active sites become more frequent, but the rise slows and the rate reaches a plateau at saturation, when adding more substrate cannot increase it further.
Sketch graph as a model

A generalized sketch of the relationship between a variable such as temperature and the rate of enzyme activity is a model: a simplified representation of a general pattern, not a record of the data from one experiment. Like other models in biology it can be evaluated using results from enzyme experiments and refined if the data disagree with it.
Rate of an enzyme-catalysed reaction

The change in the amount (mass, volume or concentration) of product formed or substrate used per unit time, for example cm³ of oxygen per second. It is found from the gradient of a graph of product or substrate against time, or as 1 divided by the time taken for a fixed change to occur.
Initial rate

The rate measured at the very start of a reaction, when the substrate concentration is known and has not yet fallen and no product has accumulated. It is found from the gradient of the first, steepest part of the graph and is the most reliable measure for comparing different conditions.
Activation energy

The energy that must be supplied to substrate molecules before a reaction can proceed, because energy is required to break bonds within the substrate. Enzymes lower the activation energy by binding the substrate in a way that strains and weakens these bonds, so that at cell temperatures far more substrate molecules have enough energy to react.
Energy yield of a reaction

The net energy released when the bonds that form the products are made, after the energy needed to break the bonds in the substrate has been supplied. On an energy graph it is the difference between the energy level of the substrate and that of the products, and it is not changed by the presence of an enzyme.
Intracellular enzyme
An enzyme that acts inside the cell that synthesized it. The enzymes of glycolysis, which act in the cytoplasm, and of the Krebs cycle, which act in the mitochondrial matrix, are intracellular.
Extracellular enzyme

An enzyme that is synthesized inside a cell and secreted to act outside cells. The digestive enzymes of the gut, such as amylase, pepsin and lipase, are extracellular: they carry out chemical digestion by hydrolysing macromolecules in the gut lumen.
Metabolic heat

Heat released by the reactions of metabolism. Energy transfers in metabolic reactions are not 100% efficient, so some energy is converted to heat in every reaction; heat generation is therefore inevitable in every living cell. Mammals, birds and some other animals depend on this heat production to maintain a constant body temperature.
Linear pathway

A metabolic pathway in which a chain of enzyme-catalysed reactions converts a starting substrate through a series of intermediates into a final product, with no intermediate regenerated. Glycolysis, which converts glucose to pyruvate, is a linear pathway.
Cyclical pathway

A metabolic pathway in which the product of the final reaction is the substrate of the first, so that one intermediate is regenerated with every turn; other substrates enter the cycle and net products leave it. The Krebs cycle, which regenerates oxaloacetate, and the Calvin cycle, which regenerates RuBP, are cyclical pathways.
Allosteric site

A binding site on an enzyme away from the active site, to which only specific substances can bind. Binding causes interactions within the enzyme that lead to conformational changes, altering the active site enough to prevent catalysis. Binding is reversible, so activity returns when the substance leaves the site.
Non-competitive inhibition

Inhibition in which an inhibitor binds reversibly to an allosteric site rather than to the active site, changing the conformation of the enzyme so that the active site no longer catalyses the reaction. Because the inhibitor does not compete with the substrate, increasing the substrate concentration does not overcome the inhibition and the maximum rate is lowered.
Competitive inhibition

Inhibition by a substance that resembles the substrate and binds reversibly to the active site, so that substrate and inhibitor compete for the same site. Increasing the substrate concentration reduces the effect of the inhibitor, and at a high enough substrate concentration the rate approaches the uninhibited maximum.
Statins

Drugs used to lower blood cholesterol. They are competitive inhibitors of HMG-CoA reductase, an enzyme in the pathway that synthesizes cholesterol: a statin resembles the enzyme's substrate and binds reversibly to the active site, reducing the rate of cholesterol synthesis in liver cells.
Feedback inhibition

Regulation of a metabolic pathway in which the end product acts as an inhibitor, usually by binding to an allosteric site on the first enzyme of the pathway. When the end product accumulates the pathway slows; as the end product is used up, inhibition is released. In the pathway that converts threonine to isoleucine, isoleucine inhibits the first enzyme, threonine deaminase.
Mechanism-based inhibition

Irreversible inhibition in which the inhibitor binds to the active site and the enzyme's own catalytic action converts it into a form that bonds covalently to the active site. The chemical change to the active site leaves the enzyme permanently inactive. Penicillin is an example.
Transpeptidase

A bacterial enzyme that forms cross-links between peptidoglycan strands in the cell wall. Penicillin binds irreversibly to its active site, so cross-linking fails, the wall is weakened and the cell bursts. In resistant bacteria a changed transpeptidase has an altered active site that still cross-links peptidoglycan but no longer binds penicillin effectively.
ATP (adenosine triphosphate)

A nucleotide made of the base adenine, the pentose sugar ribose and a chain of three phosphate groups. It is the molecule that distributes energy within cells: energy released from carbon compounds in cell respiration is used to make ATP, and ATP then supplies that energy to the processes that need it.
Nucleotide

A molecule made of a pentose sugar, a nitrogenous base and one or more phosphate groups. Nucleotides are the monomers of DNA and RNA, but ATP is also a nucleotide, one in which ribose carries adenine and three phosphates.
Energy currency

The role ATP plays as the immediate, universal supplier of energy to reactions in the cell. ATP is suited to this because it is soluble in water and moves freely through the cytoplasm, is stable at cell pH until an enzyme hydrolyses it, cannot diffuse out through the plasma membrane, releases energy in an amount suited to single reactions, and is regenerated from ADP and phosphate within seconds. It is a short-term supply that is recycled continuously, not a long-term store.
Active transport

Movement of a substance across a membrane against its concentration gradient by a protein pump, using energy from ATP. It is one of the principal uses of ATP in cells; passive processes such as diffusion, facilitated diffusion and osmosis do not use ATP.
Anabolism

The synthesis of larger molecules from smaller ones, such as building polypeptides from amino acids, polysaccharides from monosaccharides or DNA from nucleotides. Anabolic reactions require an input of energy, which ATP supplies.
Movement powered by ATP

Movement of a whole cell (for example a sperm cell swimming, or a leucocyte crawling) or of components within a cell (for example chromosomes being moved to the poles during mitosis, or vesicles being transported along the cytoskeleton). All of these depend on motor proteins that use energy released by hydrolysis of ATP.
Hydrolysis of ATP

The reaction in which ATP reacts with water to form ADP (adenosine diphosphate) and a phosphate group. Energy is released, and in the cell this energy is coupled to a process that needs it. The amount released per ATP is sufficient for many tasks in the cell.
Phosphorylation of ADP

The synthesis of ATP by joining a phosphate group to ADP. This is a condensation reaction that requires an input of energy, supplied in cell respiration (and photosynthesis). ATP and ADP are therefore interconverted continuously: hydrolysis releases energy, synthesis stores it.
Cell respiration

The controlled release of energy from carbon compounds (organic compounds) inside cells, used to produce ATP. It is a chemical process carried out by every living cell and is distinct from gas exchange.
Gas exchange

The movement of gases such as oxygen and carbon dioxide across a surface, for example between alveolar air and blood in the lungs or between the air and the cells of a leaf. It supplies oxygen for aerobic respiration and removes carbon dioxide, but it is not itself respiration.
Respiratory substrate

A carbon compound whose oxidation releases energy for ATP production. Glucose and fatty acids are the principal substrates in most cells, but a wide range of carbon compounds, including other sugars, glycerol and amino acids, can be respired.
Aerobic cell respiration

Respiration that requires oxygen. Glucose (or another substrate such as a fatty acid) is completely oxidized to carbon dioxide and water with a large yield of ATP. In humans the word equation with glucose is: glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water. Glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm; the later reactions occur in the mitochondria, so mitochondria are required.
Anaerobic cell respiration

Respiration that does not use oxygen. In humans, glucose is converted to lactate with a small yield of ATP (glucose → lactate); no carbon dioxide is formed. Only carbohydrate can be used as the substrate. All of the reactions occur in the cytoplasm, so mitochondria are not required.
Lactate

The three-carbon product of anaerobic cell respiration in humans, formed from pyruvate in the cytoplasm. It is the waste product that accumulates in muscle during intense exercise when oxygen supply is insufficient.
Mitochondrion

The organelle in which the oxygen-requiring stages of aerobic cell respiration take place, releasing most of the ATP that a eukaryotic cell produces. Mitochondria are required for aerobic respiration but not for anaerobic respiration, which is completed in the cytoplasm.
Rate of cell respiration

The amount of oxygen consumed (or carbon dioxide produced) per unit time, usually expressed per unit mass of tissue, for example in cm³ g⁻¹ min⁻¹. It is affected by variables such as temperature, availability of substrate and of oxygen, and pH, and is calculated by dividing the measured change in volume by the time taken and by the mass of tissue.
Respirometer

Apparatus for measuring the rate of respiration of living material. Carbon dioxide released is absorbed by an alkali such as potassium hydroxide, so the decrease in gas volume, followed by the movement of a drop of coloured liquid along a capillary tube, is due to oxygen being taken up. A control tube containing non-living material of the same volume shows the effect of any change in temperature or pressure.
Oxidation

The loss of electrons from a substance. In cell respiration this usually happens by removal of hydrogen atoms, each of which carries an electron, so a substrate that loses hydrogen (is dehydrogenated) has been oxidized. Gaining oxygen is also oxidation, but oxygen need not be involved.
Reduction

The gain of electrons by a substance, in cell respiration usually by accepting hydrogen. Oxidation and reduction occur together as a redox reaction: when a substrate is oxidized by losing hydrogen, the carrier that accepts the hydrogen is reduced.
NAD

A coenzyme that acts as a hydrogen carrier in cell respiration. NAD accepts hydrogen (with electrons) removed from substrates and becomes reduced NAD; reduced NAD later gives up the electrons and is converted back to NAD, so a small pool of NAD is used over and over again.
Dehydrogenation

Removal of hydrogen atoms from a substrate by a dehydrogenase enzyme. Because each hydrogen atom carries an electron, dehydrogenation oxidizes the substrate, and the hydrogen is passed to a carrier such as NAD.
Glycolysis

The stepwise conversion of one glucose (6C) to two pyruvate (3C) in the cytoplasm, with no oxygen required. It involves phosphorylation of glucose using ATP, lysis (splitting) of the phosphorylated hexose into two three-carbon molecules, oxidation of these by dehydrogenation to form reduced NAD, and ATP formation. Each step is catalysed by a different enzyme.
Phosphorylation of glucose

The first stage of glycolysis, in which phosphate groups from two ATP molecules are added to glucose. This uses ATP rather than making it; it makes the sugar more reactive and unable to leave the cell.
Net yield of glycolysis
Per glucose, glycolysis uses 2 ATP in phosphorylation and forms 4 ATP later, so the net yield is 2 ATP. It also forms 2 reduced NAD and 2 pyruvate.
Regeneration of NAD

Conversion of reduced NAD back to NAD so that glycolysis can continue. In anaerobic respiration in humans this is done by reducing pyruvate to lactate; no ATP is formed in this step, but it allows glycolysis to go on yielding a net two ATP per glucose.
Anaerobic respiration in yeast

Glycolysis followed by regeneration of NAD in which pyruvate is decarboxylated, releasing carbon dioxide, and the product is reduced to ethanol: glucose → ethanol + carbon dioxide. The pathway is the same as in humans up to pyruvate; only the NAD-regenerating step and therefore the final products differ. The carbon dioxide raises bread dough in baking and the ethanol is the alcohol in beer and wine in brewing.
Link reaction

The oxidation and decarboxylation of pyruvate (3C) in the mitochondrial matrix to form an acetyl group (2C), carbon dioxide and reduced NAD. The acetyl group is attached to coenzyme A, forming acetyl coenzyme A, which transfers it to the Krebs cycle.
Acetyl coenzyme A (acetyl-CoA)

A two-carbon acetyl group bound to the carrier molecule coenzyme A. Coenzyme A is not an enzyme: it carries acetyl groups, formed from pyruvate in the link reaction or from the breakdown of fatty acids, and hands them to oxaloacetate in the Krebs cycle, being released to be reused.
Decarboxylation

Removal of a carboxyl group from a substrate as carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide released in aerobic respiration comes from decarboxylations in the link reaction and the Krebs cycle, not from a reaction of carbon with oxygen.
Krebs cycle

A cycle of reactions in the mitochondrial matrix in which the acetyl group (2C) from acetyl-CoA is transferred to oxaloacetate (4C) to form citrate (6C). Citrate is then converted back to oxaloacetate by a series of reactions that include two decarboxylations, releasing carbon dioxide, and four oxidations by dehydrogenation, most of which form reduced NAD; one ATP is formed directly per turn.
Citrate
The six-carbon compound formed at the start of the Krebs cycle by transfer of a two-carbon acetyl group from acetyl-CoA to four-carbon oxaloacetate.
Oxaloacetate
The four-carbon compound that accepts an acetyl group to form citrate and is regenerated by the reactions of the Krebs cycle, so it is not used up.
Electron transport chain

A series of electron carriers in the inner mitochondrial membrane.
