Reduced NAD (from glycolysis, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle) transfers a pair of electrons to the first carrier, becoming NAD again; the electrons then pass from carrier to carrier, releasing energy at each transfer, until they reach oxygen.
Proton gradient

A difference in hydrogen ion (proton) concentration across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Energy released as electrons flow along the electron transport chain is used to pump protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space, so the intermembrane space becomes more concentrated in protons than the matrix.
Intermembrane space

The narrow space between the outer and inner membranes of the mitochondrion into which protons are pumped by the electron transport chain, and from which they flow back into the matrix through ATP synthase.
Chemiosmosis

The use of a proton gradient across a membrane to drive ATP synthesis. Protons diffuse down their concentration gradient from the intermembrane space back into the matrix through ATP synthase, and the energy released is coupled to the phosphorylation of ADP.
ATP synthase

An enzyme embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane that provides the only route for protons to flow back into the matrix. The flow of protons through it releases energy that it uses to join phosphate to ADP, forming ATP on the matrix side of the membrane.
Terminal electron acceptor

The substance that accepts electrons from the last carrier of the electron transport chain. In aerobic respiration this is oxygen, which combines with the electrons and with protons from the matrix to form water. Without a terminal acceptor the carriers remain reduced and electron flow stops.
Metabolic water

Water formed in aerobic respiration when oxygen accepts electrons from the electron transport chain and protons from the matrix. It is the fate of the oxygen consumed in respiration; the carbon dioxide released comes from decarboxylation, not from oxygen.
Lipids as a respiratory substrate

Fatty acids are broken down into two-carbon acetyl groups that enter aerobic respiration as acetyl-CoA and are oxidized in the Krebs cycle. Lipids yield roughly twice as much energy per gram as carbohydrates because they contain less oxygen and more oxidizable hydrogen and carbon. Fatty acids cannot enter glycolysis, so they cannot be used in anaerobic respiration; glycolysis and anaerobic respiration occur only with carbohydrate as the substrate.
Photosynthesis

The process in which light energy absorbed by pigments is transformed into chemical energy held in carbon compounds. Carbon dioxide is reduced to carbohydrates such as glucose using hydrogen obtained by splitting water, so photosynthesis both fixes carbon and stores energy in the bonds of the carbon compounds it produces.
Chemical energy in carbon compounds

Energy stored in the bonds of organic molecules such as glucose, released for use by a cell when the molecules are broken down in cell respiration. The chemical energy captured by photosynthesis passes along food chains, so this one energy transformation supplies most of the chemical energy needed for life processes in ecosystems.
Word equation for photosynthesis

carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen, with light energy absorbed by chlorophyll. The equation summarises reactants and products only: it does not show that the hydrogen used to reduce carbon dioxide comes from water, or that the oxygen released comes from water rather than from carbon dioxide.
Splitting of water

The breaking apart of water molecules during photosynthesis to obtain hydrogen. The hydrogen, as protons and electrons, is used to reduce carbon dioxide to glucose, and the oxygen left over is released as a by-product. Water is therefore a genuine reactant of photosynthesis, not merely a solvent.
By-product

A substance formed by a process but not needed by it. Oxygen is the by-product of photosynthesis: it is left over when water is split to obtain hydrogen and is released to the surroundings. The useful products are the carbon compounds; the oxygen is a waste product from the point of view of the photosynthesizing cell, even though it sustains aerobic organisms.
Cyanobacteria

Photosynthetic prokaryotes that, like plants and algae, split water and release oxygen. They have no chloroplasts; their photosynthetic pigments are held in membranes within the cell. Cyanobacteria were responsible for the first release of oxygen into the Earth's oceans and atmosphere, long before plants existed.
Chromatography

A technique for separating the components of a mixture. A spot of pigment extract is placed on an origin line near one end of a stationary phase (chromatography paper, or a thin layer of silica on a plate) and a solvent moves through it. Each pigment travels a characteristic distance according to its solubility in the solvent and its attraction to the stationary phase, so the pigments separate into coloured spots.
Rf value

The distance moved by a pigment from the origin divided by the distance moved by the solvent front from the origin. Rf lies between 0 and 1, has no units, and is constant for a given pigment in a given solvent and stationary phase, so it can be used together with colour to identify the pigment.
Photosynthetic pigments

Coloured molecules that absorb light for photosynthesis. Leaf extracts separated by chromatography typically show carotene (orange, highest Rf), xanthophylls (yellow), chlorophyll a (blue-green) and chlorophyll b (yellow-green, lowest Rf), each identified by its colour and its Rf value.
Absorption spectrum

A graph of the percentage of light absorbed by a pigment, or by a mixture of pigments, plotted against wavelength, with the horizontal axis labelled with both wavelengths in nanometres and the corresponding colours. Chlorophyll absorbs mainly in the blue (about 400–500 nm) and red (about 600–700 nm) regions and absorbs little green light, which is reflected or transmitted.
Excitation of an electron

The raising of an electron in a pigment molecule to a higher energy level when the molecule absorbs a photon. This is the step in which light energy is transformed into chemical energy: the excited electron carries the energy absorbed, which can be passed to other molecules and eventually used to make ATP and reduced NADP.
Wavelength and photon energy

Visible light spans wavelengths of roughly 400 nm (violet) to 700 nm (red). Light is absorbed as photons, and the shorter the wavelength the greater the energy of each photon. A pigment absorbs only photons whose energy matches the difference between an electron's ground state and an available excited state, which is why each pigment absorbs some wavelengths and not others.
Action spectrum

A graph of the rate of photosynthesis plotted against the wavelength of light supplied, usually as a percentage of the maximum rate, obtained by measuring oxygen production or carbon dioxide consumption under light of different wavelengths. Its shape is similar to the absorption spectrum of the photosynthetic pigments, with peaks in blue and red, but it shows more photosynthesis in green light than the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a alone would suggest, because accessory pigments absorb some of those wavelengths.
Rate of photosynthesis

The amount of photosynthesis taking place per unit time, measured indirectly as the volume of oxygen produced, the amount of carbon dioxide consumed, or the increase in biomass, per unit time. Because a rate is an amount divided by a time, measurements made over different durations must be converted to a common time before they are compared or plotted.
Limiting factor

The factor that, at a given moment, is in shortest supply relative to demand and so sets the rate of photosynthesis. Light intensity, carbon dioxide concentration and temperature can each be limiting; increasing the limiting factor raises the rate until another factor becomes limiting, when the rate levels off.
Independent variable

The variable that the investigator deliberately changes, such as light intensity altered by moving a lamp, carbon dioxide concentration altered with sodium hydrogencarbonate solution, or temperature altered with a water bath.
Dependent variable

The variable that is measured to find the effect of the independent variable, such as the rate of oxygen production by an aquatic plant measured as bubbles counted per minute or as the volume of gas collected in a fixed time.
Hypothesis

A provisional explanation for an observation, or a proposed relationship between variables, that can be tested by experiment and must survive repeated testing before it is accepted. A hypothesis can be based on a theory and then tested, or based on evidence from an experiment already carried out; a single experiment never proves it.
Carbon dioxide enrichment experiment

An experiment in which plants are grown at a carbon dioxide concentration higher than the current atmospheric level in order to predict how future rates of photosynthesis and plant growth will respond to rising atmospheric carbon dioxide. Enclosed greenhouse experiments allow precise control of variables; free-air experiments test plants growing in the field.
FACE (free-air carbon dioxide enrichment)

A field experiment in which carbon dioxide is released from pipes arranged in a ring around a plot of crops or natural vegetation, raising the concentration in the air over the plot to a chosen level, while control plots nearby remain at the ambient concentration. Because the plants grow with natural light, temperature, soil, water and other organisms, the results predict responses in real ecosystems more realistically than greenhouse experiments, at the cost of less control of variables.
Controlled variable

A variable that could affect the dependent variable and is therefore kept constant across all treatments, so that any difference in results can be attributed to the independent variable. In a greenhouse enrichment experiment, temperature, light, water supply and mineral supply are controlled variables; in a FACE experiment they cannot be held constant and are instead matched by control plots exposed to the same weather and soil.
Photosystem

A molecular array of chlorophyll and accessory pigment molecules, held in a membrane, that absorbs light and generates and emits excited electrons. Photosystems occur in the thylakoid membranes of chloroplasts in photosynthetic eukaryotes and in the membranes of cyanobacteria; they are never found free in solution.
Reaction centre

A special chlorophyll at the heart of a photosystem to which the other pigments pass the energy they absorb. When the reaction centre chlorophyll receives this energy one of its electrons is excited and emitted to an electron acceptor, leaving the chlorophyll positively charged until the electron is replaced.
Accessory pigment

A pigment other than the reaction-centre chlorophyll in a photosystem, such as chlorophyll b or a carotenoid, that absorbs wavelengths that chlorophyll a absorbs poorly and passes the absorbed energy to the reaction centre. Accessory pigments do not emit electrons themselves.
Light-harvesting array

The organised arrangement of many pigment molecules around a reaction centre. Its advantages are that pigments of different types absorb a broad range of wavelengths, that energy from hundreds of pigment molecules is funnelled to a single reaction centre so that electrons are emitted far more often than any one molecule could achieve by absorbing photons itself, and that the reaction centre is positioned in the membrane next to the electron acceptor. A single molecule of chlorophyll or any other pigment in isolation could not perform any part of photosynthesis.
Photolysis of water

The splitting of water into electrons, protons (hydrogen ions) and oxygen, carried out by photosystem II. The electrons replace those emitted by the reaction centre chlorophyll of photosystem II, the protons are released into the thylakoid lumen and contribute to the proton gradient, and the oxygen is a waste product that diffuses away.
Photosystem II

The photosystem that begins non-cyclic photophosphorylation. Its reaction centre absorbs light most strongly at 680 nm, emits excited electrons to the chain of electron carriers, and replaces them by splitting water; it is the only site of oxygen production in photosynthesis. Its evolution in the ancestors of cyanobacteria led to the oxygenation of the Earth's oceans and atmosphere.
Chemiosmosis

The synthesis of ATP using the energy of a proton gradient across a membrane. In the chloroplast, electron carriers in the thylakoid membrane use energy from excited electrons to pump protons from the stroma into the thylakoid lumen; the protons flow back into the stroma down their concentration gradient through ATP synthase, which uses the energy released to phosphorylate ADP to ATP.
ATP synthase

The enzyme embedded in the thylakoid membrane through which protons flow from the thylakoid lumen into the stroma. The flow of protons drives rotation of part of the enzyme, which catalyses the joining of a phosphate group to ADP, releasing ATP on the stroma side of the membrane where the Calvin cycle uses it.
Chain of electron carriers

A series of molecules in the thylakoid membrane that pass excited electrons from one to the next, from photosystem II (non-cyclic) or photosystem I (cyclic) towards photosystem I. As electrons pass along the chain their energy is used to pump protons into the thylakoid lumen, building the gradient used for chemiosmosis; the chain does not make ATP directly.
Non-cyclic photophosphorylation

ATP production in which electrons emitted by photosystem II pass along the chain of carriers to photosystem I and finally to NADP. Water is split to replace the electrons lost by photosystem II, so oxygen is released, and reduced NADP is produced as well as ATP.
Cyclic photophosphorylation

ATP production in which excited electrons emitted by photosystem I are passed to the chain of electron carriers and returned to photosystem I instead of reducing NADP. Protons are pumped and ATP is made by chemiosmosis, but no water is split, no oxygen is released and no reduced NADP is formed; it allows the chloroplast to make additional ATP when the Calvin cycle needs more ATP than reduced NADP.
NADP and reduced NADP

NADP (NADP+) is the electron carrier reduced at the end of the non-cyclic electron pathway. It accepts two electrons that have come from photosystem I and one hydrogen ion from the stroma, forming reduced NADP (NADPH), which carries the electrons and hydrogen to the Calvin cycle. The terms must be paired consistently: NADP with reduced NADP, or NADP+ with NADPH.
Photosystem I

The photosystem whose reaction centre absorbs most strongly at 700 nm. It receives electrons from the chain of carriers, re-excites them with light energy and emits them to a carrier on the stroma side of the membrane, from which they are used to reduce NADP in non-cyclic photophosphorylation or returned to the chain in cyclic photophosphorylation.
Thylakoid

A flattened membrane-bound sac inside the chloroplast, arranged in stacks called grana. The thylakoid membrane holds the photosystems, the chain of electron carriers and ATP synthase; the space it encloses is the thylakoid lumen. All the light-dependent reactions take place in or across the thylakoid membrane: photolysis on the lumen side of photosystem II, ATP synthesis as protons pass through ATP synthase into the stroma, and reduction of NADP on the stroma side of photosystem I.
Thylakoid lumen

The fluid-filled space enclosed by the thylakoid membrane. Protons from photolysis and from pumping by the electron carriers accumulate here, making the lumen more acidic than the stroma; this proton gradient drives ATP synthesis as protons flow out through ATP synthase.
Stroma

The fluid that surrounds the thylakoids inside the chloroplast. It contains the enzymes of the Calvin cycle, including very high concentrations of Rubisco, and it is where ATP and reduced NADP are released by the light-dependent reactions and consumed by the light-independent reactions.
Rubisco

Ribulose bisphosphate carboxylase: the enzyme that catalyses carbon fixation by joining carbon dioxide to RuBP, producing two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate. It is the most abundant enzyme on Earth because it works relatively slowly and is not effective at low carbon dioxide concentrations, so chloroplasts need very high concentrations of it in the stroma to fix carbon at a useful rate.
Carbon fixation

The conversion of inorganic carbon dioxide into an organic compound. In the Calvin cycle, Rubisco combines one molecule of carbon dioxide with one molecule of RuBP (a five-carbon compound); the unstable six-carbon product immediately splits into two molecules of glycerate 3-phosphate (three carbons each). No ATP or reduced NADP is used in this step.
RuBP (ribulose bisphosphate)

The five-carbon sugar with two phosphate groups that accepts carbon dioxide in the Calvin cycle. It is the substrate of Rubisco, together with carbon dioxide, and must be continually regenerated from triose phosphate for the cycle to continue.
Glycerate 3-phosphate (GP)

The three-carbon compound that is the first stable product of carbon fixation: two molecules are formed for each carbon dioxide fixed. It is not yet a carbohydrate; it must be reduced to triose phosphate using reduced NADP and ATP.
Triose phosphate (TP)

A three-carbon sugar phosphate formed by the reduction of glycerate 3-phosphate in a reaction that uses ATP to phosphorylate GP and reduced NADP to reduce it. It is the first carbohydrate of the Calvin cycle: most of it is used to regenerate RuBP, and the remainder is used to make glucose and other carbon compounds.
Calvin cycle

The cycle of light-independent reactions in the stroma in which carbon dioxide is fixed by Rubisco onto RuBP, the glycerate 3-phosphate formed is reduced to triose phosphate using ATP and reduced NADP, and RuBP is regenerated from triose phosphate using ATP. For every six molecules of triose phosphate produced, five are used to regenerate three molecules of RuBP and one is available for making glucose and other products.
Regeneration of RuBP

The conversion of five molecules of triose phosphate (fifteen carbon atoms) into three molecules of RuBP (fifteen carbon atoms), using ATP from the light-dependent reactions. Without regeneration the supply of RuBP would run out and carbon fixation would stop. If glucose is the product, five-sixths of all the triose phosphate produced must be recycled in this way.
Calvin cycle products as precursors

Triose phosphate and other intermediates of the Calvin cycle are the starting points of the metabolic pathways that make all the carbon compounds of a photosynthesizing organism: glucose, sucrose, starch and cellulose, fatty acids and lipids, and, when combined with nitrogen and other elements from mineral nutrients, amino acids and nucleotides. Every carbon atom in these compounds was fixed in the Calvin cycle.
Mineral nutrients

Inorganic ions absorbed from the soil or water, such as nitrate, ammonium, phosphate and sulfate, that supply the elements other than carbon, hydrogen and oxygen needed to build carbon compounds. Nitrogen from nitrate or ammonium is combined with carbon skeletons derived from Calvin cycle intermediates to make amino acids; mineral nutrients supply no carbon and no energy.
Light-dependent reactions

The reactions in the thylakoids that use light energy: photolysis of water, electron transport with proton pumping, ATP synthesis by chemiosmosis and reduction of NADP. They supply the ATP and reduced NADP that the light-independent reactions consume, and they depend in turn on the light-independent reactions returning ADP, phosphate and NADP for re-use; without light they stop at once.
Light-independent reactions

The reactions of the Calvin cycle in the stroma, which do not use light directly but depend on the ATP and reduced NADP made in the light-dependent reactions. In darkness they stop within minutes as ATP and reduced NADP are used up. If carbon dioxide is absent they stop consuming ATP and reduced NADP, so NADP and ADP are not regenerated, electrons cannot leave photosystem I, and the light-dependent reactions including photosystem II come to a halt.
Receptor

A protein with a binding site whose shape and chemical properties are complementary to a specific signalling chemical. Binding of the signalling chemical is reversible and non-catalytic: the receptor changes conformation rather than changing the chemical, and this conformational change is what starts the cell's response. Receptors may be transmembrane proteins in the plasma membrane or intracellular proteins in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
Ligand

The IB term for a signalling chemical that binds to the binding site of a receptor. Hormones, neurotransmitters, cytokines and autoinducers are all ligands for their receptors. A cell responds to a ligand only if it possesses a receptor with a binding site specific to that ligand, which is why the same chemical circulating through a whole body affects only particular target cells.
Quorum sensing

Cell signalling among bacteria in which each cell secretes a small signalling chemical (an autoinducer) into its surroundings. The concentration of autoinducer rises with population density; once it passes a threshold it binds to receptors in the cells and changes gene expression across the whole population, so behaviours that are only worthwhile at high density are switched on together.
Bioluminescence in Vibrio fischeri

The marine bacterium Vibrio fischeri lives free in seawater at low density, where it does not glow, and at very high density in the light organ of the Hawaiian bobtail squid, where it does. Each cell secretes an autoinducer (an acyl-homoserine lactone); when the population is dense enough for the autoinducer to reach its threshold concentration, it binds a receptor protein that promotes transcription of the lux genes, which encode luciferase, the enzyme that produces light.
Hormone

A signalling chemical secreted by endocrine cells or glands into the blood, which transports it throughout the body. It acts on distant target cells that carry receptors for it, typically over minutes to hours and often on cells in several organs at once. Hormones are a functional category defined by how the chemical is released and delivered, not by its chemistry.
Neurotransmitter

A signalling chemical released from the presynaptic membrane of a neuron into a synaptic gap, across which it diffuses to bind receptors on the postsynaptic cell within a millisecond. Its effect is localized to that synapse and short-lived, because it is rapidly broken down or reabsorbed. Some chemicals, such as noradrenaline, serve as neurotransmitters at synapses and as hormones when released into the blood.
Cytokine

A small protein signalling chemical secreted by cells, especially cells of the immune system, that mostly acts on nearby cells (or on the secreting cell itself) to coordinate responses such as inflammation, cell division and differentiation of immune cells. Cytokines are not produced by endocrine glands and are distinguished from hormones by their mainly local action and their cellular sources.
Calcium ions as signalling chemicals

Calcium ions (Ca2+) are kept at a very low concentration in the cytoplasm by pumps. When channels open in the plasma membrane or in intracellular stores such as the endoplasmic reticulum, Ca2+ floods into the cytoplasm and binds to proteins that trigger rapid responses, including muscle contraction and release of neurotransmitter from a presynaptic neuron. Unlike the other categories, calcium ions are not synthesized by the cell and act as signals within the cell.
Amine hormones

Hormones that are small molecules derived from a single amino acid, mostly tyrosine. Epinephrine (adrenaline) and noradrenaline are amines made from tyrosine; thyroxine is also tyrosine-derived. Being hydrophilic, epinephrine cannot cross the plasma membrane and binds to transmembrane receptors.
Protein and peptide hormones

Hormones that are chains of amino acids, from short peptides to full proteins. Insulin is a protein hormone of 51 amino acids in two chains. Protein hormones are hydrophilic and so remain outside the cell, binding to transmembrane receptors in the plasma membrane.
Steroid hormones

Hormones that are lipids synthesized from cholesterol, with a characteristic four-ring carbon skeleton. Oestradiol, progesterone and testosterone are steroid hormones. Being hydrophobic, they pass through the phospholipid bilayer and bind intracellular receptors in the cytoplasm or nucleus.
Chemical groups of neurotransmitters

Neurotransmitters are chemically diverse: amino acids (glutamate, GABA and glycine), peptides (such as endorphins), amines (such as dopamine, noradrenaline and serotonin) and a gas, which the guide lists as nitrous oxide (the gas that acts as a neurotransmitter is nitric oxide, NO). Acetylcholine, the transmitter at neuromuscular junctions, is a small molecule that fits none of these groups.
Reasons for chemical diversity of signalling chemicals

A body sends many different messages at the same time through the same blood and tissue fluid. Because each receptor binds only a ligand with a complementary shape, using chemically distinct signalling chemicals lets each message be read only by cells with the matching receptor, without cross-talk. Different chemistries also suit different jobs: hydrophobic steroids can enter cells and act on genes over hours, while small hydrophilic amines and amino acids act on surface receptors within seconds and are quickly removed.
Distant signalling by hormones

Hormones are secreted into the blood and carried to every part of the body, so a hormone released in one place can act on cells in several distant organs simultaneously. The response develops over seconds to hours, and the hormone persists until it is removed by the liver or kidneys. Only cells carrying receptors for that hormone respond, so distribution is general but the effect is targeted.
Localized signalling by neurotransmitters

A neurotransmitter is released into the synaptic gap, a space about 20 nm wide between the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes, and diffuses across it in under a millisecond. Its effect is confined to the postsynaptic cell of that synapse and is ended quickly by enzymic breakdown or reuptake, so neurotransmitters give fast, precise, local effects, in contrast to the widespread, slower effects of hormones in the blood.
Transmembrane receptor

A receptor protein spanning the plasma membrane. Its membrane-spanning region is made of hydrophobic amino acids that sit among the hydrocarbon tails of the phospholipids, while the extracellular part carrying the ligand-binding site and the cytoplasmic part are made largely of hydrophilic amino acids. The ligand remains outside the cell; the signal, not the chemical, is passed across the membrane.
Intracellular receptor

A receptor protein located in the cytoplasm or nucleus, with a largely hydrophilic surface so that it is soluble in the aqueous interior of the cell, and a hydrophobic pocket that binds its ligand. Its ligands are hydrophobic chemicals such as steroid hormones, which penetrate the phospholipid bilayer to reach it. Activated intracellular receptors typically act on DNA to change gene expression.
Signal transduction

The sequence of responses within a cell that is set off when a ligand binds to a receptor. Binding changes the shape of the receptor, and this change is passed on through a series of molecular events (activation of proteins, production of second messengers, phosphorylation of enzymes) that ends in a response such as an enzyme becoming active, a channel opening or a gene being transcribed. The receptor initiates the pathway; the ligand itself usually never enters the cell.
Signal amplification

A feature of many transduction pathways in which each activated component acts on many molecules of the next component, so that binding of a small number of ligand molecules produces a very large response. For example, one activated G protein activates an enzyme that makes many cAMP molecules, and each cAMP-activated kinase phosphorylates many enzyme molecules.
Acetylcholine receptor (ligand-gated ion channel)

A transmembrane receptor at synapses and neuromuscular junctions that is itself an ion channel. When two acetylcholine molecules bind to sites on its extracellular part, the receptor changes shape and the channel through its centre opens, allowing positively charged ions (chiefly Na+) to diffuse into the cell down their concentration gradient. Acetylcholine itself stays outside the cell.
Depolarization of the membrane potential

The membrane potential is the voltage across the plasma membrane, about -70 mV inside relative to outside in a resting neuron. Inflow of positively charged ions through opened acetylcholine receptor channels makes the inside less negative; this change is depolarization. If the depolarization reaches the threshold, it can trigger other changes such as an action potential in a neuron or contraction of a muscle fibre.
G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR)

A transmembrane receptor with seven membrane-spanning helices. Binding of its ligand on the outside changes its shape, and the cytoplasmic part then activates a G protein attached to the inner face of the membrane. Humans have many hundreds of different GPCRs, responding to hormones, neurotransmitters, odours and light, and they are the targets of a large fraction of medicinal drugs.
G protein

A protein on the cytoplasmic face of the plasma membrane that binds guanine nucleotides. In its inactive state it holds GDP; an activated GPCR causes it to exchange GDP for GTP, on which an activated subunit separates and switches on an effector such as the enzyme adenylyl cyclase. The G protein hydrolyses its GTP back to GDP after a short time, which switches it off, so the signal is conveyed into the cell but not left on.
Epinephrine (adrenaline)

An amine hormone secreted by the adrenal glands during stress or exercise. It binds to G protein-coupled receptors in the plasma membrane of target cells such as liver cells, and its effects, including breakdown of glycogen to release glucose, are brought about via cAMP. Both names come from the hormone's production by the adrenal gland (Latin ad = at, ren = kidney; Greek epi = above, nephros = kidney) and remain in use in different parts of the world.
Cyclic AMP (cAMP) as a second messenger

A small molecule made from ATP by the membrane enzyme adenylyl cyclase when it is switched on by an activated G protein. cAMP diffuses through the cytoplasm and activates protein kinases that phosphorylate enzymes, for example switching on glycogen breakdown in a liver cell. It is called a second messenger because it carries the message of the first messenger, the hormone that remained outside the cell, to targets inside it.
Tyrosine kinase receptor

A transmembrane receptor whose cytoplasmic domain is a kinase: when its ligand binds to the extracellular part, the receptor transfers phosphate groups from ATP onto tyrosine residues of its own cytoplasmic domain. These phosphorylated tyrosines start a sequence of reactions inside the cell. The insulin receptor is the IB example.
Insulin signalling to glucose transporters

Insulin, a protein hormone, binds to the extracellular part of its receptor in the plasma membrane and stays outside the cell. Binding causes phosphorylation of tyrosine on the cytoplasmic side of the receptor, which triggers a sequence of reactions ending with vesicles that contain glucose transporter proteins moving to and fusing with the plasma membrane. The extra transporters increase the rate at which the cell takes up glucose from the blood.
Steroid hormone receptor

An intracellular receptor for a steroid hormone such as oestradiol, progesterone or testosterone. The hormone diffuses through the plasma membrane and binds to a site on the receptor in the cytoplasm or nucleus, activating it. The activated hormone-receptor complex binds to specific DNA sequences near particular genes and promotes their transcription, so the response is a change in the proteins the cell makes and develops over minutes to hours.
Effect of oestradiol on GnRH-secreting cells

Oestradiol acts on cells in the hypothalamus that secrete gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH). At the moderate concentrations found through most of the cycle it inhibits GnRH secretion (negative feedback). When oestradiol rises to a high, sustained level as a follicle matures, its effect switches and it stimulates GnRH secretion (positive feedback), which drives the surge of luteinizing hormone that triggers ovulation.
Effect of progesterone on endometrial cells

Progesterone, secreted mainly after ovulation, acts on cells of the endometrium (the lining of the uterus). It maintains and thickens the endometrium, stimulates its glands to secrete and increases its blood supply, preparing it to receive an embryo. If progesterone secretion falls, the endometrium can no longer be maintained and is shed in menstruation.
Negative feedback

Regulation in which the response to a stimulus acts to reduce or reverse that stimulus, so the system tends to return to a set level. Example: oestradiol, secreted by the ovary when GnRH has stimulated the pituitary to release gonadotropins, inhibits the hypothalamic cells that secrete GnRH, limiting further oestradiol production. Negative feedback counteracts change in either direction; it does not mean simply 'lowering'.
Positive feedback

Regulation in which the response to a stimulus increases that stimulus, so the process is amplified until an end point is reached. Example: during birth, stretching of the cervix stimulates secretion of oxytocin, which strengthens uterine contractions, which stretch the cervix further; the loop ends with delivery. Positive feedback is a normal part of regulation used to drive a process rapidly to completion.
Neuron

A cell of the nervous system that carries electrical impulses. It consists of a cell body, containing the cytoplasm and nucleus, with elongated nerve fibres of varying length projecting from it, along which impulses are conducted.
Cell body
The part of a neuron that contains the nucleus and most of the cytoplasm. The nerve fibres, both the axon and the dendrites, project from it.
Axon

A long single nerve fibre projecting from the cell body of a neuron, along which impulses are conducted. In some human motor neurons a single axon extends about a metre from the spinal cord to a muscle.
Dendrite
One of the multiple shorter nerve fibres projecting from the cell body of a neuron. Impulses are conducted along dendrites as well as along the axon.
Nerve fibre

An elongated projection of a neuron, either an axon or a dendrite, along which electrical impulses are conducted. A nerve fibre is part of a single neuron; a nerve, by contrast, is a bundle of many fibres from many neurons.
Sodium–potassium pump

A transmembrane protein in the plasma membrane of a neuron that uses energy from ATP to move sodium ions out of the cell and potassium ions into it, against their concentration gradients. Three sodium ions are moved out for every two potassium ions moved in, so the cytoplasm becomes low in sodium ions and high in potassium ions.
Membrane potential

The difference in electrical potential (voltage) between the inside and the outside of a cell membrane, conventionally stated as the potential of the inside relative to the outside. It arises because charged ions are unequally distributed across the membrane.
Membrane polarization

The state of a membrane that has a difference in charge across it, one side being more positive and the other more negative. A resting neuron is polarized because its inside is negatively charged relative to its outside.
Resting potential

The membrane potential of a neuron that is not conducting an impulse, typically about −70 mV (inside negative). It is generated and maintained by the sodium–potassium pump, which establishes concentration gradients, together with the greater leakage of potassium ions out of the cell than of sodium ions into it and the presence of negatively charged proteins inside the cell that cannot cross the membrane.
Nerve impulse

An action potential that is propagated along a nerve fibre. It is an electrical signal because it involves movement of positively charged ions (sodium and potassium ions) across the membrane, which changes the membrane potential.
Action potential

A rapid, temporary reversal of the membrane potential of a nerve fibre, in which the inside briefly becomes positive relative to the outside (depolarization) and then returns to the negative resting potential (repolarization). It is propagated along the fibre without decreasing in size.
Giant axon of squid

A very wide non-myelinated axon, up to about 1 mm in diameter, that conducts impulses at about 25 m s⁻¹. This is far faster than narrow non-myelinated fibres, which may be only about 1 µm wide and conduct at around 1 m s⁻¹, showing that conduction speed is positively correlated with axon diameter.
Myelinated fibre

A nerve fibre surrounded by a myelin sheath. Myelinated fibres conduct impulses much faster than non-myelinated fibres of similar diameter; myelinated fibres in mammals can conduct at over 100 m s⁻¹, faster even than a squid giant axon many times wider.
Correlation coefficient (r)

A statistic between −1 and +1 that measures the strength and direction of a linear relationship between two variables. The sign shows the direction (positive when the variables rise together, negative when one falls as the other rises) and the magnitude shows the strength, with values near ±1 indicating a strong correlation and values near 0 a weak one. A correlation, however strong, does not by itself show that one variable causes the other.
Coefficient of determination (R²)

The square of the correlation coefficient, r², expressed as a value from 0 to 1 or as a percentage. It gives the proportion of the variation in the dependent variable that is explained by variation in the independent variable; for example, if r = 0.9 then R² = 0.81, so 81% of the variation is explained. R² has no sign and so does not indicate the direction of a correlation.
Positive and negative correlation

A positive correlation is one in which the dependent variable tends to increase as the independent variable increases, as conduction speed does with axon diameter. A negative correlation is one in which the dependent variable tends to decrease as the independent variable increases, as conduction speed does with animal size.
Synapse

A junction between a neuron and another cell, either another neuron or an effector cell such as a muscle fibre or gland cell, across which a signal passes by means of a chemical neurotransmitter. A signal can pass across a typical synapse in one direction only.
Presynaptic and postsynaptic neuron

The presynaptic neuron is the neuron that brings an impulse to a synapse and releases neurotransmitter from its presynaptic membrane. The postsynaptic cell is the neuron or effector cell whose membrane carries the receptors for that neurotransmitter and which is stimulated as a result.
Effector cell

A cell that carries out a response when it is stimulated by a neuron, such as a muscle fibre that contracts or a gland cell that secretes. The synapse between a motor neuron and a muscle fibre is a neuromuscular junction.
Neurotransmitter

A chemical stored in vesicles in the presynaptic neuron and released into the synaptic cleft when an impulse arrives. It diffuses across the cleft and binds to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane, passing the signal to the postsynaptic cell.
Calcium as an intracellular signalling chemical

When an action potential depolarizes the presynaptic membrane, calcium channels in that membrane open and calcium ions diffuse into the presynaptic neuron from the surrounding fluid. Inside the neuron the calcium ions act as a signal that causes vesicles of neurotransmitter to fuse with the presynaptic membrane.
Exocytosis of neurotransmitter

The release of neurotransmitter from the presynaptic neuron by fusion of vesicles with the presynaptic membrane, so that their contents are emptied into the synaptic cleft. It is triggered by the entry of calcium ions.
Synaptic cleft
The narrow fluid-filled gap, about 20 nm wide, between the presynaptic membrane and the postsynaptic membrane. Neurotransmitter crosses it by diffusion.
Transmembrane receptor

A protein in the postsynaptic membrane to which a neurotransmitter binds. In an excitatory synapse the receptor is, or opens, a channel that lets positively charged ions such as sodium ions diffuse into the postsynaptic cell.
Excitatory postsynaptic potential (EPSP)

A depolarization of the postsynaptic membrane caused by an excitatory neurotransmitter binding to its receptors and opening channels through which positively charged ions, mainly sodium ions, enter. It brings the membrane potential closer to the threshold for an action potential.
Acetylcholine

A neurotransmitter used at many types of synapse, including synapses between neurons in the central and peripheral nervous systems and neuromuscular junctions between motor neurons and skeletal muscle fibres. Binding of acetylcholine to its receptors on the postsynaptic membrane generates an excitatory postsynaptic potential.
Neuromuscular junction

The synapse between a motor neuron and a skeletal muscle fibre. Acetylcholine released from the motor neuron binds to receptors on the muscle fibre membrane and depolarizes it, leading to contraction.
Threshold potential

The membrane potential, typically about −55 mV, that must be reached for voltage-gated sodium channels to open and an action potential to be produced. A depolarization that does not reach threshold fades away without producing an action potential.
Voltage-gated sodium channel

A channel protein in the membrane of a nerve fibre that opens when the membrane potential reaches the threshold. Sodium ions then diffuse into the fibre down their concentration gradient, causing depolarization; the channels then close before the membrane repolarizes.
Voltage-gated potassium channel

A channel protein in the membrane of a nerve fibre that opens in response to the depolarization of an action potential, slightly later than the sodium channels. Potassium ions diffuse out of the fibre down their concentration gradient, causing repolarization.
Depolarization

The change in membrane potential during an action potential from the negative resting value to a positive value (about +30 mV), caused by the entry of sodium ions through voltage-gated sodium channels.
Repolarization

The return of the membrane potential from its positive peak to the negative resting value, caused by the exit of potassium ions through voltage-gated potassium channels. The sodium–potassium pump does not cause repolarization, but afterwards restores the concentration gradients that the action potential has slightly reduced.
Local current

The movement of ions along a nerve fibre, inside and outside it, between a region that is depolarized and the adjacent resting region. Sodium ions that have entered diffuse along the inside of the fibre away from the depolarized region, and outside the fibre sodium ions diffuse towards it, reducing the membrane potential of the adjacent region until it reaches threshold.
Propagation of an action potential

The passage of an action potential along a nerve fibre, in which local currents from each depolarized region bring the next region to threshold, opening its voltage-gated sodium channels so that it produces its own action potential. Each region regenerates the action potential in turn, so the impulse does not fade as it travels.
Oscilloscope trace

A graph of membrane potential (usually in millivolts) against time (usually in milliseconds), recorded from electrodes placed inside and outside a nerve fibre. A resting potential appears as a steady line at about −70 mV; an action potential appears as a spike that rises to about +30 mV during depolarization, falls during repolarization, may briefly dip below the resting potential, and then returns to it.
Impulse frequency

The number of action potentials passing along a nerve fibre per second, found from an oscilloscope trace by counting the spikes and dividing by the time in seconds that the trace covers. A stronger stimulus produces a higher frequency of impulses, not larger action potentials.
Myelin sheath

An insulating layer of membrane, laid down by Schwann cells, that wraps around a myelinated nerve fibre. It is interrupted at intervals by nodes of Ranvier and prevents ion movement across the parts of the membrane it covers.
Node of Ranvier
A short gap in the myelin sheath of a myelinated fibre where the membrane is exposed. Ion pumps and voltage-gated channels are clustered at the nodes, so action potentials occur only there.
Saltatory conduction

Propagation of an action potential along a myelinated fibre from one node of Ranvier to the next. Local currents spread rapidly along the insulated section between nodes and depolarize the next node to threshold, so the action potential appears to jump from node to node. Because only the nodes have to be depolarized, conduction is much faster than in a non-myelinated fibre.
Neonicotinoid

A type of pesticide that binds to acetylcholine receptors at synapses in the central nervous system of insects. The receptors can then no longer respond normally to acetylcholine, so synaptic transmission is blocked and the insect is paralysed and dies.
Cocaine

A drug that blocks reuptake of the neurotransmitter dopamine by binding to the transporter proteins that would return dopamine to the presynaptic neuron. Dopamine therefore remains in the synaptic cleft and continues to stimulate the postsynaptic neuron.
Reuptake

The removal of neurotransmitter from the synaptic cleft by transporter proteins that move it back into the presynaptic neuron, ending its action on the postsynaptic receptors. Blocking reuptake prolongs and intensifies the stimulation of the postsynaptic cell.
Inhibitory neurotransmitter

A neurotransmitter, such as GABA, whose binding to receptors on the postsynaptic membrane opens channels that make the inside of the postsynaptic cell more negative, for example by letting chloride ions in or potassium ions out. This hyperpolarizes the membrane and makes an action potential less likely.
Hyperpolarization
A change in membrane potential to a value more negative than the resting potential, for example from −70 mV to −75 mV. A hyperpolarized membrane is further from the threshold potential.
Inhibitory postsynaptic potential (IPSP)

A hyperpolarization of the postsynaptic membrane caused by an inhibitory neurotransmitter, which moves the membrane potential further from threshold and so reduces the likelihood that the postsynaptic neuron will produce an action potential.
Summation

The adding together of the postsynaptic potentials produced by several presynaptic neurons acting on one postsynaptic neuron. Excitatory potentials depolarize and inhibitory potentials hyperpolarize, so the combined effect is their net sum; an action potential is produced only if this net change reaches threshold.
All-or-nothing response

The principle that a postsynaptic neuron either produces a full-sized action potential, if the summed postsynaptic potentials reach threshold, or produces none at all. Postsynaptic potentials themselves are graded in size, but the action potential they may trigger is not.
Free nerve ending

The unspecialized ending of a sensory neuron in the skin that responds to painful stimuli. Its membrane has channels for positively charged ions that open in response to high temperature, acid, or certain chemicals such as capsaicin. Entry of positively charged ions depolarizes the membrane to threshold, and impulses then pass along the neuron to the brain.
Capsaicin

The chemical in chilli peppers that produces a burning sensation. It opens channels for positively charged ions in free nerve endings, the same response these endings give to high temperature, so the brain perceives pain even though the tissue is not hot.
Perception of pain

The awareness of pain, which occurs in the brain when impulses from free nerve endings reach it. The nerve endings in the skin detect the stimulus and generate the impulses, but the pain itself is perceived in the brain, not in the skin.
Emergent property

A property of a whole system that arises from the interaction of its components and is not a property of any component on its own. Consciousness is an emergent property of the brain: it arises from the interaction of very many neurons, and no individual neuron is conscious.
Consciousness

The state of awareness of oneself and one's surroundings. It emerges from the interaction of the individual neurons of the brain and cannot be located in, or explained by, any single neuron or its signals.
System integration

The coordination of the component parts of a living system so that together they perform an overall function that no part could perform alone. Integration is a necessary process in living systems at every level, from organelles within a cell to organs within a body.
Hierarchy of subsystems

The organization of a multicellular organism in levels: cells are grouped into tissues (groups of similar cells performing a shared function), tissues into organs, organs into body systems, and body systems into the whole organism. Each level is a subsystem of the level above and is integrated with the others.
Emergent property

A property of a whole system that its component parts do not have on their own and that arises from the interaction of those parts. A cheetah becoming an effective predator is an emergent property of the integration of its muscular, skeletal, nervous, respiratory and circulatory systems; no single system makes it a predator.
Nervous signalling

Communication between organs by electrical impulses conducted along neurons, with chemical transmission across synapses. A message travels rapidly along a fixed pathway of neurons to a specific target, so nervous responses are fast, precisely targeted and usually short-lived.
Hormonal (endocrine) signalling

Communication between organs by hormones, chemical messengers secreted by endocrine glands directly into the blood. The blood carries a hormone to every part of the body, but only cells with receptors for that hormone respond. Hormonal responses are typically slower to begin and longer-lasting than nervous responses, and one hormone can affect many organs at once.
Transport by the blood system

The movement of materials between organs by the circulating blood, which integrates organs that are far apart. Examples: oxygen absorbed in the lungs is carried to respiring tissues; glucose absorbed in the small intestine is carried to the liver and to muscles; urea produced by the liver is carried to the kidneys; and hormones are carried from endocrine glands to their target organs.
Brain as central information integration organ

The brain receives information from many receptors at once, combines it with stored information from previous experience and uses the combined result to decide on responses. This processing of combined inputs, together with learning (changes in behaviour as a result of experience) and memory (the storage and later retrieval of information), makes the brain the central integrating organ of the body.
Conscious and unconscious processes

A conscious process is one of which the person is aware and which involves processing in the cerebral hemispheres, such as deciding to pick up a cup. An unconscious process takes place without awareness or a decision, such as a reflex or the adjustment of heart rate; it can be integrated in the spinal cord or in parts of the brain such as the medulla, without the cerebral hemispheres deciding on the response.
Spinal cord as an integrating centre

The part of the central nervous system inside the vertebral column, with grey matter (cell bodies, interneurons and synapses) surrounded by white matter (myelinated nerve fibres). As well as conducting impulses to and from the brain, the spinal cord integrates unconscious processes such as reflexes: it receives sensory input and sends motor output without the cerebral hemispheres being involved in the decision.
Receptor cell

A cell that detects a stimulus (a change in the internal or external environment) and produces a signal that is passed to a sensory neuron. Examples are photoreceptor cells in the retina and hair cells in the cochlea. In the skin, the free nerve ending of a sensory neuron itself acts as a pain receptor.
Sensory neuron

A neuron that conveys messages, as nerve impulses, from receptor cells to the central nervous system. Sensory neurons provide the input to the spinal cord and, via the spinal cord or the cranial nerves, to the cerebral hemispheres. Impulses travel along a sensory neuron in one direction only, towards the CNS.
Motor neuron

A neuron that carries nerve impulses from the central nervous system to an effector. Motor neurons carrying output from the cerebral hemispheres end at skeletal muscle fibres, where their impulses stimulate the muscle to contract. A muscle can only be stimulated to contract; it relaxes when stimulation stops and is lengthened by the contraction of an antagonistic muscle.
Nerve

A bundle of nerve fibres (the long axons of neurons) enclosed in a protective sheath of connective tissue. Most nerves contain fibres of both sensory and motor neurons, so a single nerve carries impulses towards the CNS in some fibres and away from it in others. A neuron is a single cell; a nerve contains fibres from many neurons.
Myelinated and unmyelinated nerve fibres

In a transverse section of a nerve, a myelinated fibre appears as an axon surrounded by a thick myelin sheath, formed by Schwann cells wrapped around it, which insulates the axon and greatly increases the speed at which impulses are conducted. An unmyelinated fibre has no such sheath and conducts more slowly. Both types are normally present in the same nerve.
Reflex arc

The pathway of neurons that produces a reflex: a rapid, involuntary response to a stimulus that does not require a decision by the brain. In the pain reflex of the hand, a free sensory nerve ending acts as the pain receptor; the sensory neuron carries the impulse to the grey matter of the spinal cord, where a single interneuron passes it to a motor neuron, which stimulates skeletal muscle in the arm (the effector) to contract and withdraw the hand.
Interneuron

A neuron located entirely within the central nervous system that connects other neurons. In the pain reflex arc a single interneuron in the grey matter of the spinal cord links the sensory neuron to the motor neuron. Other interneurons pass the sensory information up the spinal cord to the brain, so the pain is felt shortly after the reflex has already withdrawn the hand.
Effector

The structure that carries out the response to a stimulus: a muscle or a gland. In the pain reflex the effector is skeletal muscle, which is stimulated to contract even though the response is involuntary; being skeletal muscle does not make a response voluntary.
Cerebellum

A region of the brain, below and behind the cerebral hemispheres, that coordinates the contraction of skeletal muscles and maintains balance and posture. It does not initiate voluntary movements, which are commanded by the cerebral hemispheres; it uses information from the eyes, the inner ear and receptors in muscles and joints to make movements smooth, accurate and well-timed.
Circadian rhythm

A cycle of physiological activity with a period of about 24 hours, generated within the body and synchronized to the day–night cycle by light detected by the eyes. The cycle of sleeping and waking is a circadian rhythm.
Melatonin

A hormone secreted by the pineal gland in the brain in a diurnal pattern: secretion rises in the evening as light fades, is highest during the night and falls to a low level during the day, because light detected by the retina suppresses it. A high melatonin concentration promotes sleepiness, so the pattern helps to establish the cycle of sleeping and waking.
Epinephrine (adrenaline)

A hormone secreted by the adrenal glands, above the kidneys, in response to danger, stress or the anticipation of vigorous activity. Its widespread effects prepare the body for intense muscle contraction: heart rate and stroke volume increase; bronchioles dilate and ventilation increases; glycogen in the liver is broken down, raising blood glucose; blood is diverted to skeletal muscle by vasodilation there and vasoconstriction in the gut and skin; and the pupils dilate.
Hypothalamus

A region of the brain that links the nervous system and the endocrine system. It monitors conditions in the blood, such as temperature and solute concentration, receives information from other parts of the brain, and controls the pituitary gland so that the pituitary secretes the hormones the body needs.
Pituitary gland

A small endocrine gland attached beneath the hypothalamus. Under the control of the hypothalamus it secretes hormones, some of which act directly on body tissues (for example growth hormone and ADH) and some of which control other endocrine glands (for example TSH controls the thyroid gland, and FSH and LH control the gonads). Through the pituitary, the hypothalamus controls much of the endocrine system.
Baroreceptor

A stretch receptor in the walls of the aorta and the carotid arteries that monitors blood pressure. When blood pressure rises the artery wall is stretched more and the baroreceptors send impulses more frequently to the medulla.
Chemoreceptor

A receptor that monitors the chemical composition of the blood: its pH and its concentrations of oxygen and carbon dioxide. Chemoreceptors are located in the walls of the aorta and the carotid arteries (the aortic and carotid bodies) and in the medulla of the brainstem.
Medulla (medulla oblongata)

The part of the brainstem that coordinates the unconscious control of heart rate and ventilation. Its cardiovascular centre receives impulses from baroreceptors and chemoreceptors and sends nerve impulses to the heart: impulses along the sympathetic nerve increase heart rate and stroke volume, and impulses along the parasympathetic (vagus) nerve decrease heart rate. Its respiratory centre sends impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles.
Stroke volume
The volume of blood pumped out of a ventricle in one heartbeat. Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume, so the medulla can increase the output of the heart by increasing either or both.
Feedback control of ventilation rate

Cell respiration produces carbon dioxide, which dissolves in blood plasma and forms carbonic acid; this releases hydrogen ions and lowers blood pH. Chemoreceptors in the brainstem detect the fall in pH and the respiratory centre of the medulla sends more frequent impulses to the diaphragm and intercostal muscles, increasing the rate and depth of ventilation. More carbon dioxide is exhaled, blood pH rises back towards normal and the stimulus is removed: negative feedback.
Peristalsis
Waves of contraction of the circular and longitudinal smooth muscle in the wall of the gut that move material along it. Peristalsis is involuntary and does not depend on gravity.
Enteric nervous system (ENS)

A network of neurons in the wall of the gut that controls peristalsis and other gut activity involuntarily, without instructions from the CNS. The ENS coordinates the contractions of the gut wall so that material passes along the gut in an orderly way at a rate suited to digestion and absorption. Initiation of swallowing and egestion of faeces are under voluntary control by the CNS; peristalsis between these points is controlled by the ENS.
Qualitative and quantitative observations

A qualitative observation is a description without numerical measurement, such as a labelled diagram recording that a seedling shoot has curved towards the light. A quantitative observation is a numerical measurement, such as the angle of curvature of the shoot measured with a protractor in degrees. Both are valid scientific data.
Precision, accuracy and reliability

Precision is how closely repeated measurements of the same quantity agree with each other; it is limited by the resolution of the instrument (for example a protractor marked in 1° divisions) and by random error. Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value; it is reduced by systematic error, such as aligning the protractor against the wrong reference line. Reliability is the consistency of results when the investigation is repeated; it is improved by using many seedlings and repeating the experiment. Repeating measurements reduces the effect of random error but does not remove a systematic error.
Positive phototropism

The directional growth of a plant shoot towards a source of light coming from one side. A tropism is a growth response in which the direction of growth is determined by the direction of the stimulus. Phototropism is caused by cells on the shaded side of the shoot elongating more than cells on the lit side; it is growth, not movement of existing tissues.
Phytohormone

A signalling chemical produced by plant cells that regulates growth, development or responses to stimuli in other cells, usually at very low concentrations. Plants use a variety of chemicals as phytohormones, including auxins, cytokinins, gibberellins, abscisic acid and the gas ethylene. Plants have no endocrine glands: phytohormones are produced in many tissues and move from cell to cell or in the xylem and phloem.
Auxin efflux carrier

A membrane protein that actively transports auxin out of a plant cell. Auxin can diffuse freely into cells but cannot diffuse out, so the position of the efflux carriers determines the direction in which auxin leaves. When all the cells in a tissue concentrate their efflux carriers on the same side, auxin is transported from cell to cell in one direction and becomes concentrated in part of the plant, maintaining a concentration gradient.
Apoplast

The continuous network of cell walls and intercellular spaces outside the plasma membranes of plant cells. Auxin promotes the secretion of hydrogen ions from the cytoplasm into the apoplast, which acidifies the cell wall.
Promotion of cell growth by auxin

Auxin stimulates proton pumps in the plasma membrane to secrete hydrogen ions into the apoplast. The resulting low pH in the cell wall loosens the cross links between cellulose molecules, so the wall can stretch and the cell elongates as it takes up water. In a shoot lit from one side, auxin is concentrated on the shaded side, so cells there elongate more and the difference in growth rate bends the shoot towards the light.
Cytokinin

A phytohormone produced in root tips and transported to the shoots, where it promotes shoot growth. Auxin is produced in shoot tips and transported to the roots. The interaction between the two phytohormones ensures that root and shoot growth remain integrated: each organ signals its growth to the other, so neither outgrows what the other can support.
Ethylene (ethene)

A gaseous phytohormone (IUPAC name: ethene) that stimulates the changes in fruits that occur during ripening, such as softening of cell walls, conversion of starch to sugars and changes in colour. Because it is a gas, ethylene diffuses through the air from one fruit to neighbouring fruits.
Positive feedback in fruit ripening

A control mechanism in which the response increases the original stimulus, so the process accelerates. Ethylene stimulates ripening, and ripening stimulates the fruit to produce more ethylene, which spreads to neighbouring cells and fruits. As a result the ripening of a fruit, and of the fruits on a plant, is rapid and synchronized, which benefits the plant by making its fruit attractive to seed-dispersing animals at the same time.
Infectious disease

A disease caused by a pathogen that can be transmitted to a host. It is distinguished from non-infectious diseases such as genetic disorders or deficiency diseases, which are not caused by another organism and cannot be transmitted from one person to another by infection.
Careful observation as a source of progress (NOS)

Careful observation of patterns can lead to important progress even before the underlying mechanism is known. In 19th-century Vienna, Semmelweis observed that deaths from childbed fever were far higher on the ward staffed by doctors who came from dissecting corpses than on the ward staffed by midwives, and showed that hand-washing in chlorinated lime reduced deaths. In London in 1854, Snow mapped cholera deaths, found they clustered around the Broad Street water pump and had its handle removed. Both acted decades before the germ theory of disease was accepted and the bacteria responsible were generally recognized.
Primary defence

The barriers that prevent pathogens from entering the body in the first place, as opposed to the immune responses that act once a pathogen is inside. The skin and the mucous membranes are the primary defences.
Skin as a physical and chemical barrier

The skin is a physical barrier because its outer layer consists of tough dead cells that pathogens cannot easily penetrate. It is also a chemical barrier: sebum secreted by sebaceous glands contains fatty acids that keep the surface at a low pH, which inhibits the growth of many pathogens.
Mucous membrane

The moist lining of surfaces that open to the outside, including the airways, the digestive tract, the reproductive tract and the eyes. These surfaces lack the tough dead outer layer of skin, but the mucus they secrete traps pathogens so that they can be removed, for example by cilia or by swallowing, before they can penetrate the epithelium.
Platelet

A small cell fragment in the blood, without a nucleus, formed from large cells in the bone marrow. When a blood vessel is damaged, platelets adhere to the damaged site and release clotting factors that start the clotting cascade.
Clotting factors

Substances released by platelets (and from damaged tissue) at the site of a cut that initiate the clotting cascade. Without their release, the cascade does not start, so clots do not form in undamaged vessels.
Clotting cascade

A sequence of reactions, started by the release of clotting factors, in which each step activates the next. Because each activated enzyme molecule can act on many molecules of the next component, the cascade amplifies the initial signal, which is why the final conversion of fibrinogen to fibrin by thrombin is rapid.
Thrombin
The enzyme produced at the end of the clotting cascade. Thrombin catalyses the rapid conversion of the soluble plasma protein fibrinogen into insoluble fibrin at the site of damage.
Fibrinogen and fibrin

Fibrinogen is a soluble protein that circulates in the plasma of healthy people all the time. Thrombin converts it into fibrin, an insoluble protein that forms a mesh of fibres across the wound. The mesh traps erythrocytes (and platelets) to form a clot that seals the cut.
Innate immune system

The part of the immune system that responds to broad categories of pathogen rather than to particular ones, and that does not change during an organism's life: it responds in the same way to a pathogen however many times that pathogen is encountered. Phagocytes are the component of the innate system that IB students need to know.
Adaptive immune system

The part of the immune system, based on lymphocytes, that responds in a specific way to particular pathogens and builds up a memory of the pathogens encountered, so that the response to a pathogen becomes faster and more effective on later exposures.
Phagocyte

A white blood cell of the innate immune system that recognizes pathogens as foreign, engulfs them by endocytosis and digests them using enzymes from lysosomes. Phagocytes are not specific to a particular pathogen: the same cell can engulf many kinds.
Amoeboid movement

Movement of a cell by extending its cytoplasm and flowing into the extension, as an amoeba does. Phagocytes use it to squeeze out between the cells of a capillary wall and crawl through tissues to sites of infection.
Endocytosis of a pathogen

The process by which a phagocyte engulfs a pathogen: the plasma membrane extends around the pathogen and fuses to enclose it in a vesicle inside the cell. The pathogen does not pass through the membrane into the cytoplasm; it remains inside the vesicle, where lysosomes fuse with it and their enzymes digest it.
Lysosome

A membrane-bound vesicle in the cytoplasm containing hydrolytic enzymes. In a phagocyte, lysosomes fuse with the vesicle containing an engulfed pathogen and their enzymes digest it, keeping the enzymes separated from the phagocyte's own cytoplasm.
Lymphocyte
A white blood cell of the adaptive immune system. Lymphocytes both circulate in the blood and are contained in lymph nodes. B-lymphocytes and helper T-lymphocytes cooperate to produce antibodies.
B-lymphocyte

A lymphocyte that can produce antibodies. An individual has a very large number of different B-lymphocytes, and each one makes a single specific type of antibody, determined before the cell ever meets an antigen. Only the B-lymphocytes whose antibody fits a particular antigen respond to it.
Lymph node

A small organ on a lymph vessel in which large numbers of lymphocytes are contained. Lymph draining from the tissues passes through lymph nodes, bringing antigens into contact with the lymphocytes there; the nodes swell during infection as lymphocytes multiply.
Antibody

A protein produced by B-lymphocytes (in their plasma cell form) that binds specifically to one type of antigen. Binding to antigens on a pathogen helps to eliminate it, for example by clumping pathogens together or marking them for destruction by phagocytes.
Antigen

A molecule that the immune system recognizes as foreign and that triggers antibody production. Most antigens are glycoproteins or other proteins, and they are usually located on the outer surface of a pathogen. An antibody's binding site is specific to one antigen.
Blood group antigens

Glycoproteins and other molecules on the surface of erythrocytes that differ between people, for example between the ABO blood groups. If erythrocytes are transfused into a person whose blood group is different, the antigens they carry are foreign to the recipient and may stimulate antibody production, so donor and recipient blood must be matched.
Helper T-lymphocyte

A lymphocyte that does not produce antibodies but is needed to activate B-lymphocytes. Helper T-cells are antigen-specific: a helper T-cell becomes activated by a particular type of antigen and can then activate B-cells specific to that same antigen.
Activation of B-lymphocytes

The process that a B-cell must undergo before it produces antibodies or becomes a memory cell. Activation requires two things: direct interaction of the B-cell with its specific antigen, and contact with a helper T-cell that has itself been activated by the same type of antigen.
Plasma cell

A B-lymphocyte that has been activated and has differentiated to secrete large quantities of antibody. Plasma cells have extensive rough endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus for the synthesis and secretion of antibody protein.
Clone of plasma cells

The large population of genetically identical plasma cells produced when an activated B-cell divides repeatedly by mitosis. Because there are only small numbers of B-cells specific to any one antigen, this multiplication is needed before enough antibody can be produced, and every cell in the clone makes the same type of antibody.
Immunity

The ability to eliminate an infectious disease from the body. It is due to the long-term survival of lymphocytes (memory cells) that are capable of making the specific antibodies needed to fight the infection, not to the antibodies themselves persisting.
Memory cell

A long-lived lymphocyte formed when a B-cell (or T-cell) is activated. Memory cells do not secrete antibodies while the pathogen is absent; if the same antigen is encountered again they respond rapidly, dividing to form plasma cells so that antibody is produced sooner and in larger amounts than on first exposure.
HIV

Human immunodeficiency virus, a retrovirus that infects and eventually destroys certain lymphocytes. Infection with HIV is not the same as AIDS: a person can carry and transmit HIV for years before AIDS develops.
Transmission of HIV in body fluids

HIV is transmitted when body fluids containing the virus, such as blood, semen, vaginal secretions or breast milk, pass from one person into another. Mechanisms include unprotected sexual intercourse, sharing of hypodermic needles by drug users, transfusion of unscreened blood or blood products, and transmission from mother to child across the placenta, during birth or in breast milk. HIV is not transmitted by casual contact, saliva, sneezing or insect bites.
AIDS

Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome, the condition that develops when HIV has killed so many helper T-lymphocytes that the adaptive immune system can no longer activate B-cells to produce antibodies. The person becomes unable to fight infections that a healthy immune system would control.
Opportunistic infection

An infection by a pathogen that rarely causes disease in a person with a functioning immune system, but which takes the opportunity provided by a weakened immune system. The illnesses that characterize AIDS are opportunistic infections caused by other pathogens, not diseases caused directly by HIV.
Antibiotic

A chemical that blocks a process occurring in bacteria but not in eukaryotic cells, so that it kills bacteria or stops them multiplying without harming the patient's cells. Examples of processes blocked are the synthesis of the peptidoglycan cell wall and protein synthesis on bacterial (70S) ribosomes.
Failure of antibiotics against viruses

Antibiotics do not control viral infections because viruses have no metabolism of their own: they lack cell walls, ribosomes and the enzymes that antibiotics target, and they reproduce using the metabolic processes of the host cell, which is a eukaryotic cell that antibiotics do not affect.
Antibiotic resistance

The ability of a strain of bacteria to survive and reproduce in the presence of an antibiotic that kills or inhibits other strains. Resistance arises by random mutation (or by acquiring a resistance gene from another bacterium) and then increases in frequency because the antibiotic kills susceptible bacteria and leaves the resistant ones to reproduce: it is evolution by natural selection.
Multiresistant bacteria

Strains of pathogenic bacteria that have accumulated resistance to several different antibiotics, each resistance requiring its own gene or mutation. Careful use of antibiotics, such as not prescribing them for viral infections and not using them unnecessarily in agriculture, reduces the selection pressure and slows the emergence of multiresistant strains.
Searching chemical libraries for new antibiotics (NOS)

A chemical library is a large collection of compounds that can be screened for a particular activity. Searching such libraries, in recent years with computer models trained to predict antibacterial activity, has identified candidate antibiotics with structures unlike existing ones. It illustrates that the development of a new technique can open up new avenues of research.
Zoonosis

An infectious disease that can transfer from other species of animal to humans. A large proportion of human infectious diseases, and most newly emerging ones, are zoonoses, and their modes of infection are varied.
Tuberculosis, rabies and Japanese encephalitis as zoonoses

Three zoonoses with different modes of infection. Tuberculosis: the bacterium Mycobacterium bovis can pass from cattle to humans in unpasteurized milk (and by inhalation). Rabies: a virus in the saliva of an infected mammal, such as a dog or bat, enters through a bite. Japanese encephalitis: a virus carried from infected pigs and wading birds to humans by mosquitoes.
COVID-19

The disease caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2, which is thought to have transferred to humans from another species, most probably bats, shortly before it was identified in 2019. Having crossed into humans it then spread between people by respiratory droplets, causing a pandemic with profound consequences for human health, societies and economies.
Vaccine

A preparation that stimulates the development of immunity to a specific pathogen without causing the disease. A vaccine contains antigens of the pathogen (for example a killed or weakened pathogen, or purified antigen molecules), or nucleic acid (DNA or RNA) with a sequence coding for an antigen so that the person's own cells produce it. The antigen triggers an adaptive immune response that leaves memory cells.
Immunization

The process of making a person immune to a disease, usually by vaccination. The vaccine's antigens activate specific B- and T-lymphocytes, which multiply and form memory cells, so a later infection by the real pathogen meets a rapid and effective response.
Herd immunity

Protection of a whole population that arises when a sufficient percentage of its members are immune to a disease, so that transmission is greatly impeded and chains of infection are broken. Members of a population are interdependent: each immune person reduces the chance that a susceptible person, including one who cannot be vaccinated, is exposed. The percentage needed depends on how easily the disease spreads.
Epidemic

An outbreak in which the number of cases of an infectious disease in a population rises rapidly above the usual level. Epidemics can be prevented by keeping the immune fraction of the population above the level at which each infected person, on average, infects fewer than one other.
Pragmatic truth and certainty (NOS)

Scientific claims are accepted as pragmatic truths, reliable enough to act on because they have survived testing and evaluation, not as absolute certainties. Scientists publish research so that others can evaluate it; the media often report results while that evaluation is still going on. Vaccines are tested rigorously and the risk of side effects is minimal but not nil, so decisions weigh a small risk against a large benefit.
Percentage change

The change in a quantity expressed as a percentage of its original value: percentage change = (final value − initial value) ÷ initial value × 100. It is negative for a decrease. The denominator is the initial value, not the final value.
Percentage difference

A comparison of two values where neither is the original or a reference value, such as case rates in two regions. In the convention used here, percentage difference = (difference between the values) ÷ (mean of the two values) × 100. Because the mean is used as the reference, the result is the same whichever value is listed first. When a question names a different reference value, use that value as the denominator instead.
Population

An interacting group of organisms of the same species living in the same area at the same time. Members of a population normally breed with one another, so a population is a reproductive unit as well as an ecological one.
Reproductive isolation between populations
