A specific base sequence in DNA, located near the start of a gene and upstream of it, to which transcription factors and RNA polymerase bind so that transcription of the gene can be initiated. The promoter is a control sequence: it is not part of the sequence that is transcribed into mRNA and it does not code for part of the polypeptide.
Enhancer

A specific base sequence in DNA to which activator transcription factors bind, increasing the rate of transcription of a gene. An enhancer may be thousands of base pairs away from the gene it regulates, upstream or downstream of it; looping of the DNA brings the proteins bound at the enhancer into contact with those bound at the promoter.
Transcription factor

A protein that binds to a specific base sequence in DNA, such as a promoter or an enhancer, and regulates transcription of a gene. In eukaryotic cells, transcription factors must bind to the promoter before RNA polymerase can bind and begin transcription; other transcription factors increase or decrease the rate of transcription, so which transcription factors are present and active in a cell helps to determine which genes are expressed.
Degradation of mRNA

The breakdown of mRNA molecules in the cytoplasm by nuclease enzymes, which hydrolyse the RNA into nucleotides. Because a molecule of mRNA can be translated repeatedly for as long as it persists, controlling how quickly it is degraded regulates how much polypeptide is made from a gene. In human cells, an mRNA may persist for anything from minutes up to days before it is broken down.
Nuclease

An enzyme that hydrolyses the phosphodiester bonds of a nucleic acid. The nucleases that degrade mRNA in the cytoplasm end the translation of that mRNA; they do not affect the gene in the nucleus, which can be transcribed again.
Epigenesis

The development of patterns of differentiation in the cells of a multicellular organism. All the body cells develop from a single zygote and contain the same genome; they become different from each other because different genes are expressed in different cells, not because their DNA base sequences differ.
Epigenetic change

A change in the pattern of gene expression of a cell that does not involve any change to the base sequence of its DNA. Epigenetic changes therefore alter the phenotype of the cell but not its genotype, which distinguishes them from mutations.
Genome

All of the genetic information of a cell or organism: the complete DNA base sequence, including every gene and the non-coding sequences. Apart from rare mutations, every body cell of a multicellular organism has the same genome, and it does not change as the cell differentiates or as conditions change.
Transcriptome

All of the RNA molecules, including mRNA, that are present in a cell at a particular time. Because no cell expresses all of its genes, the transcriptome contains transcripts of only part of the genome; it differs between cell types and changes as a cell responds to its conditions.
Proteome

All of the proteins present in a cell at a particular time. The proteome differs between cell types and changes over time, and it does not simply mirror the transcriptome: the amount of each protein also depends on how rapidly its mRNA is translated and degraded and on how long the protein itself persists.
Epigenetic tag

A chemical group added to DNA or to the histone proteins of a nucleosome that alters gene expression without altering the DNA base sequence. Methylation of cytosine in a promoter and methylation of amino acids in histones are examples.
Methylation of the promoter

The addition of methyl groups to cytosine bases in the DNA of a gene's promoter. This represses transcription and therefore the expression of the gene downstream of the promoter. The methylated cytosine is still cytosine and still pairs with guanine, so the base sequence is unchanged.
Histone methylation

The addition of methyl groups to amino acids in the histone proteins around which DNA is wound in nucleosomes. Depending on which amino acids are methylated, this can cause transcription of the associated genes to be repressed or activated; the details of how this is achieved are not required.
Epigenetic inheritance

The passing on of a change in gene expression, and so of a phenotypic change, to daughter cells or to offspring without any change in the nucleotide sequence of the DNA. It is possible when epigenetic tags such as DNA methylation or histone modification remain in place during mitosis (giving daughter cells the same pattern of expression) or during meiosis (so that the tags are present in gametes).
Environmental effect on gene expression

A change in which genes a cell or organism expresses, caused by a factor in its surroundings rather than by a change in its genes. Such factors often act by altering epigenetic tags, so the pattern of expression, and therefore the phenotype, changes while the genotype stays the same.
Air pollution and methyl tags

The example named in the guide: studies of people exposed to air pollution, such as particulate matter from traffic, have found altered patterns of methyl tags on the DNA of their cells, including on genes involved in inflammation and immune responses. The DNA base sequence is not changed by the pollution; its effect is on gene expression.
Removal of epigenetic tags from gametes

During the formation of sperm and ova and in the early embryo, most of the epigenetic tags carried on the DNA and histones are removed. This allows the cells of the embryo to develop a fresh pattern of differentiation. Some tags are not removed, so a few genes carry different tags depending on whether they came from the sperm or the ovum, and are expressed differently according to the parent that supplied them.
Ligers and tigons

Lion–tiger hybrids. A liger has a lion father and a tiger mother and grows much larger than either parent species; a tigon has a tiger father and a lion mother and does not. Both receive one set of lion chromosomes and one set of tiger chromosomes, so the size difference is not due to different genes. It arises because tags that were not removed from the sperm and ovum cause growth-related genes to be expressed differently depending on which parent supplied them.
Monozygotic twin study

An investigation that compares monozygotic (identical) twins, who developed from one zygote and so have the same genome. Because their genes are the same, differences in gene expression or phenotype between the twins must be due to differences in their environment, so such studies are used to investigate the effects of the environment on gene expression, for example by comparing the patterns of DNA methylation in twins of different ages or with different lifestyles.
lac operon

A group of genes in the bacterium Escherichia coli, transcribed together as one unit, that code for the proteins needed to take up and break down lactose, including the enzyme beta-galactosidase. Transcription is controlled by a repressor protein binding to the operator, a base sequence next to the promoter. The lactose-metabolizing genes are expressed only when lactose is present.
Repressor protein

A protein that binds to a specific base sequence in DNA and prevents transcription. The lac repressor binds to the operator of the lac operon, blocking RNA polymerase, when lactose is absent. When lactose is present, lactose (as its isomer allolactose) binds to the repressor and changes its shape so that it can no longer bind to the operator, allowing the genes to be transcribed.
Hormonal control of gene expression

The example of estrogen: a steroid hormone that passes through the plasma membrane of a target cell and binds to a receptor protein inside the cell. The hormone–receptor complex acts as a transcription factor, binding to specific base sequences in DNA and altering the transcription of target genes, so the hormone changes the pattern of gene expression in the cell.
Solvation

The process in which solute particles become separated from one another and surrounded by solvent molecules, so that the solute dissolves. With water as the solvent, solvation depends on the polarity of water: the oxygen atom carries a partial negative charge and the hydrogen atoms partial positive charges, so water molecules are attracted to charged ions and to polar molecules.
Hydrogen bonding between water and polar solutes

The attraction that holds polar molecules such as glucose in solution: hydrogen bonds form between the partially charged atoms of water molecules and polar groups on the solute, for example the hydroxyl (–OH) groups of a sugar. Non-polar molecules such as triglycerides have no such groups, so water cannot form hydrogen bonds with them and they do not dissolve.
Hydration of ions

The attraction of polar water molecules to charged ions when an ionic compound dissolves. Positively charged ions such as Na⁺ are attracted to the partially negative oxygen atoms of water molecules, and negatively charged ions such as Cl⁻ are attracted to the partially positive hydrogen atoms. Each ion becomes surrounded by a shell of oriented water molecules that keeps it separated from other ions.
Osmosis

The net movement of water across a partially permeable membrane from a solution with a lower solute concentration to a solution with a higher solute concentration. The direction is expressed in terms of solute concentration: water moves from the hypotonic solution to the hypertonic solution.
Hypotonic solution

A solution that has a lower solute concentration than the solution it is being compared with, such as the cytoplasm of a cell. Water moves by osmosis out of a hypotonic solution into the solution with which it is compared.
Hypertonic solution

A solution that has a higher solute concentration than the solution it is being compared with, such as the cytoplasm of a cell. Water moves by osmosis into a hypertonic solution from the solution with which it is compared.
Isotonic solution

A solution that has the same solute concentration as the solution it is being compared with. There is no net movement of water by osmosis between two isotonic solutions, although water molecules continue to cross the membrane in both directions.
Dynamic equilibrium of water movement

The state of a cell in an isotonic environment: water molecules cross the membrane into and out of the cell at equal rates, so there is no net movement of water even though individual molecules are moving in both directions all the time. This is different from water movement stopping.
Isotonic solute concentration of a tissue

The solute concentration of a bathing solution at which plant tissue shows no net change in mass or length, because the solution is isotonic with the cells. It is deduced from the results of bathing samples of tissue in a range of concentrations: percentage change in mass or length is plotted against concentration, and the isotonic concentration is where the line crosses zero change, which is usually between two of the concentrations tested rather than one of them.
Standard deviation

A statistic that describes the spread of a set of repeat measurements around their mean. A small standard deviation shows that the repeats are close together; a large one shows they are widely scattered. In the plant-tissue experiment it can be calculated for the repeats at each concentration and used to compare the reliability of length measurements with the reliability of mass measurements.
Standard error

A statistic that indicates how close the mean of a sample of repeats is likely to be to the true mean. It is smaller than the standard deviation of the same data and becomes smaller as the number of repeats increases. Standard error can be shown on a graph as error bars extending above and below each plotted mean.
Crenation

The shrinkage of a cell that lacks a cell wall when it is placed in a hypertonic medium: water leaves the cell by osmosis, its volume decreases and the cell membrane develops a crinkled, scalloped outline. In a hypotonic medium the same kind of cell swells and can burst, because there is no wall to resist its expansion.
Contractile vacuole

A membrane-bound structure in freshwater unicellular organisms such as Paramecium that fills with water and then contracts to expel it from the cell. Because the cytoplasm is hypertonic to fresh water, water enters the cell continuously by osmosis; the contractile vacuole removes it, preventing the cell from swelling and bursting.
Isotonic tissue fluid

The condition that multicellular organisms maintain in the fluid surrounding their cells so that the cells, which lack walls, neither gain water and burst nor lose water and shrink. Keeping tissue fluid isotonic with the cytoplasm prevents these harmful changes.
Turgor pressure

The pressure exerted by the cell contents against the cell wall of a plant cell that has taken in water by osmosis in a hypotonic medium. The wall resists expansion, so pressure builds up inside the cell until net uptake of water stops; the cell is then turgid. Turgor pressure is what makes non-woody plant tissue firm.
Plasmolysis

The condition of a plant cell in a hypertonic medium: water leaves the cell by osmosis, the protoplast (the cell contents inside the membrane) shrinks and the cell membrane pulls away from the cell wall. The wall itself keeps its shape, and the space between wall and membrane is filled by the external solution, which passes freely through the wall.
Isotonic intravenous fluid

Fluid given into a patient's vein during medical treatment, for example 0.9% sodium chloride solution (normal saline), which is isotonic with blood plasma. Because it has the same solute concentration as the plasma, the patient's blood cells neither take in water and burst nor lose water and crenate; pure water could not be given for this reason.
Isotonic bathing of organs for transplantation

The practice of storing an organ that has been removed for transplantation in a solution isotonic with the cytoplasm of its cells. This prevents net osmotic movement of water into or out of the cells, so they are not damaged by swelling or shrinkage before the organ is transplanted.
Water potential (ψw)

The potential energy of water per unit volume. It indicates the tendency of water to move: water moves from a region of higher water potential to a region of lower water potential. The units are usually kilopascals (kPa).
Reference state for water potential

Pure water at atmospheric pressure and 20°C, which is assigned a water potential of zero. The absolute quantity of potential energy in water cannot be measured, so water potentials are always given relative to this reference. Dissolving solutes lowers water potential, so every solution at atmospheric pressure has a negative water potential.
Water potential gradient

A difference in water potential between two regions. Water moves down the gradient, from the region of higher water potential to the region of lower water potential, because in doing so it loses potential energy; the movement needs no input of energy from a cell. Net movement stops when the two regions have the same water potential.
Solute potential (ψs)

The contribution of dissolved solutes to water potential. Solute potential is zero for pure water and becomes more negative as solute concentration increases, so it ranges from zero downwards and is negative for every solution.
Pressure potential (ψp)

The contribution of pressure to water potential. Inside plant cells pressure potential is generally positive, because the cell wall presses back on the contents of a cell that has taken in water. In xylem vessels where sap is being transported under tension, pressure potential is negative.
Water potential equation

ψw = ψs + ψp: the water potential of a cell with a wall is the sum of its solute potential and its pressure potential. Because ψs is zero or negative and ψp inside a cell is usually positive, a cell's water potential is less negative than its solute potential; for example, ψs = −700 kPa and ψp = +200 kPa give ψw = −500 kPa.
Full turgor

The state of a plant cell bathed in a hypotonic solution such as pure water once net uptake of water has stopped. Water entering the cell raises the pressure potential as the wall resists expansion; at full turgor in pure water the pressure potential has risen until it equals the magnitude of the solute potential, so ψw = ψs + ψp = 0, the same as the water outside, and there is no further net movement.
Incipient plasmolysis

The point reached by a plant cell losing water to a hypertonic solution at which the protoplast has just stopped pressing on the cell wall. The pressure potential has fallen to zero, so the cell's water potential equals its solute potential (ψw = ψs). If the external solution has a still lower water potential, water continues to leave and the membrane pulls away from the wall.
Asexual reproduction

Reproduction by a single parent without meiosis or the fusion of gametes, so that the offspring are genetically identical to the parent and to each other (clones). Its relative advantage is that an individual already adapted to an existing, stable environment passes on the whole of its successful genotype to every offspring, and reproduction can be rapid because no mate is needed.
Sexual reproduction

Reproduction in which two gametes, produced by meiosis, fuse to form a zygote. The offspring carry new combinations of alleles, so a population reproducing sexually shows the genetic variation on which natural selection can act; its relative advantage is that some offspring are likely to be adapted to a changed environment. Its costs are that it takes longer, requires a mate, and breaks up the parent's own successful allele combination.
Meiosis in the sexual life cycle

The nuclear division that halves the chromosome number to produce haploid gametes. Because homologous chromosomes are separated at random (independent assortment) and exchange segments by crossing over, meiosis breaks up the parental combinations of alleles: no gamete carries the same allele combination as the parent's body cells.
Fertilization (fusion of gametes)

The fusion of a male gamete with a female gamete to form a diploid zygote. Fertilization restores the diploid number and, because any male gamete may fuse with any female gamete, it produces new combinations of alleles that neither parent possessed. Fusion of gametes and fertilization are the same event.
Gamete

A haploid sex cell produced by meiosis. In animals the male gamete is a sperm and the female gamete an egg; in flowering plants the male gametes develop inside pollen grains and the female gamete inside an ovule. Two gametes fuse at fertilization to form a diploid zygote.
Male gamete

The gamete that travels to the female gamete. Because it must move, it is small and motile with very little stored food, and it can be produced in very large numbers at low cost to the parent. In humans the male gamete is a sperm, with a flagellum for swimming and many mitochondria to supply ATP for movement.
Female gamete

The gamete that stays in place and is reached by the male gamete. It is large and non-motile, with food reserves in its cytoplasm to support the early embryo, so it is costly to make and is produced in far smaller numbers than male gametes. In humans the female gamete is the egg, which is released one at a time at ovulation.
Reproductive strategy

The pattern of investment a sex makes in producing gametes and in its offspring. Because male gametes are small, cheap and numerous, a male can potentially father very many offspring and typically competes for mates; because female gametes are large, costly and few, a female's reproductive success is limited by the number of eggs she can make and provision, so females typically invest more in each offspring and are more selective in mating.
Testis

The male gonad, held in the scrotum outside the body cavity where the slightly lower temperature favours sperm production. The testes produce sperm by meiosis in the seminiferous tubules and secrete the hormone testosterone.
Epididymis
A long coiled tube on the surface of each testis in which sperm produced in the testis mature and are stored until ejaculation.
Sperm duct (vas deferens)
The muscular tube that carries sperm from the epididymis to the urethra during ejaculation, passing the seminal vesicle and prostate gland on the way.
Seminal vesicle and prostate gland

Accessory glands that add fluid to the sperm to form semen. The seminal vesicles secrete an alkaline fluid containing fructose, which the sperm respire for ATP; the prostate gland secretes an alkaline fluid that neutralizes the acidity of the vagina. Neither gland makes or stores sperm.
Urethra
The tube running through the penis that carries semen out of the body during ejaculation and urine out of the body from the bladder at other times; the two never pass at the same time.
Ovary

The female gonad. Each ovary contains follicles in which eggs develop and mature; one follicle bursts at ovulation each cycle to release an egg. The ovary also secretes the hormones oestradiol (from developing follicles) and progesterone (from the corpus luteum).
Oviduct (fallopian tube)

The tube leading from near each ovary to the uterus. Its funnel-shaped opening collects the egg released at ovulation, ciliated cells move the egg towards the uterus, and it is the site where fertilization normally takes place.
Uterus and endometrium

The uterus is the muscular organ in which the embryo implants and the foetus develops. Its inner lining, the endometrium, thickens and becomes rich in blood vessels during each uterine cycle in readiness for implantation, and is shed at menstruation if no embryo implants.
Cervix and vagina

The cervix is the narrow neck of the uterus that opens into the vagina; it produces mucus and dilates during childbirth. The vagina is the muscular tube leading from the cervix to the outside of the body; it receives the penis and semen during sexual intercourse and is the birth canal.
Menstrual cycle

The roughly 28-day cycle of changes in the ovary (ovarian cycle) and in the endometrium of the uterus (uterine cycle), which together constitute the menstrual cycle. It is regulated by FSH and LH from the pituitary gland and by oestradiol and progesterone from the ovary, through both negative and positive feedback.
Ovarian cycle

The sequence of events in the ovary: FSH stimulates a group of follicles to develop, one dominant follicle matures and secretes oestradiol (follicular phase), a surge of LH causes it to burst and release its egg (ovulation, around day 14), and the remains of the follicle form the corpus luteum, which secretes progesterone (luteal phase) before degenerating if no pregnancy occurs.
Uterine cycle

The sequence of changes in the endometrium: it is shed during menstruation (days 1 to about 5), rebuilt and thickened under the influence of oestradiol, and maintained and further thickened with a rich blood supply under progesterone from the corpus luteum. When the corpus luteum degenerates and progesterone falls, the endometrium breaks down and the next menstruation begins.
Follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)

A hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary gland at the start of the cycle. It stimulates the development of follicles in the ovary and stimulates the developing follicles to secrete oestradiol. Its secretion is inhibited by negative feedback from progesterone and by low levels of oestradiol.
Luteinizing hormone (LH)

A hormone secreted by the anterior pituitary gland. A sharp surge of LH, triggered by positive feedback from the high level of oestradiol from the mature follicle, causes ovulation and then stimulates the ruptured follicle to become the corpus luteum.
Oestradiol

A steroid hormone secreted by the developing follicles in the ovary. It stimulates the endometrium to thicken after menstruation, and its rising level in the days before ovulation acts by positive feedback on the pituitary to trigger the surge of LH (and a smaller rise in FSH) that causes ovulation. At low levels, together with progesterone, it inhibits FSH and LH secretion by negative feedback.
Progesterone

A steroid hormone secreted by the corpus luteum after ovulation (and by the placenta during pregnancy). It maintains and further thickens the endometrium and, by negative feedback on the pituitary, inhibits FSH and LH secretion so that no further follicles develop during the luteal phase. When the corpus luteum degenerates the fall in progesterone causes menstruation.
Corpus luteum

The yellow body formed from the wall of the follicle after ovulation, under the influence of LH. It secretes progesterone (and some oestradiol) for about ten days. If no embryo implants it degenerates, hormone levels fall and menstruation follows; if pregnancy occurs it is maintained by hCG from the embryo.
Positive and negative feedback in the menstrual cycle

Negative feedback: progesterone and low-level oestradiol inhibit the pituitary's secretion of FSH and LH, holding the cycle in check during the luteal phase. Positive feedback: the rising oestradiol from the mature follicle stimulates the pituitary to secrete more LH (and FSH), which stimulates more oestradiol secretion, so LH rises steeply to the surge that causes ovulation.
Fusion of gamete membranes

The event in human fertilization in which the cell membrane of the sperm fuses with the cell membrane of the egg. Only the sperm nucleus enters the egg cytoplasm; the sperm's tail (flagellum) and its mitochondria are destroyed, so all the mitochondria of the zygote come from the egg.
Joint mitosis of the zygote

After the sperm nucleus has entered the egg, the nuclear membranes of the sperm nucleus and the egg nucleus dissolve, and all the condensed chromosomes from both nuclei line up together on a single spindle in a joint mitosis. The result is two diploid nuclei, one in each of the first two cells of the embryo; the two haploid nuclei do not first fuse into a single diploid nucleus.
In vitro fertilization (IVF)

A fertility treatment in which eggs are collected from the ovaries and fertilized with sperm outside the body (in vitro means in glass), and one or more of the resulting embryos are transferred to the uterus. Hormone treatment is used first to suspend the woman's own cycle and then to induce superovulation.
Superovulation

The maturation and release of many eggs in a single cycle, induced in IVF by injecting artificial doses of FSH (with LH or hCG to trigger final maturation) after the normal secretion of pituitary hormones has been suspended with a drug. It allows several eggs to be collected at once so that several embryos can be produced.
Ovule

The structure inside the ovary of a flower in which the female gamete is produced by meiosis followed by mitosis. After fertilization the ovule develops into a seed containing the embryo, and the ovary around it develops into the fruit.
Pollen grain

The structure produced in the anther, by meiosis followed by mitosis, that contains the male gametes of a flowering plant. The pollen grain is not itself a gamete: it carries the gamete nuclei to the stigma and, on germinating, grows a pollen tube that delivers them to the ovule.
Pollination

The transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma. Pollination is not fertilization: it is followed by pollen development (growth of a pollen tube down the style) and only then by the fusion of a male gamete with the female gamete inside the ovule.
Pollen tube

The tube that grows from a germinating pollen grain on the stigma, down through the style to an ovule, carrying the male gametes. When it reaches the ovule a male gamete fuses with the female gamete (fertilization) to produce a zygote, which develops into the embryo of the seed.
Hermaphroditic plant

A plant whose flowers produce both male gametes (in pollen) and female gametes (in ovules). Its reproduction is still sexual, because gametes are produced by meiosis and fuse at fertilization, even when a flower fertilizes itself; the offspring may differ genetically from the parent if it is heterozygous, and in any case are produced by meiosis and fertilization rather than by mitosis alone.
Stamen (anther and filament)

The male part of a flower. The anther produces pollen grains, containing the male gametes, and releases them when ripe; the filament is the stalk that holds the anther in a position where visiting insects brush against it.
Carpel (stigma, style and ovary)

The female part of a flower. The stigma is the sticky surface that receives pollen grains; the style is the stalk through which pollen tubes grow; the ovary contains the ovules, in which the female gametes are produced and which become seeds after fertilization.
Petal and nectary

In an insect-pollinated flower the petals are large and brightly coloured, often scented and marked, to attract insects; the nectary at the base of the flower secretes sugary nectar as a reward, positioned so that an insect feeding on it touches the anthers and stigma.
Sepal
One of the outer, usually green, leaf-like parts of a flower that enclose and protect the flower while it is a bud.
Cross-pollination

The transfer of pollen from the anther of a flower on one plant to the stigma of a flower on a different plant of the same species. It brings together gametes from two parents and so increases genetic variation in the offspring. Pollen is carried between plants by animals (mainly insects) or by wind.
Self-pollination
The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma of the same flower or of another flower on the same plant. The gametes come from one parent, so the offspring are less varied and inbreeding results.
Methods of promoting cross-pollination

Features that make self-pollination unlikely: the anthers and stigma of a flower maturing at different times, so a flower's own pollen is shed before or after its stigma is receptive; separate male and female flowers on the same plant (monoecious species); male and female flowers on separate plants (dioecious species); and reliance on animals or wind to carry pollen from plant to plant.
Self-incompatibility

A genetic mechanism in many plant species that prevents a plant's own pollen (or pollen from a genetically similar plant) from fertilizing its eggs, for example by stopping the pollen tube growing down the style when the pollen and the carpel carry matching alleles of the self-incompatibility gene. It ensures that the gametes fusing at fertilization come from different plants, increasing genetic variation within the species.
Inbreeding

Breeding between closely related individuals, of which self-pollination is the extreme case. It decreases genetic diversity in the population and, by increasing the proportion of offspring homozygous for harmful recessive alleles, reduces vigour (inbreeding depression).
Seed dispersal

The transport of seeds away from the parent plant, for example by wind, water or animals that eat fruits or carry hooked seeds. It is distinct from pollination, which is the transfer of pollen and happens before fertilization; dispersal happens after fertilization and reduces competition between the parent and its offspring.
Germination

The growth and development of the embryo in a seed into a seedling. The seed absorbs water, the embryo produces gibberellin which stimulates the mobilization of food reserves, the radicle (embryonic root) emerges and then the shoot, until the seedling's leaves can photosynthesize.
Mobilization of food reserves

The conversion of the insoluble food stores of a seed, such as starch, into soluble substances that can be transported to the growing embryo and respired: in germinating cereal grains, amylase is synthesized in response to gibberellin and hydrolyses starch to maltose, which is converted to glucose for cell respiration and growth.
Gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH)

A hormone secreted by the hypothalamus that stimulates the anterior pituitary gland to release the gonadotropins LH and FSH. Increased GnRH release towards the end of childhood triggers the increase in LH and FSH secretion that starts puberty.
Puberty

The period of developmental change during which the reproductive system becomes functional. It begins when the hypothalamus increases its release of GnRH, which raises LH and FSH secretion by the pituitary; these stimulate the testes to secrete testosterone or the ovaries to secrete oestradiol and progesterone, and the increased steroid sex hormones cause the physical changes associated with puberty.
Spermatogenesis

The production of sperm in the seminiferous tubules of the testes from puberty onwards. Cells in the outer layer of the tubule divide by mitosis to maintain their numbers, some grow slightly, then each undergoes the two divisions of meiosis to give four haploid cells of equal size, which differentiate into sperm. Millions of sperm are produced each day throughout adult life.
Oogenesis

The production of eggs in the ovaries. Before birth, cells divide by mitosis, grow, and begin meiosis but stop early in the first division. From puberty, each cycle a few of these cells resume meiosis: the first division is unequal, giving a large secondary oocyte and a small polar body; the secondary oocyte is released at ovulation and completes the second division, again unequally, only if a sperm enters it. One functional egg with a large cytoplasm results, and only a few hundred are ever released.
Polar body

A tiny cell produced by the unequal cytoplasmic division at each meiotic division of oogenesis. It receives a haploid set of chromosomes but almost no cytoplasm, and degenerates; this is how one cell entering meiosis gives a single egg that keeps nearly all the cytoplasm and food reserves.
Acrosome reaction

The release of hydrolytic enzymes from the acrosome, a membrane-bound vesicle in the head of the sperm, when the sperm contacts the zona pellucida. The enzymes digest a path through the zona pellucida so that the sperm can reach and fuse with the egg cell membrane.
Cortical reaction

The release, by exocytosis, of the contents of cortical granules from the egg cytoplasm into the space around the egg as soon as a sperm's membrane fuses with the egg membrane. The enzymes released alter the zona pellucida so that it hardens and no longer binds sperm, preventing any further sperm from passing through and so preventing polyspermy.
Zona pellucida

The glycoprotein coat surrounding the egg cell membrane. A sperm must digest its way through it (acrosome reaction) to fuse with the egg; after fertilization the cortical reaction changes it into a barrier that blocks all other sperm.
Polyspermy

The entry of more than one sperm nucleus into an egg. It would give a zygote with too many sets of chromosomes, which cannot develop normally, so it is prevented by the cortical reaction that follows entry of the first sperm.
Blastocyst

The stage of the human embryo, reached about five to seven days after fertilization by repeated mitotic divisions while it is moved down the oviduct to the uterus. It is a hollow ball of cells with a fluid-filled cavity, an inner cell mass that will form the foetus, and an outer layer of cells that attaches to the endometrium at implantation and later contributes to the placenta.
Implantation

The attachment of the blastocyst to the endometrium and its sinking into the lining, about seven days after fertilization. The outer cells of the blastocyst begin to secrete hCG and to draw nutrients from the endometrium, and the embryo can then continue its development inside the uterus.
Human chorionic gonadotropin (hCG)

A hormone secreted by the embryo, from its outer cells at implantation, and then by the developing placenta. It maintains the corpus luteum so that progesterone secretion continues and the endometrium is not shed. Because it is made only by an embryo, its presence in the mother's urine is the basis of pregnancy testing.
Monoclonal antibody

An antibody produced by a single clone of identical cells, so every molecule binds the same specific antigen. Pregnancy tests use monoclonal antibodies that bind hCG: one, attached to a coloured marker, binds hCG in urine as it flows along the test strip, and a second, fixed in a line on the strip, captures the hCG-antibody complexes so that a coloured line appears only when hCG is present.
Placenta

The disc-shaped organ formed from foetal tissue and the endometrium through which the foetus exchanges substances with the mother. Oxygen, glucose, amino acids, lipids, water, vitamins, minerals and antibodies pass from maternal to foetal blood, and carbon dioxide, urea and other wastes pass the other way, without the two bloods mixing. By providing for the foetus in this way it allows the foetus to be retained in the uterus to a much later stage of development than in mammals without a placenta; it also secretes progesterone and oestradiol.
Placental villi

Finger-like projections of foetal tissue, containing foetal capillaries, that extend into pools of maternal blood in the placenta. Their very large total surface area, and the short distance between maternal blood and foetal capillaries, allow rapid exchange of materials by diffusion and active transport.
Hormonal maintenance of pregnancy

Pregnancy continues only while progesterone levels remain high: progesterone maintains the endometrium and inhibits contractions of the uterine muscle. In the first weeks the progesterone is secreted by the corpus luteum, kept alive by hCG from the embryo; by about the end of the first trimester the placenta has taken over progesterone (and oestradiol) secretion and the corpus luteum degenerates.
Oxytocin

A hormone secreted by the posterior pituitary gland that stimulates contraction of the uterine muscle during childbirth. At the end of pregnancy a fall in progesterone removes the inhibition of contractions; each contraction stretches the cervix, stretch receptors signal to the pituitary and more oxytocin is secreted, causing stronger contractions. This positive feedback continues until the baby is delivered.
Hormone replacement therapy (HRT)

Treatment of women during and after the menopause with oestrogen (with or without progesterone) to replace the hormones the ovaries no longer secrete, relieving menopausal symptoms. Early epidemiological studies reported that women on HRT had a lower incidence of coronary heart disease, but later randomized controlled trials showed that HRT causes a small increase in CHD risk.
Epidemiological study

An observational study that looks for correlations between a factor (such as taking HRT) and a health outcome (such as coronary heart disease) across a population, without the researchers controlling who is exposed. Because the groups being compared may differ in other ways (confounding variables), a correlation found in such a study cannot by itself establish cause and effect.
Randomized controlled trial

An experiment in which participants are allocated at random to receive the treatment or a placebo, so that confounding variables such as socioeconomic status are spread evenly between the groups. It can test cause and effect: randomized controlled trials of HRT showed that HRT slightly increases the risk of CHD, overturning the conclusion drawn from the earlier correlation.
Haploid gamete

A sex cell produced by meiosis that contains one set of chromosomes (n) and therefore one copy of each autosomal gene. In sexual reproduction each parent contributes one haploid gamete, so each parent passes on one allele of each gene to the offspring.
Diploid zygote

The cell formed by the fusion of two haploid gametes at fertilization. It contains two sets of chromosomes (2n), one from each parent, and so has two copies of each autosomal gene. Every body cell produced from it by mitosis carries the same two copies.
Sexual life cycle

A life cycle in which haploid gametes are produced by meiosis in the parents and fuse to form a diploid zygote. This pattern of inheritance is common to all eukaryotes that reproduce sexually, including plants, fungi and animals, even though the organisms differ in which stage of the cycle is dominant.
P, F1 and F2 generations

The generations named in a genetic cross. The P (parental) generation is the pair of organisms first crossed; the F1 (first filial) generation is their offspring; the F2 (second filial) generation is produced by crossing F1 individuals with each other or by allowing them to self-fertilize.
Punnett grid

A grid used to predict the outcome of a genetic cross. The possible gametes of one parent head the columns and those of the other parent head the rows; each cell shows a possible offspring genotype, and the cells are counted to give the expected genotypic and phenotypic ratios.
Pollination in a plant cross

The transfer of pollen from an anther to a stigma. Pollen contains the male gametes and the female gametes are located in ovules inside the ovary, so pollination must take place before the gametes can fuse. To cross two chosen plants, the breeder transfers pollen from one plant to the stigma of the other, usually after removing the anthers of the recipient flower so that it cannot self-pollinate.
Self-pollination and self-fertilization

Plants such as peas produce both male and female gametes on the same plant, so pollen can be transferred to a stigma of the same plant (self-pollination) and a male gamete can then fuse with a female gamete of the same plant (self-fertilization). Self-fertilization of an F1 plant is a standard way of producing an F2 generation. Genetic crosses of this kind are widely used to breed new varieties of crop and ornamental plants.
Genotype

The combination of alleles that an organism has inherited, for one gene or for many. For a single autosomal gene the genotype consists of two alleles, one inherited from each parent, and is written with two symbols such as Tt.
Gene and allele

A gene is a length of DNA at a particular locus that codes for a polypeptide or has another specific function; an allele is one of the alternative forms of that gene, differing from other alleles in its base sequence. All the alleles of a gene occupy the same locus, so a diploid organism carries two alleles of each autosomal gene, which may be the same or different.
Homozygous

Having two copies of the same allele of a gene, for example TT or tt. A homozygous organism produces only one type of gamete with respect to that gene and, if self-fertilized or crossed with an identical homozygote, breeds true for the trait.
Heterozygous

Having two different alleles of a gene, for example Tt. A heterozygous organism produces two types of gamete for that gene in equal numbers, one carrying each allele, because the two alleles segregate during meiosis.
Phenotype

The observable traits of an organism, including its structure, physiology and behaviour, resulting from its genotype and from environmental factors. Some human traits are due to genotype only (for example ABO blood group), some to environment only (for example scars or the language first spoken) and many to interaction between genotype and environment (for example height or skin colour).
Dominant allele

An allele that has the same effect on the phenotype whether it is present in the homozygous or the heterozygous state. Typically a dominant allele codes for a functional protein and one copy is enough to produce the trait, so a homozygous-dominant genotype and a heterozygous genotype give the same phenotype.
Recessive allele

An allele that affects the phenotype only when it is present in the homozygous state. Many recessive alleles code for a non-functional or absent protein; in a heterozygote the dominant allele still produces enough functional protein for the trait, so the recessive allele has no observable effect there, although it is still present and can be passed to offspring.
Phenotypic plasticity

The capacity of an organism to develop traits suited to the environment it experiences, by varying its patterns of gene expression rather than by any change in its genotype. Because the genotype is unchanged, the altered traits may be reversible during the lifetime of the individual if the environment changes again, as with the darkening of skin on exposure to sunlight.
Phenylketonuria (PKU)

A human disease inherited as a recessive condition, caused by mutation in an autosomal gene that codes for the enzyme needed to convert the amino acid phenylalanine to tyrosine. A person homozygous for the mutant allele lacks a functional enzyme, so phenylalanine accumulates and causes damage to the developing brain unless dietary phenylalanine is restricted from birth.
Carrier

An individual heterozygous for a recessive disease allele who does not have the disease but can pass the allele to offspring. Two carriers of PKU are unaffected, because one functional allele produces enough enzyme, but each child they have has a 1 in 4 chance of inheriting the mutant allele from both parents and having PKU.
Single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP)

A position in the genome at which a single nucleotide differs between individuals in a population. SNPs are the most common source of the different alleles of a gene: two alleles that differ at one SNP may code for polypeptides differing in a single amino acid, or may differ in how much the gene is expressed.
Multiple alleles

The existence of more than two alleles of a gene in a gene pool. Any number of alleles of a gene can exist in the population, because mutations at different positions produce different variants, but a diploid individual inherits only two of them, one from each parent.
Gene pool

All the alleles of all the genes carried by the members of an interbreeding population. The gene pool is where multiple alleles of a gene exist together, even though each individual carries at most two of them.
ABO blood group alleles

The gene for the ABO blood group has three alleles in the human gene pool, denoted IA, IB and i. IA and IB are codominant with each other and both are dominant to i, so the genotypes IAIA and IAi give group A, IBIB and IBi give group B, IAIB gives group AB and ii gives group O.
Codominance

A pattern of inheritance in which both alleles of a heterozygote are fully expressed, so the heterozygote has a dual phenotype showing the effects of both alleles at once. The AB blood type (genotype IAIB) is an example: both the A and the B antigens are present on the red blood cells.
Incomplete dominance

A pattern of inheritance in which the heterozygote has a phenotype intermediate between the two homozygotes, because neither allele is fully dominant. In the four o'clock flower or marvel of Peru (Mirabilis jalapa), red-flowered and white-flowered homozygotes produce pink-flowered heterozygotes, and pink × pink gives red, pink and white offspring in a 1:2:1 ratio.
Sex determination in humans

Humans have one pair of sex chromosomes: XX in females and XY in males. Every egg carries an X chromosome, whereas a sperm carries either an X or a Y, so it is the sex chromosome in the sperm that determines whether the zygote develops male-typical or female-typical physical characteristics. The X chromosome carries far more genes than the much smaller Y chromosome.
Sex-linked gene

A gene located on a sex chromosome, in practice almost always the X chromosome because it carries far more genes than the Y. Males have only one X chromosome, so they have a single copy of each X-linked gene and a single recessive allele produces the recessive phenotype; females have two copies. Alleles on the X chromosome are shown as superscript letters on an uppercase X, for example XH and Xh, and a male genotype is written XHY or XhY.
Haemophilia

A sex-linked genetic disorder in which blood fails to clot normally, caused by a recessive allele (Xh) of a gene on the X chromosome. A male with genotype XhY has haemophilia because he has no second X chromosome to carry the dominant allele; a female XHXh is an unaffected carrier, and an affected female (XhXh) is rare because she must inherit Xh from both parents. Sons receive their X chromosome from their mother, so a carrier mother passes the allele to half her sons on average.
Pedigree chart

A diagram showing the family relationships and phenotypes of individuals over several generations, used to deduce the pattern of inheritance of a genetic disorder. For example, an affected child born to two unaffected parents shows that the condition is recessive and that both parents are heterozygous; an affected daughter with an unaffected father rules out X-linked recessive inheritance. Because close relatives are more likely to carry the same recessive allele inherited from a common ancestor, marriage between close relatives raises the chance of children being homozygous for a recessive disorder, which is the genetic basis for its prohibition in many societies.
Inductive reasoning

Reasoning that draws a general conclusion from observations of some but not all cases. Scientists use it when they base a theory on the cases they have observed, for example deducing that a disorder is inherited as an autosomal recessive condition from the pattern seen in part of a pedigree chart.
Deductive reasoning

Reasoning from a general principle or theory to a conclusion about a specific case. Once a pattern of inheritance has been proposed for a pedigree, it can be used deductively to work out the genotypes of specific individuals, for example that the unaffected parents of an affected child must both be heterozygous.
Continuous variation

Variation in a trait that can take any value within a range, with no distinct categories, so that a population shows a continuous distribution of values. It results from polygenic inheritance, from environmental factors, or from both: human skin colour is continuously variable because several genes each contribute to the amount of melanin and exposure to sunlight also affects it.
Polygenic inheritance

The control of a single trait by two or more genes, each usually with a small additive effect. Because many combinations of alleles are possible, polygenic traits such as human skin colour show many phenotypes grading into one another rather than a few discrete classes.
Discrete variable

A variable that falls into a limited number of separate categories with no intermediates, such as ABO blood group (A, B, AB or O). Discrete variables are usually controlled by one gene, whereas continuous variables such as skin colour or height take any value across a range.
Mean, median and mode

Measures of central tendency for a set of values. The mean is the sum of the values divided by the number of values; the median is the middle value when the values are arranged in order (or the mean of the two middle values); the mode is the value that occurs most often. For a continuous variable the mean is the usual measure, but the median is less affected by outliers.
Box-and-whisker plot

A plot that displays six aspects of data for a continuous variable such as student height: the minimum, the first quartile, the median, the third quartile, the maximum and any outliers. The box extends from the first quartile to the third quartile with a line at the median; the whiskers extend to the smallest and largest values that are not outliers, and outliers are plotted as separate points.
Interquartile range and outlier

The interquartile range (IQR) is the difference between the third quartile and the first quartile and contains the middle half of the data. A data point is categorized as an outlier if it is more than 1.5 × IQR above the third quartile or more than 1.5 × IQR below the first quartile.
Segregation

The separation of the two alleles of a gene into different gametes during meiosis, because the homologous chromosomes carrying them are pulled to opposite poles in anaphase I. A heterozygote Aa therefore produces gametes carrying A and gametes carrying a in equal numbers.
Independent assortment

The random orientation of each bivalent on the equator in metaphase I of meiosis, independently of every other bivalent, so that the alleles of genes on different chromosomes are combined at random in the gametes. A double heterozygote AaBb for two unlinked genes therefore produces the gametes AB, Ab, aB and ab in equal proportions, which is the basis of the ratios seen in dihybrid crosses.
Dihybrid cross

A cross that follows the inheritance of two genes at once. For two unlinked autosomal genes, a cross between two double heterozygotes (AaBb × AaBb) gives a 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio, derived by combining the 3:1 ratio for each gene (3/4 × 3/4 = 9/16, 3/4 × 1/4 = 3/16, 1/4 × 3/4 = 3/16, 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/16). A test cross of a double heterozygote with a double homozygous recessive (AaBb × aabb) gives a 1:1:1:1 ratio, because the four equally frequent gametes of the heterozygote each combine with the single gamete type ab.
Mendel's second law

The law of independent assortment: alleles of different genes assort independently of one another during gamete formation. The 9:3:3:1 and 1:1:1:1 dihybrid ratios rest on this law, which holds only if the genes are on different chromosomes or are far enough apart on one chromosome for the recombination rate to reach 50%. Linked genes are an exception, illustrating that biological laws hold only under certain conditions.
Locus

The specific position of a gene on a particular chromosome. The locus of a human gene is the same in every individual, and a genome database records each gene's chromosome, its position on that chromosome and the polypeptide it codes for. Two genes may have loci on different chromosomes, in which case they are unlinked, or loci in close proximity on the same chromosome, in which case they are linked.
Autosomal gene linkage

The tendency of alleles of two genes to be inherited together because their loci are on the same autosome. Alleles of linked genes do not assort independently: the combination on each chromosome is passed on intact unless crossing over between the two loci in prophase I separates them, and the closer the loci the less often this happens. In crosses the allele symbols are shown alongside vertical lines representing the homologous chromosomes.
Recombinant

A gamete, or an offspring genotype or phenotype, that has a combination of alleles of two genes different from the combinations in the parents. For unlinked genes recombinants arise by independent assortment and make up half the offspring of a test cross; for linked genes they arise only by crossing over between the loci and are the two less frequent classes of offspring.
Test cross

A cross between an individual heterozygous for both genes and an individual homozygous recessive for both genes. Because the homozygous recessive parent contributes only recessive alleles, the phenotype of each offspring reveals which gamete it received from the heterozygous parent, so the proportions of parental and recombinant phenotypes among the offspring equal the proportions of parental and recombinant gametes.
Chi-squared test

A statistical test of whether observed results differ significantly from those expected under a hypothesis. For each class, (observed − expected)² / expected is calculated and the values are summed to give chi-squared; the degrees of freedom are the number of classes minus one. If the calculated value exceeds the critical value at p = 0.05 the null hypothesis is rejected; if it is smaller, the null hypothesis is not rejected and the observed results are consistent with the expected ratio.
Null and alternative hypotheses

In a chi-squared test on a dihybrid cross, the null hypothesis (H0) states that there is no significant difference between the observed and expected numbers, so any difference is due to chance and the genes assort independently. The alternative hypothesis (H1) states that the observed results differ significantly from the expected ratio, for example because the genes are linked.
Statistical significance and sampling

A difference is statistically significant at the p = 0.05 level if the probability of obtaining a difference at least as large by chance alone, when the null hypothesis is true, is less than 5%. Statistical testing uses a sample to represent a population: in a dihybrid cross the sample is the F2 generation counted, and in many experiments it is the set of replicated or repeated measurements.
Homeostasis

The maintenance of the internal environment of an organism, in which variables such as body temperature, blood pH, blood glucose concentration and blood osmotic concentration are kept within preset limits despite fluctuations in the external environment. The variable is not held at one fixed value: it oscillates within a narrow range around a set point.
Set point and preset limits

The set point is the value of a homeostatic variable that the control system works to restore, such as a core body temperature of about 37 °C, a blood pH of about 7.4, a blood glucose concentration of about 4–6 mmol L−1 between meals and a blood osmotic concentration of about 0.3 osmol L−1. The preset limits are the narrow range either side of the set point within which the variable is allowed to fluctuate before corrective responses become strong.
Negative feedback

A control mechanism in which a change in a variable away from its set point triggers responses that reverse the change, returning the variable towards the set point. It operates in both directions: a value above the set point is brought down and a value below is brought up. Negative feedback is used in homeostasis because it is self-correcting and stabilizing.
Positive feedback

A control mechanism in which a change in a variable triggers responses that increase the change further, driving the variable away from its starting value until some end point is reached. Positive feedback amplifies deviations rather than correcting them, so it is unsuitable for homeostasis; it is used where a rapid, one-way completion is needed, such as the oxytocin-driven contractions of childbirth.
Insulin

A peptide hormone secreted by the beta cells of the pancreatic islets when blood glucose concentration rises above the set point, for example after a meal. It is transported dissolved in the blood plasma to all tissues but acts only on cells with insulin receptors. In its target cells it increases the uptake of glucose from the blood, stimulates the conversion of glucose to glycogen in liver and skeletal muscle cells, and increases the use of glucose in cell respiration, so blood glucose concentration falls.
Glucagon

A peptide hormone secreted by the alpha cells of the pancreatic islets when blood glucose concentration falls below the set point, for example during fasting or exercise. Carried in the blood plasma, it acts on liver cells, stimulating the breakdown of stored glycogen to glucose and the release of that glucose into the blood, so blood glucose concentration rises.
Pancreatic endocrine cells (islet alpha and beta cells)

Clusters of hormone-secreting cells in the pancreas, the islets of Langerhans, that monitor blood glucose concentration directly. Beta cells secrete insulin in response to high glucose and alpha cells secrete glucagon in response to low glucose; each hormone is released into the blood, not into a duct, which is what makes these cells endocrine. The two hormones are antagonistic, so together they return blood glucose to the set point from above and from below.
Glycogen

A branched polysaccharide of glucose stored as granules in liver and skeletal muscle cells. Insulin stimulates its synthesis from glucose when blood glucose is high; glucagon stimulates its breakdown to glucose in the liver when blood glucose is low. Glycogen is the short-term glucose store, not to be confused with glucagon, the hormone.
Type 1 diabetes

A form of diabetes in which the beta cells of the pancreatic islets are destroyed by the person's own immune system (an autoimmune disease), so little or no insulin is secreted and blood glucose concentration rises to dangerously high values after meals. It usually develops in childhood or adolescence; the main risk factor is a genetic predisposition and it cannot be prevented by lifestyle. It is treated by regular injections or pump delivery of insulin, timed and dosed against food intake and blood glucose testing.
Type 2 diabetes

A form of diabetes in which insulin is still secreted, at least at first, but the target cells no longer respond to it normally (insulin resistance) because of changes in their receptors and signalling, so glucose is not taken up and blood glucose concentration stays high. Beta-cell output may decline later. Risk factors are obesity, especially abdominal fat, diets rich in sugar and fat, physical inactivity, increasing age and family history. It can be largely prevented, and initially treated, by diet and exercise; drugs that increase insulin sensitivity or secretion are added when needed, and some patients eventually need insulin.
Peripheral thermoreceptors

Sensory receptors in the skin that detect the temperature of the skin and of the external environment and send nerve impulses to the hypothalamus. They provide an early warning of heat loss or gain before the core temperature changes. The hypothalamus also contains central thermoreceptors that monitor the temperature of the blood flowing through it.
Hypothalamus (thermoregulatory centre)

The part of the brain that acts as the control centre for body temperature. It compares the temperature of the blood passing through it, and the input from peripheral thermoreceptors, with the set point of about 37 °C, then coordinates responses: nerve impulses to effectors such as skeletal muscle, arteriole smooth muscle, sweat glands and arrector pili muscles, and hormonal signals via the pituitary gland.
Thyroxin

A hormone secreted by the thyroid gland that raises the metabolic rate of most body cells, increasing the rate of cell respiration and so the amount of heat released. Its secretion is stimulated by thyroid-stimulating hormone from the pituitary gland, which is in turn controlled by the hypothalamus. Thyroxin release rises in prolonged cold exposure, providing a slower, longer-lasting increase in heat generation than the rapid nervous responses.
Effectors of temperature change

Birds and mammals regulate their body temperature by physiological means (the effector tissues below) and by behavioural means such as seeking shade, sun or shelter; the guide requires the details only for humans. The tissues that carry out thermoregulatory responses. Muscle effectors include skeletal muscle (shivering), smooth muscle in the walls of skin arterioles (vasoconstriction and vasodilation) and the arrector pili muscles (hair erection). Adipose tissue effectors include brown adipose tissue, which generates heat by uncoupled respiration; white adipose tissue insulates. Sweat glands are the effector for evaporative cooling.
Vasodilation and vasoconstriction

Changes in the diameter of the arterioles supplying capillaries near the skin surface, brought about by smooth muscle in the arteriole walls. Vasodilation widens the arterioles so more warm blood flows through the surface capillaries and more heat is lost by radiation, conduction and convection. Vasoconstriction narrows them so less blood reaches the surface and heat is retained in the core. The capillaries themselves do not move and cannot constrict.
Shivering

Rapid, involuntary, rhythmic contractions of skeletal muscle triggered by the hypothalamus when the body is cold. The contractions do little useful work, so most of the energy released by the increased cell respiration in the muscle fibres is released as heat, which warms the blood passing through the muscle.
Sweating

Secretion of sweat, a dilute salt solution, onto the skin surface by sweat glands when the body is too hot. Cooling occurs only when the water in the sweat evaporates, because evaporation absorbs latent heat from the skin; sweat that drips off without evaporating removes very little heat, which is why sweating is less effective in humid air.
Uncoupled respiration in brown adipose tissue

Heat generation in brown adipose tissue, found especially in infants and around the neck and shoulders of adults. Its mitochondria contain an uncoupling protein in the inner membrane that lets protons flow back into the matrix without passing through ATP synthase, so the energy of the proton gradient built by the electron transport chain is released as heat instead of being used to make ATP. The tissue is brown because of its very many mitochondria and rich blood supply.
Hair erection (piloerection)

Contraction of the arrector pili muscles attached to hair follicles, pulling the hairs upright when the body is cold. In furred mammals the raised hairs trap a thicker layer of still air next to the skin, reducing heat loss; in humans the hair is too sparse for this to insulate effectively, and the response persists as 'goose bumps'.
Excretion

The removal from the body of the waste products of metabolism, such as urea from the breakdown of excess amino acids and carbon dioxide from cell respiration, together with other toxic or unwanted solutes. The kidneys excrete urea and other solutes in urine. Excretion is distinct from egestion, the elimination of undigested food that was never part of the body's metabolism.
Osmoregulation

The regulation of the osmotic concentration of the blood and other body fluids, achieved in humans mainly by the kidneys adjusting how much water is reabsorbed from the filtrate and therefore the volume and concentration of the urine. Osmoregulation and excretion are separate roles of the kidney: one controls water balance, the other removes metabolic waste.
Osmotic concentration (osmol L−1)

The total concentration of osmotically active solute particles in a solution, measured in osmoles per litre (osmol L−1); a solute that dissociates into two ions contributes two osmoles per mole. Human blood plasma is kept at about 0.3 osmol L−1 (300 mosmol L−1). Water moves by osmosis from a solution of lower osmotic concentration to one of higher osmotic concentration.
Ultrafiltration

Filtration of blood plasma under pressure in the glomerulus, a knot of capillaries inside Bowman's capsule. High blood pressure in the glomerular capillaries, caused by the efferent arteriole being narrower than the afferent arteriole, forces water and small solutes (glucose, amino acids, salts, urea) through the fenestrated capillary wall, the basement membrane and the slits between podocytes into Bowman's capsule. Blood cells and plasma proteins are too large to pass, so the filtrate is plasma minus its proteins.
Selective reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule

The recovery of useful substances from the glomerular filtrate back into the blood in the proximal convoluted tubule. All of the glucose and amino acids and most of the sodium ions are reabsorbed by active transport through the tubule cells, and water follows by osmosis, so about 80% of the filtrate volume is returned. Urea and other toxins are not actively reabsorbed and so remain in the filtrate to be excreted in urine. The tubule cells have microvilli and many mitochondria for this task.
Loop of Henle

The hairpin-shaped section of the nephron that dips from the cortex into the medulla and back. Cells of the ascending limb actively transport sodium ions out of the filtrate into the medullary interstitial fluid, and the ascending limb is impermeable to water, so the medulla is kept at a high osmotic concentration that increases with depth. This high concentration is what allows water to be drawn by osmosis out of the collecting ducts, which pass down through the medulla, when aquaporins are present.
Antidiuretic hormone (ADH)

A peptide hormone produced by neurosecretory cells of the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary gland when osmoreceptors in the hypothalamus detect a rise in blood osmotic concentration. ADH acts on the cells of the collecting ducts, increasing their permeability to water so that more water is reabsorbed into the medulla and blood; the urine becomes smaller in volume and more concentrated. When blood osmotic concentration falls, ADH secretion falls and dilute urine is produced.
Osmoreceptors

Cells in the hypothalamus that monitor the osmotic concentration of the blood, shrinking when the blood becomes more concentrated. Their signals increase the rate of ADH secretion from the pituitary gland and also produce the sensation of thirst; when the blood is dilute they signal less, ADH secretion falls and water is excreted.
Aquaporins in collecting duct cells

Water channel proteins whose location in collecting duct cells is switched by ADH. When ADH binds to receptors on the duct cells, intracellular vesicles carrying aquaporins fuse with the plasma membrane facing the filtrate, so water can pass by osmosis into the cells and on into the concentrated medulla. When ADH is absent the aquaporins are withdrawn by endocytosis back into vesicles, the membrane becomes almost impermeable to water and dilute urine leaves the duct.
Redistribution of blood supply

The change in the share of cardiac output sent to different organs as activity changes, brought about by vasodilation of arterioles in organs that need more blood and vasoconstriction in those that need less. During vigorous physical activity skeletal muscles receive the great majority of a much increased cardiac output while flow to the gut and kidneys is sharply reduced; during wakeful rest the gut and kidneys receive large shares; during sleep cardiac output is lower and flow to skeletal muscle is minimal. Blood flow to the brain is held nearly constant in all three states.
Natural selection

The mechanism driving evolutionary change: individuals in a population vary in heritable traits, more offspring are produced than can survive, and those whose traits are better adapted to the selection pressures of their environment are more likely to survive and reproduce, so the alleles they carry become more frequent in the population over generations. It has operated continuously over billions of years and is the source of the biodiversity of life on Earth.
Paradigm shift

A fundamental change in the accepted framework of ideas within which scientists interpret observations. In Darwin's time it was widely accepted that species evolved, but the mechanism was unclear; Darwin's theory of natural selection supplied a convincing mechanism and replaced Lamarckism, which is an example of a paradigm shift.
Lamarckism

The earlier explanation of evolutionary change, associated with Lamarck, in which characteristics acquired by an individual during its lifetime through use, disuse or the environment are passed on to its offspring. It was replaced by Darwin's mechanism of natural selection because acquired characteristics are not encoded in genes and so are not heritable.
Mutation as a source of variation

A change in the base sequence of DNA. Mutation is the only source of new alleles: it generates the new heritable variants on which natural selection can act, and it occurs randomly rather than in response to the needs of the organism.
Sexual reproduction as a source of variation

Meiosis (through crossing over and the random orientation of bivalents) and the random fusion of gametes at fertilization produce offspring with new combinations of existing alleles. Sexual reproduction does not create new alleles; it generates new combinations of the alleles already present.
Overproduction of offspring

The tendency of populations to produce more offspring than the environment can support. Because more individuals are produced than can survive to reproduce, individuals compete for limited resources, and this competition is a factor that promotes natural selection.
Carrying capacity

The maximum population size of a species that a particular environment can sustain over time, set by the limiting resources available. Food is one such resource; others include water, light, space, nesting or breeding sites, and shelter from predators and weather.
Abiotic factor

A non-living component of the environment, such as temperature, water availability, light intensity, salinity or soil pH, that can affect the survival of individuals and so act as a selection pressure on a population.
Density-independent factor

A factor whose effect on the proportion of individuals surviving does not depend on the density (number per unit area) of the population. Abiotic factors such as unusually high or low temperatures, drought, flooding or fire are typically density-independent: they can kill a similar proportion of a crowded population and a sparse one.
Selection pressure

Any factor in the environment, biotic or abiotic, that affects the chances of survival and reproduction of individuals with particular heritable traits, and so changes which alleles are passed on to the next generation.
Adaptation

A heritable characteristic that makes an individual better suited to its environment and so increases its chances of survival and reproduction. Individuals within a population differ in how well adapted they are, and these differences are the basis of natural selection.
Fitness

The survival value and reproductive potential of a genotype: how successful individuals with that genotype are at surviving and leaving offspring that themselves survive, relative to other genotypes in the population. Fitness is not physical strength or size; a genotype that produces more surviving offspring has higher fitness.
Intraspecific competition

Competition between individuals of the same species for the same limited resources or for mates. Because these individuals differ in their adaptations, some survive and reproduce more successfully than others, and this is the competition on which natural selection is based.
Heritable trait

A characteristic that is determined by an individual's genes, encoded in the base sequence of its DNA, and so can be passed on to offspring through the gametes. Only heritable traits can be changed in frequency by natural selection, so traits must be heritable for evolutionary change to occur.
Acquired characteristic

A characteristic that develops during an individual's life as a result of environmental factors, such as enlarged muscles from exercise, scars, or skills that have been learned. Acquired characteristics are not encoded in the base sequence of genes and so are not heritable.
Sexual selection

A selection pressure in animal species arising from differences in success at attracting or competing for a mate. Physical and behavioural traits that can be used as signs of overall fitness, such as plumage, size or courtship display, increase mating success, so the alleles for them become more frequent even when they carry a survival cost.
Plumage of birds of paradise

The elaborate, brightly coloured feathers and courtship displays of male birds of paradise, used as an example of sexual selection: females choose males with the most impressive plumage and display, so alleles for these traits have increased in frequency over generations even though the plumage is costly to grow and makes males more conspicuous.
Endler's guppy experiments

John Endler's experiments with guppies (Poecilia reticulata) from streams in Trinidad, in which he controlled the selection pressures experimentally. In artificial ponds and in stream transplants he varied the presence of predators (the dangerous pike cichlid Crenicichla and the weaker predator Rivulus) and the size of the gravel. Where predation was strong, males evolved fewer, smaller and duller spots; where predators were absent, sexual selection by females produced more numerous, larger and brighter spots within a few generations.
Gene pool
All the genes, and their different alleles, present in a population. Natural selection, mutation, migration and genetic drift change the frequencies of alleles in the gene pool over generations.
Allele frequency

The proportion of all the copies of a gene in a population's gene pool that are a particular allele, expressed as a decimal fraction between 0 and 1 or as a percentage. In a diploid population each individual contributes two copies of each autosomal gene, so allele frequency is not the same as the proportion of individuals showing a phenotype or carrying the allele.
Geographically isolated populations

Populations of the same species that are separated by a physical barrier so that little or no interbreeding occurs between them. Because their gene pools are separate, natural selection, genetic drift and founder effects can lead them to have different allele frequencies. Allele-frequency databases show this for human populations: for example, the frequencies of the ABO blood group alleles differ markedly between populations in different parts of the world.
Neo-Darwinism

The integration of genetics with Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection. It explains evolution as a change in allele frequencies in the gene pool, with mutation generating new alleles and natural selection acting on individuals according to differences in their heritable traits, so that alleles conferring higher fitness increase in frequency.
Directional selection

Selection that favours individuals at one extreme of the range of variation in a trait, so that the mean of the trait shifts in that direction over generations and the frequency of the alleles for that extreme increases. An example is the increase in antibiotic resistance in bacteria exposed to an antibiotic.
Disruptive selection

Selection that favours individuals at both extremes of the range of variation over those with intermediate values, so that the population becomes more variable or divides into two distinct forms, and allele frequencies change in favour of the alleles for the extremes.
Stabilizing selection

Selection that favours individuals with intermediate values of a trait over those at either extreme, so that the mean stays the same but variation is reduced. Allele frequencies still change, because the alleles for the extreme phenotypes are removed from the gene pool.
Hardy–Weinberg equation

For a gene with two alleles whose frequencies are p and q, p + q = 1, and if the population is in genetic equilibrium the genotype frequencies are given by p² + 2pq + q² = 1, where p² is the frequency of one homozygote, q² the frequency of the other homozygote and 2pq the frequency of heterozygotes. If one genotype frequency is known (usually the homozygous recessive, q²), the allele frequencies can be calculated from it.
Genetic equilibrium

The state of a population in which allele frequencies, and hence genotype frequencies, remain constant from generation to generation, so that the genotype frequencies fit the Hardy–Weinberg equation. A population in genetic equilibrium is not evolving.
Hardy–Weinberg conditions

The conditions that must be maintained for a population to remain in genetic equilibrium: the population is large, mating is random, there is no mutation, no migration into or out of the population, and no natural selection (all genotypes have equal survival and reproductive success). If observed genotype frequencies do not fit the Hardy–Weinberg equation, one or more of these conditions is not being met.
Artificial selection

Selection by deliberate human choice of traits: in crop plants and domesticated animals, humans choose the individuals with desirable traits to breed from, so the alleles for those traits increase in frequency over generations.
