Unintended consequences of human actions, such as the evolution of antibiotic resistance in bacteria, are due to natural rather than artificial selection.
Ecosystem stability

The property of a natural ecosystem by which it persists over long periods, keeping the same overall structure and type of community, even though the populations within it fluctuate and individual organisms are continually replaced. Stability is a property of the ecosystem as a whole, not of its individual members.
Evidence of long-term ecosystem continuity

Evidence that a type of ecosystem has occupied a region continuously through geological time, obtained from dated sediment cores, fossil pollen, fossil leaves and wood, and fossil animals. Such evidence indicates that some ecosystems have persisted for millions of years: tropical rainforest in parts of the Amazon basin and northern Australia is estimated to have persisted for tens of millions of years, and the Namib Desert of southern Africa is estimated to have been arid for around 55 million years.
Supply of energy as a requirement for stability

A continuous input of energy, almost always light from the Sun captured by producers in photosynthesis, that an ecosystem needs in order to remain stable. Energy flows through an ecosystem and is lost as heat at every trophic level, so it cannot be recycled and must be supplied continuously.
Recycling of nutrients as a requirement for stability

The return of chemical elements such as carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus from dead organic matter and waste to the abiotic environment, mainly through decomposition by saprotrophic bacteria and fungi, so that producers can take them up again. Because the supply of nutrients in an ecosystem is finite, this recycling is essential for the ecosystem to persist.
Genetic diversity as a requirement for stability

The variety of alleles present in the populations of an ecosystem. A genetically diverse population is likely to contain some individuals with alleles that allow survival when a new disease, pest or change in conditions arrives, so the population and the ecosystem that depends on it are less likely to collapse.
Tolerance levels of climatic variables

The range of values of a climatic variable such as temperature, rainfall or humidity within which the organisms of an ecosystem can survive and reproduce. An ecosystem can remain stable while climatic variables fluctuate, provided the fluctuations stay within the tolerance levels of the species present.
Tipping point

A threshold beyond which a small further change in a variable causes a large, rapid and often irreversible change in the state of an ecosystem. Deforestation of the Amazon rainforest is a possible example: beyond some minimum area of forest, moisture recycling may fail and forest may be replaced by drier savanna-like vegetation.
Moisture recycling by the Amazon rainforest

The generation of atmospheric water vapour by transpiration from a very large area of trees. The water vapour cools the air as it evaporates, drives air flows across the region, and condenses to give rainfall on which the forest itself depends. A large area of intact forest is needed to maintain these processes, and the minimum area that is sufficient is uncertain.
Percentage change

The change in a quantity expressed as a percentage of its original value: percentage change = (new value − original value) ÷ original value × 100. A decrease gives a negative value. The extent of deforestation is assessed as the percentage change from the original area of forest.
Mesocosm

A small, enclosed experimental ecosystem set up as a model of a natural ecosystem, containing producers, consumers and decomposers with abiotic components such as water, sediment or soil, so that the effect of a variable on stability can be investigated. Aquatic or microbial mesocosms are more likely to be successful than terrestrial ones.
Sealed mesocosm as a system closed to matter but open to energy

A mesocosm in a sealed glass vessel is preferable to one in an open tank because entry and exit of matter is prevented, so nutrients must be recycled within it, while energy transfer remains possible: light enters through the glass and heat leaves. Care and maintenance of mesocosms should follow IB experimental guidelines, so that organisms do not suffer.
Keystone species

A species that has a disproportionately large effect on the structure of its community relative to its abundance or biomass. Removal of a keystone species can change the whole community and risks ecosystem collapse. Examples include sea otters in kelp forests, the starfish Pisaster on rocky shores, wolves in Yellowstone and beavers.
Community structure

The set of species present in a community and their relative abundances and trophic relationships. A keystone species maintains community structure, for example by preventing one competitor or herbivore from dominating; its removal can lead to a cascade of changes through the food web.
Renewable natural resource

A resource harvested from a natural ecosystem that is replaced by natural processes such as growth and reproduction, for example timber or nuts from wild trees and fish from the sea. A renewable resource can still be depleted if it is harvested faster than it is replaced.
Sustainable harvesting

Harvesting a renewable resource at a rate lower than the rate at which it is replaced by growth and reproduction, so that the stock does not decline and the harvest can continue indefinitely. Harvesting above the replacement rate depletes the stock and can lead to collapse.
Assessing sustainability of harvesting

Judging whether harvesting is sustainable by comparing harvest rate with replacement rate, using indicators such as the size of the stock, trends in the catch or yield, the effort needed to obtain it, and the age structure of the population. For a marine fish such as Atlantic cod, a rising fishing effort for the same catch and a fall in the mean age of fish caught indicate over-harvesting. For a terrestrial plant such as the Brazil nut tree, the presence of seedlings and young trees indicates that harvesting of nuts is leaving enough seeds for replacement.
Sustainability of agriculture

The extent to which a system of farming can continue indefinitely without degrading the resources it depends on. Factors to consider include soil erosion, leaching of nutrients, the supply of fertilizers and other inputs, pollution due to agrochemicals, and the carbon footprint of the farming.
Leaching

The washing of soluble substances, such as nitrate and phosphate from fertilizers, down through the soil by rainwater or irrigation into groundwater, streams, lakes and the sea. Leaching both depletes soil nutrients and pollutes water.
Carbon footprint of agriculture

The total greenhouse gas emissions attributable to a farming system, including carbon dioxide from fuel used by machinery and from the manufacture of fertilizers and other inputs, methane from livestock, nitrous oxide released from fertilized soils, and carbon dioxide from clearing land.
Eutrophication

The enrichment of a body of water with nutrients, especially nitrate and phosphate leached from fertilized farmland. The nutrients cause rapid growth of algae (an algal bloom); the algae then die and are decomposed by aerobic saprotrophic bacteria, whose respiration lowers the concentration of dissolved oxygen so that fish and other aerobic organisms die. Eutrophication affects lakes, rivers and coastal marine waters.
Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD)

The quantity of dissolved oxygen consumed by aerobic microorganisms as they decompose the organic matter in a sample of water, usually measured over five days. A high BOD indicates a large amount of decomposable organic matter and therefore a high rate of oxygen removal from the water; eutrophication increases BOD.
Biomagnification

The increase in the concentration of a persistent toxin in the tissues of organisms at each successive trophic level of a food chain. A consumer takes in the toxin from every prey organism it eats and, because the toxin is not broken down or excreted, it accumulates, so top consumers carry the highest concentrations.
DDT as an example of biomagnification

An insecticide that is fat-soluble and persistent in the environment. DDT sprayed on crops and wetlands entered food chains and became concentrated in birds of prey and fish-eating birds, where it caused thinning of eggshells and breeding failure. Its use was banned in many countries from the 1970s.
Mercury as an example of biomagnification

A toxic metal released by industry, mining and the burning of coal. In water and sediments bacteria convert mercury to methylmercury, which is retained in tissues and biomagnified along aquatic food chains, reaching high concentrations in large predatory fish such as tuna and swordfish. People eating contaminated fish and shellfish at Minamata in Japan suffered severe nervous system damage.
Microplastic and macroplastic

Macroplastics are visible items of plastic debris such as bags, bottles and fishing nets; microplastics are fragments smaller than about 5 mm, produced by the breakdown of macroplastics or manufactured as fibres and beads. Macroplastics harm marine animals by entanglement and by blocking the gut when swallowed; microplastics are ingested by filter feeders and other animals, can carry adsorbed pollutants, and pass along food chains.
Persistence of plastics

Plastics remain in the environment for very long periods because they are not biodegradable: decomposers lack enzymes able to break down these synthetic polymers. Plastics fragment into ever smaller pieces but the material is not removed. Clear communication of research on the effects of plastics on marine life changed public perception globally and drove measures to reduce plastic pollution.
Rewilding

Restoration of natural processes in a degraded ecosystem so that it can maintain itself with little further intervention. Methods include reintroduction of apex predators and other keystone species, re-establishment of connectivity between habitats over large areas, and minimization of human impact, including by ecological management such as removing livestock or controlling introduced species.
Habitat connectivity

The degree to which areas of habitat are linked so that organisms can move between them. Re-establishing connectivity by corridors and by removing barriers allows animals to migrate, disperse and breed across a large area, maintaining population sizes and genetic diversity.
Hinewai Reserve

A reserve of more than 1000 hectares on Banks Peninsula, New Zealand, where former farmland has been allowed to return to native forest since 1987 by minimal interference. Grazing livestock were removed and introduced browsing mammals are controlled, but the invasive shrub gorse was left in place as a nurse canopy: native tree seedlings grow up through it and shade it out, and native forest has regenerated naturally.
Ecological succession

The process by which the community in an area changes over time, with one community being replaced by another, until a relatively stable climax community is reached. Succession can be triggered by changes in the abiotic environment, such as a volcanic eruption or glacial retreat, and by biotic factors, such as organisms altering the soil or shading the ground.
Primary and secondary succession

Primary succession begins in an area where no soil and no previous community exist, such as bare rock or sand exposed by a retreating glacier or created by a volcano. Secondary succession begins where a previous community has been removed but soil remains, for example after a fire or the abandonment of farmland.
Pioneer community

The first community to colonise bare ground in primary succession, typically lichens, mosses and small hardy plants that can tolerate the lack of soil, water and nutrients. Pioneers begin to form soil by trapping particles and adding organic matter, changing the environment so that other species can establish.
Changes during primary succession

As primary succession proceeds, the size of plants increases, the amount of primary production increases, species diversity increases, food webs become more complex and the amount of nutrient cycling increases, as soil depth and organic content build up.
Cyclical succession

A pattern in which a community passes repeatedly through a cycle of phases rather than settling into a single unchanging climax community. In heather moorland, heather plants pass through pioneer, building, mature and degenerate phases; when old plants die back, the gap is colonised by lichens, mosses and other plants before heather seedlings re-establish and the cycle begins again.
Climax community

The relatively stable community that ecological succession tends to lead to under a given set of environmental conditions, such as temperate deciduous woodland or tropical rainforest. Its composition depends on the climate and soil of the area.
Arrested succession

Prevention of the development of the climax community by a human influence, so that the community is held at an earlier stage of succession. Grazing by farm livestock, which removes tree and shrub seedlings and keeps land as grassland, and drainage of wetlands for agriculture are examples; if the influence is removed, succession can resume.
Anthropogenic climate change

Change in the Earth's climate caused by human activity, in particular the warming that results from anthropogenic increases in the atmospheric concentrations of greenhouse gases. The IB limits the causes studied to carbon dioxide and methane, whose concentrations have risen since pre-industrial times because of human activities.
Anthropogenic sources of carbon dioxide and methane

Carbon dioxide concentration has risen (from about 280 ppm before industrialization to over 420 ppm) mainly through combustion of fossil fuels, deforestation and other land-use change, and cement production. Methane concentration has more than doubled mainly through enteric fermentation in ruminant livestock, rice paddies, landfill sites and leakage during the extraction and transport of fossil fuels. Both gases absorb long-wave radiation re-emitted by the Earth's surface, so their increase enhances the greenhouse effect.
Positive and negative correlation

A correlation is a relationship between two variables. In a positive correlation, higher values of one variable are associated with higher values of the other; in a negative correlation, higher values of one variable are associated with lower values of the other. Antarctic ice cores show a positive correlation between global temperature and atmospheric carbon dioxide concentration over hundreds of thousands of years.
Correlation and causation

A correlation between two variables does not by itself show that one causes the other: both could be affected by a third factor, or the causal direction could be the reverse. The ice-core correlation between carbon dioxide and temperature does not prove that carbon dioxide raises global temperature; the causal link is established by other evidence, including laboratory measurements of the absorption of infrared radiation by carbon dioxide and the physics of the greenhouse effect.
Positive feedback cycle

A cycle in which the consequence of a change increases the original change, moving the system further from its starting state. In global warming, warming triggers processes that release more greenhouse gases or increase the absorption of solar radiation, which causes further warming. Examples are release of carbon dioxide from the deep ocean, loss of reflective snow and ice, accelerated decomposition of peat and previously undecomposed organic matter in permafrost, release of methane from melting permafrost, and increases in droughts and forest fires.
Albedo

The fraction of incoming solar radiation that a surface reflects. Snow and ice have a high albedo and reflect most of the solar radiation reaching them, whereas open water and bare ground have a low albedo and absorb most of it. Loss of snow and ice therefore increases the absorption of solar radiation, warming the surface and melting more snow and ice: a positive feedback.
Permafrost

Ground that has remained frozen for at least two consecutive years, found across large areas of the Arctic and sub-Arctic. It contains vast quantities of organic matter that has accumulated without decomposing because it is frozen. When permafrost thaws, decomposers become active: aerobic decomposition releases carbon dioxide and anaerobic decomposition by methanogenic archaea in waterlogged thawed ground releases methane, both of which cause further warming.
Drought, forest fire and peat decomposition as positive feedbacks

Warming increases evaporation and the frequency of droughts, and drier vegetation and soil make forest fires more frequent and intense; fires release carbon dioxide from biomass and soil organic matter, causing further warming and more drought. Warming and drying of peat, and thawing of permafrost, also speed up decomposition of organic matter that had accumulated undecomposed, releasing carbon dioxide (and methane where the ground is waterlogged), which causes further warming.
Tipping point

A threshold beyond which a small further change causes an ecosystem to shift abruptly to a different state, which may be difficult or impossible to reverse. The change of boreal forests from net carbon accumulation to net carbon loss is an example: once drought, browning and fire outweigh primary production, the forest switches from a carbon sink to a carbon source.
Boreal forest (taiga)

The coniferous forest biome of high northern latitudes, with long cold winters and short growing seasons. Boreal forests have historically accumulated carbon, storing much of it in thick soil organic layers. Warmer temperatures and decreased winter snowfall are increasing the incidence of drought, reducing primary production and causing forest browning and more frequent and more intense forest fires.
Forest browning

A decline in the greenness and productivity of forest vegetation, detected from satellite measurements and ground surveys, caused by drought stress, reduced growth, needle loss and tree death. Browning in the taiga indicates a reduction in primary production and therefore in the uptake of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere.
Legacy carbon

Carbon in the soil organic layer of a boreal forest that escaped combustion in previous fires and has accumulated over many fire cycles, so it is older than the trees now growing. In the past, most fires burnt only the carbon that had been fixed since the last fire. When fires become more frequent and intense, they burn deeper and combust this legacy carbon, releasing carbon that had been stored for centuries and contributing to the switch from net accumulation to net loss.
Landfast ice

Sea ice that is attached to the coast, to the sea floor or to grounded icebergs, so that it does not drift with winds and currents. Emperor penguins (Aptenodytes forsteri) breed on landfast ice around Antarctica through the winter; the ice must persist until the chicks fledge in December and January. Warming is causing landfast ice to break out earlier, before the chicks have grown waterproof adult plumage, and colonies have suffered breeding failure as a result.
Sea ice

Frozen sea water floating on the ocean surface. Arctic sea ice provides walruses (Odobenus rosmarus) with a resting platform over the shallow continental shelf, close to the sea-floor molluscs on which they feed. As summer sea ice retreats into deep water beyond the shelf, walruses must haul out on land in large, crowded groups and make longer journeys to their feeding grounds, so the loss of sea ice is a loss of habitat.
Nutrient upwelling

The rise of cold, nutrient-rich water from the deep ocean to the sunlit surface, where the nutrients (such as nitrate and phosphate) allow high rates of phytoplankton production. Nutrients accumulate at depth because dead organic matter sinks and is decomposed there. Warmer, less dense surface water forms a stable layer over the colder water below, so changes in ocean currents and surface warming can reduce or prevent upwelling, lowering ocean primary production and the energy flow through marine food chains.
Range shift

A change in the geographical area occupied by a species. As the climate warms, temperate species tend to shift poleward and upslope so that they remain within the range of temperatures they can tolerate. Evidence includes upslope shifts of montane bird species in New Guinea and the northward spread, with contraction at the southern edge of the range, of tree species in North America. For plants the shift occurs across generations, through seed dispersal and differential survival, not by movement of individuals.
Ocean acidification

The decrease in the pH of the oceans caused by the dissolving of additional atmospheric carbon dioxide. Dissolved carbon dioxide forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions; these react with carbonate ions, lowering the carbonate ion concentration. Seawater remains slightly alkaline (mean surface pH has fallen from about 8.2 to about 8.1) but the lower carbonate concentration suppresses calcification, so corals build their calcium carbonate skeletons more slowly.
Coral bleaching

The loss of colour by reef-building corals when, stressed by unusually high water temperature, they expel the mutualistic photosynthetic algae (zooxanthellae) living in their tissues. The coral is left alive but pale and deprived of most of its food supply; if the stress is prolonged the coral starves and dies, whereas if the water cools soon enough it can regain its algae and recover.
Reef ecosystem collapse

The breakdown of a coral reef ecosystem that follows the death of its corals. Corals build the three-dimensional structure that provides habitat, shelter and food for a very large number of fish and invertebrate species; when the corals die the structure erodes and most of these species are lost, so the whole ecosystem collapses rather than a single species.
Carbon sequestration

The removal of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and its long-term storage in a carbon sink such as biomass, soil or peat. Afforestation, forest regeneration and restoration of peat-forming wetlands are approaches that use natural processes to sequester carbon, offsetting anthropogenic emissions.
Afforestation

The planting of trees on land that has not recently been forested, to create a new carbon sink. There is active scientific debate over whether plantations of fast-growing non-native tree species or rewilding with native species offer the best approach to carbon sequestration: plantations sequester carbon rapidly at first, but native woodland may store more carbon in the long term, including in soil, and supports greater biodiversity.
Forest regeneration

The regrowth of forest on land that was previously forested and has been cleared or degraded, either by natural regeneration from seeds and regrowth or with assistance. As the regenerating forest grows, carbon is sequestered in biomass and soil.
Peat

Partially decomposed plant material that accumulates in waterlogged soils, where the lack of oxygen inhibits the saprotrophs that would otherwise decompose it fully. Peat formation naturally occurs in temperate and boreal zones and also very rapidly in some tropical ecosystems. Peatlands store large amounts of carbon; drained peat decomposes and releases carbon dioxide, so restoring peat-forming wetlands by re-wetting them is an approach to carbon sequestration.
Phenology

Research into the timing of biological events, such as flowering, budburst and bud set in deciduous trees, and bird migration and nesting, and into the variables that influence that timing. Photoperiod and temperature patterns are examples of variables that act as cues, and long-term phenological records show how the timing of events is changing as the climate warms.
Photoperiod

The length of the daily period of light, which at a given latitude follows the same annual pattern every year because it depends on the Earth's orbit and not on the weather. Many organisms use photoperiod as a cue for the timing of biological events, for example bud set in deciduous trees in autumn and the migration of many bird species, so events cued by photoperiod do not advance when the climate warms.
Disruption of phenological synchrony

The loss of the matching in time between interdependent biological events in different populations when climate change shifts one event but not the other. Within an ecosystem, temperature may be the cue in one population while photoperiod is the cue in another. In the Arctic, spring growth of the mouse-ear chickweed (Cerastium arcticum) is cued by temperature and so is occurring earlier, whereas migration of reindeer (Rangifer tarandus) to the calving grounds is cued by photoperiod and has not advanced, so calves are born after the peak in plant growth and have less nutritious food.
Great tit and caterpillar mismatch

An example of disrupted synchrony in north European forests: the peak biomass of the caterpillars that great tits (Parus major) feed to their nestlings has advanced with warmer springs, while the birds' egg-laying date has advanced less, so chicks hatch after the food peak and fewer survive. Life cycles per year (voltinism)

The number of generations an insect completes in a year. Insects are ectotherms whose development rate rises with temperature, so warmer springs and summers allow more generations to be completed. The spruce bark beetle (Ips typographus or Dendroctonus micans) has one generation per year in cool conditions but two or more in warm ones, so climate change increases beetle populations and the damage to spruce forests.
Fitness

The relative contribution of an individual of a particular genotype or phenotype to the next generation, through survival and reproduction. Climate change alters which phenotypes have the highest fitness: in tawny owls (Strix aluco) the brown colour morph survives snowy winters less well than the grey morph, so as snow cover has decreased the fitness of the brown morph has risen relative to the grey morph.
